I stood on the balcony, the chill night air doing nothing to cool the sudden, searing heat radiating from my face. "I found Jupiter again, Dad!" Toby yelled from the living room, proudly wiping his mouth with his sleeve. He had been commandeering my observatory-grade telescope every single night, utterly fixated on the sky. I gripped the aluminum casing, my nails digging into the metal. I had explicitly shown him how to never, ever touch the optics. A thick vein pulsed erratically on the side of my forehead. I closed my eyes, but all I could see was the ruined anti-reflective coating, the hundreds of dollars in damage from his careless, sticky hands. I slowly dismantled the heavy mount, my movements stiff, robotic, and completely silent.

Sarah’s breath hitched in her throat. She dropped her palette on the hardwood floor, not caring as cerulean blue splattered against the baseboards. Her easel, which had held a delicate seascape, now featured a glaring yellow sun painted thickly over the moody clouds. Seven-year-old Mia, who had developed a relentless fascination with "finishing" Sarah's work, stood beside it. She held Sarah's finest sable brush, its delicate bristles utterly crushed. "I fixed the gloomy weather!" Mia chirped. Sarah closed her eyes. Her jaw muscles bulged as she clenched her teeth. She could feel her heartbeat pounding in her fingertips. Without looking at her daughter, Sarah reached out and snapped the wooden brush in two. The sharp crack made Mia jump. Dropping the splintered halves onto the floor, Sarah turned and marched out of the studio, her footsteps heavy, sharp, and echoing down the corridor.

I found my hand-carved mahogany knights buried in the sandbox. The horse heads—which had cost me three months of meticulous whittling—were deeply scratched, their polished lacquer ruined by jagged grit. Ever since I taught Jake the pieces' names, he refused to play with anything else. "They're fighting the army men!" Jake yelled, running over with a handful of my pawns. He threw them aggressively onto the driveway. The violent clack of chipping wood hit my ears like a physical blow. Heat rushed instantly to my face. My hands curled into tight, shaking fists at my sides. I wanted to seize his entire bucket of toys and empty it into the trash compactor. I stared at the deep gouge on the white queen's crown, my chest rising and falling in rapid, jagged heaves. I picked up the surviving pieces in dead silence, my jaw locked.

Helen stood at the threshold of the living room, her posture entirely rigid. The space was transformed into a chaotic spiderweb of neon and pastel lines. Her daughter, Zoe, had abandoned her toys, obsessively constructing these massive string traps every afternoon. Helen’s eyes tracked the lines back to the source: her artisanal, hand-dyed merino wool skeins, unwound and tied in tight, impossible knots around door knobs and lamp switches. The expensive Peruvian yarn was fraying against the rough brick fireplace. "I'm a spy, Mom!" Zoe announced. Helen didn’t speak. A fierce flush crept up her neck, staining her cheeks crimson. She pulled heavy fabric shears from her apron pocket. Her breathing was loud and labored through her nose. With swift, aggressive snips, Helen marched through the room, brutally severing the taut lines, ignoring Zoe’s startled protests as the intricate web collapsed around them.

The harsh scraping noise from the garage sent a cold shiver down my spine. I rounded the corner to see twelve-year-old Sam diligently rubbing the hood of my '67 Mustang. He had become completely fixated on the vehicle, spending hours detailing it. My eyes locked onto the tool in his hand: a coarse wire grill brush. A constellation of deep, silver scratches swirled across the previously flawless cherry-red clear coat. "Getting the bug marks off, Dad!" he called out. My blood instantly felt like battery acid. I stomped forward, snatching the brush from his grip so forcefully the wooden handle bruised my palm. I stared at the ruined hood, my breathing coming in short, sharp bursts. My vision tunneled. I pointed a trembling finger toward the open driveway. "Out," I rasped, kicking the metal trash can across the concrete.

The distinct clinking of metal drew Julian to the playroom. He froze in the doorway. His son, Max, had completely abandoned his video games for the thrill of physical coins, and was gleefully dropping ancient Roman denarii into a plastic toy register. "Arr, pirate treasure!" Max cheered. Julian’s eyes darted to the empty velvet-lined display case on the rug. The airtight acrylic capsules had been pried open and discarded. Julian’s hands clenched into fists, the fingernails biting painfully into his flesh. He marched over and upended the toy register. A shower of irreplaceable silver scattered across the floor. Max began to cry, but Julian didn’t look at him. His face was flushed, his lips pressed into a thin, bloodless line. He dropped to his knees, frantically sweeping the two-thousand-year-old artifacts into a pile, squeezing a scratched silver piece until his arm violently shook.

I stood over the dining room table, my vision blurring at the edges. For two months, I had been assembling the five-thousand-piece replica of the Sistine Chapel. Recently, eight-year-old Emma decided she loved puzzles too, refusing to leave my workstation alone. Now, chunks of the sky were entirely missing, while others were glued together haphazardly into a crude, three-dimensional cube. "Look, Mom! I made a puzzle block!" she said, proudly holding up a lumpy box of superglued cardboard pieces. The acrid smell of the adhesive stung my nose. My stomach churned, and a hot prickle of sweat broke out across my forehead. I grabbed the edge of the mahogany table, my knuckles stark white, gripping the wood so hard my joints popped. I wanted to swipe my arm across the surface and send the remaining pieces flying. Instead, I spun around and stormed out.

Elias stared at the email from HarperCollins. He actually clicked 'print', needing a physical manifestation of the polite, two-line dismissal. When the printer hummed and spat out the page, he snatched it, ripping it down the middle, then again, and again, until it was nothing but jagged confetti snowing down on his shoes. He swiped his arm across his desk. A ceramic mug, a stack of research notes, and a framed photograph crashed onto the hardwood. His breath came in ragged, sharp pulls. His jaw ached from how hard he was grinding his teeth. "Not the right fit," he hissed to the empty room, his fingernails digging deep into his palms. He kicked the shattered remains of his mug, sending a shard flying into the drywall.

I stared at the glowing screen, the words 'We pass on this project' burning into my retinas. Tor Books. Five years of world-building dismissed in three generic sentences. My fingers hovered over the keyboard, trembling so hard I kept hitting the wrong keys. Dear Editor, I typed, striking the keys with enough force to rattle the monitor. Thank you for your profound lack of vision. I hit backspace, my breathing loud in the silent apartment. I hope your imprint crumbles into dust. Backspace. I slammed the laptop shut so violently the hinge cracked. Heat radiated from my cheeks, and a loud ringing filled my ears. They hadn't even read past the first chapter. I paced the length of my tiny kitchen, kicking a stray dining chair until it tipped over backward.

Sarah didn't cry when the letter arrived from Macmillan. Instead, she stood perfectly still in the driveway, the thick cream paper crinkling in her tightening grip. Her face grew hot, a flush creeping up her neck. She marched straight past the front door, ignoring the barking dog, and headed for the backyard fire pit. She didn't bother with kindling. She dropped the neatly folded letter into the metal bowl, pulled a lighter from her pocket, and touched the flame to the corner. She watched the polite, evasive words curl, blacken, and turn to ash. Her jaw was locked so tight her temples throbbed. She grabbed the garden hose and blasted the ashes, squeezing the nozzle until the water shot out in a violently pressurized stream, obliterating every trace of their message.

"Did you get the email?" Mark asked from the kitchen. I didn't answer right away. I was too busy glaring at the Simon & Schuster logo at the top of the rejection. A high-pitched ringing started in my ears. "Well?" he pushed. I spun around, my chair scraping harshly against the floorboards. "Yes, Mark, I got it!" I snapped, my voice sharp enough to make him flinch. "And guess what? They loved it so much they decided they never want to speak to me again." I grabbed the nearest object—a stapler—and hurled it into the wastebasket. It missed and struck the wall, leaving a deep dent in the plaster. "Are you happy now? Everyone was right. It’s a waste of time!" I stormed past him, shoving my shoulder into the doorframe as I retreated into the bedroom.

The cursor blinked relentlessly at the end of the email. Gollancz. It was supposed to be the pinnacle. David stared unblinking, a bitter taste flooding his mouth. He minimized the window and found the folder labeled 'Masterpiece'. His chest tightened, a suffocating pressure building behind his ribs. He right-clicked. Delete. A prompt asked if he was sure. His mouse hand shook violently. He slammed the left button down. Yes. Then he opened the recycling bin. Empty. He wasn't done. He yanked the power cord from the wall outlet, plunging his desktop into sudden darkness. The silence of the room was deafening, save for his rapid, shallow breaths. He gripped the edge of his desk and shoved. The heavy oak didn't move, so he kicked the leg of it, hard enough to bruise his toes. "Idiots," he spat.

The barista called my name, but the sound was muffled behind the rushing blood in my ears. I sat at the corner table of the crowded café, staring down at my phone. The subject line read: Orbit Books - Submission Update. The body was a polite, copy-pasted rejection. I looked at the three-hundred-page printed manuscript sitting in front of me, neatly bound in a black folder. My face burned. I grabbed the first fifty pages, my hands gripping the paper so hard my knuckles were stark white. I ripped them down the middle. The sound turned heads, but I didn't care. I grabbed the next chunk, tearing through cardstock and paper alike, throwing the mangled halves onto the floor. "Miss?" the barista asked, stepping closer. "Don't," I hissed through clenched teeth, my chest heaving as I reached for the rest.

Arthur sat at the polished mahogany table, a crystal glass of bourbon in his hand. The letter from Vintage Classics lay flat on the placemat. "Not quite what we are looking for." The words mocked him, dancing on the expensive letterhead. He took a slow, deep breath through his nose, holding it in until his lungs burned. His grip on the glass tightened. He stared at the signature of the editor—a twenty-something intern, no doubt, who had skimmed his life's work on a morning commute. The glass groaned under the pressure of his tightening fingers. He imagined the editor's smug face, sipping a latte, dismissing five years of historical research. His jaw muscles feathered. With a sudden, sharp crack, the crystal shattered in his palm, sending golden liquid and shards cascading over the polite, dismissive letter.

The audacity of their response was breathtaking. Farrar, Straus and Giroux had kept my manuscript tied up for fourteen months, only to send a two-sentence form rejection. I stood up so fast my office chair rolled backward and slammed into the bookshelf. I paced the floor, my hands balled into tight fists, nails biting into my palms. I marched back to the keyboard, my breathing loud and ragged. Dear Editorial Team, I typed, pressing the keys hard enough to risk breaking the switches. I truly appreciate the fourteen months it took you to read zero pages of my work. Your dedication to inefficiency is genuinely staggering. I hovered over the send button. My face felt like it was radiating heat. I clicked send, stood up, and immediately swept my arm across the desk, sending a pile of reference books crashing down.

Looking at the email on her phone, Chloe stopped walking in the middle of the park. It was from Baen Books. A flat negative. A jogger bumped her shoulder, muttering an apology. Chloe didn't apologize back. She turned and glared at him with such ferocity he stumbled slightly before hurrying away. She looked back at the screen. Her nostrils flared. She marched toward the nearest trash can, dropping her phone right into the muck of half-eaten hotdogs and coffee cups. Instantly regretting it, she plunged her hand in and snatched the device back, wiping it aggressively on her jeans. She stomped toward her apartment, shoulders hitched high, muttering under her breath. Every person who looked her way received a lethal scowl. When a pigeon landed in her path, she kicked a spray of gravel at it, scattering the bird into the sky.

It wasn't the rejection from Scholastic that set me off; it was the phrase "best of luck finding a home for your little story." Little story. My teeth ground together so forcefully I heard a distinct pop in my jaw. I grabbed the printed copy of my middle-grade fantasy from the shelf. It weighed exactly three pounds. I marched to the home office and turned on the heavy-duty paper shredder. I didn't feed it gently. I shoved entire chapters into the slot, forcing the motor to whine and groan as it choked on the thick paper. "Little story," I mimicked, my voice dripping with venom. The machine jammed on chapter twelve. I grabbed the plastic housing and shook the entire unit, finally kicking the side of the metal bin. The plastic cracked, but I just grabbed another handful of pages.

The notification from HarperCollins chimed halfway through Maya's dinner party. She glanced at her watch, saw the preview text, and froze. Her friends were laughing, passing a bowl of salad, completely unaware. Maya's face flushed a deep crimson. She set her wine glass down with a heavy clunk that silenced the table. "Everything okay?" Greg asked. Maya didn't look at him. She stared at the wall, her chest rising and falling in sharp, erratic movements. "Fine," she said, her voice clipped and dangerously low. "Just perfectly fine." She picked up her steak knife, her grip white-knuckled, and began sawing into her meat with unnecessary force. The blade screeched against the ceramic plate, a horrific, grating sound. Nobody spoke. She kept sawing, her eyes fixed and narrowed, cutting the piece of chicken into tiny, shredded, unrecognizable pieces.

I pulled over on the shoulder of the highway, threw the car in park, and read the email from Subterranean Press again. My vision blurred, not with tears, but with a searing heat. I gripped the steering wheel, squeezing the leather until my forearms cramped. I let out a sound that was half-scream, half-growl, slamming my palms against the wheel again and again. The horn blared into the empty desert landscape. I punched the dashboard, the plastic cracking under my knuckles, but I barely felt the sting. "Four revisions!" I yelled at the windshield, my voice hoarse. "You asked for four revisions!" I threw the phone onto the passenger seat, slammed the car into drive, and stomped on the gas pedal. The tires shrieked, spinning out in a cloud of gravel and dust before I merged recklessly back onto the asphalt.

I stared at the photo on my monitor, my jaw tight enough to crack a tooth. DragonSlayer99 had finally posted a selfie in our discord channel. The background wasn't some distant basement in Ohio like he had claimed for three years; it was the unmistakable peeling yellow wallpaper of the apartment complex directly across from mine. Worse, it was the exact guy who plays bass guitar at two in the morning. My fingernails dug half-moons into my palms. I had spent countless late nights messaging him, pouring out my soul about my miserable living situation, and he had sat there, typing out sympathetic replies while literally being the source of my exhaustion. I shoved my keyboard away, the plastic slamming loudly against the wall. Three years of secrets were completely mocked by the heavy thumping of a bass guitar starting up right on cue across the alleyway.

Clara’s screen glowed with the location ping. Two miles away. The phone trembled in her grip. CoffeeBean wasn't in Seattle. He was right here in Austin. A quick cross-reference of the background in his recent photo confirmed it: the exact chalkboard menu of the cafe on 4th Street. The cafe Clara visited every single morning. The barista there—a guy with a smug smirk who always spelled her name with a 'K' and never looked her in the eye—wore the exact same silver thumb ring visible in the picture. Her blood rushed in her ears, drowning out the ambient noise of her bedroom. She had confessed her deepest insecurities to him online, and he had served her burnt espresso with a scoff just hours ago. She threw her phone onto the mattress, marching to her closet to grab her coat, breathing heavily.

"Sorry man, time zones are brutal," he had typed last night. "Going to sleep, it's 2 AM here in London." I scoffed, glaring at the geolocated tag he accidentally left on his latest tweet. It didn't say London. It said Westside Mall, Chicago. Ten minutes from my front door. My breathing grew shallow and hot as I pieced it all together. The weird excuses about not wanting to turn on his webcam, the delayed responses when I suggested we do a real-life meetup halfway across the globe. He wasn’t across the Atlantic. He was taking the same subway lines I did. I aggressively clicked on his profile, my mouse rattling against the desk pad. He let me buy him digital gifts and pay for international shipping, knowing full well he could have just driven over. My teeth ground together as I slammed the delete key.

The cursor blinked on Marcus’s screen. The attachment had finally downloaded. He clicked it open, expecting a picture of his gaming buddy’s new apartment. Instead, his eyes locked onto the street sign in the corner. Elm Street. Then, the familiar red front door. It wasn't just in his city; it was his ex-girlfriend’s house. The guy grinning in the photo, holding a cardboard box, was the same person Marcus had spent the last eight months helping through a rough patch online. The heat creeping up his neck felt like a physical weight. Marcus gripped the edge of his desk, the wood creaking under the pressure of his thumbs. Every late-night conversation, every piece of advice he had given 'ShadowHawk' about wooing his new girl, echoed mockingly in his head. He abruptly yanked the power cord from the wall, plunging his room into total darkness.

I ripped the headphones off my head and threw them onto the floor. They bounced, emitting a sharp squeal of feedback. For two years, 'Atlas' told me he was a college student in New York, giving me advice on handling the jerks in my high school. Today, he forgot to blur his stream background. Pinned to the wall was a bright orange lanyard from my exact school in Denver. My eyes narrowed, mentally matching his voice to the faces in my homeroom. It was Jeremy. The same Jeremy who snickered when I tripped in the cafeteria yesterday. A hot, tight sensation seized my throat. I kicked my desk chair back so hard it violently crashed against the closet door. I had laid bare all my daily humiliations to the person secretly laughing at them in person.

Sarah’s heel tapped a frantic, relentless rhythm against the linoleum. The app showed her online chess partner’s distance as less than fifty feet away. She stepped out into her apartment hallway, glaring at the door of 4B. The tenant there was notorious for leaving leaking garbage bags out. As she watched, the door opened and the messy neighbor stepped out, phone in hand. "Just sent my next move," the neighbor muttered into a voice note. Sarah’s phone buzzed instantly with a chess notification. Her lips pressed into a thin, bloodless line. She had spent a year swapping deeply personal poetry with this woman, believing she lived in Montreal. Sarah marched forward, her boots stomping heavily on the floorboards. She snatched the rotting garbage bag from the floor, marching straight toward the woman, fully intending to shove it right back through her open doorway.

My thumb hovered over the screen, trembling so fiercely I could barely read the text. It was a local dating app profile. The bio was a word-for-word copy of a joke my long-distance gaming partner, Elias, had claimed to invent. I swiped through the pictures. It was him. And the location said "One mile away." My breathing hitched, coming out in sharp, ragged bursts. He had told me he was from Toronto. Worse, I realized why his face looked familiar locally. We had matched on this exact app a month ago under his real name, and he had completely stood me up for coffee. I had literally cried on his virtual shoulder about being ghosted, and he had comforted me through the headset. My grip on the phone tightened until the glass screen protector groaned. I slammed the device face-down on the counter.

David stared at the shipping manifesto. His knuckles turned white as he gripped the steering wheel of his delivery van. His online coding partner, ‘ZeroCool,’ had claimed to be based in Tokyo, leaving David to handle all the grueling physical distribution of their tech startup in Miami alone. But the return address on the prototype package he just intercepted wasn’t Japan. It was a luxury condo complex three blocks from David’s current route. A low growl vibrated in David’s throat. For three years, he had ruined his back hauling heavy server racks, sweating in the Florida heat, while his partner was apparently sitting in air-conditioned comfort just down the street, claiming international immunity. David shoved the van into gear, the tires screeching against the asphalt as he violently yanked the steering wheel toward the condo complex. The prototype box bounced off the dashboard.

I stared at the livestream, my fingernails digging deeply into the armrests of my chair. My favorite online debate buddy, the one who spent hours discussing ethical philosophy with me, adjusted his webcam. The camera panned too far to the left, revealing the distinct skyline view from our local City Hall. Then, he took off his headset, turning to answer someone off-screen. It was Councilman Roberts. The exact politician who just voted to bulldoze my neighborhood's community garden. A rushing sound filled my ears, hot and suffocating. The sheer hypocrisy tasted like ash in my mouth. I had actively protested his policies on the street, then come home to politely chat about "civic duty" with the man himself on Discord. I grabbed my mug of cold coffee and violently hurled it into the trash can, watching the ceramic shatter into dozens of jagged pieces.

The rain plastered Maya’s hair to her forehead, but she didn’t move. She stood frozen on the sidewalk outside the city’s most expensive steakhouse. Stepping out of the valet line under a large umbrella was Leo. He was the online friend she had sent three hundred dollars to last week because he claimed he was starving in a rural town in Nebraska. She recognized his distinct laugh and the custom leather jacket he had showed off on stream. Maya’s teeth ground together, producing a sharp, grating noise in her head. She had skipped lunches for a month to scrape together that money. Her hands balled into tight fists inside her coat pockets, her fingernails biting into her skin. She watched him carelessly hand a twenty-dollar tip to the valet driver. A hot flush crept up her neck, her breaths shooting out in white clouds of vapor.

The metadata on the photo didn't lie. GPS coordinates: right here in boring old Springfield. I scoffed, a harsh, ugly sound that echoed in my empty bedroom. For five years, Chloe had spun extravagant tales about her life in Paris. She described the smell of the bakeries, the view of the Seine, the chic parties she attended. I had eaten up every word, feeling utterly inadequate about my small-town existence. Now, zooming in on the supposedly European brick wall in her selfie, I recognized the spray-painted graffiti tag from the alley behind our local gas station. She lived ten minutes away. My jaw locked. I felt the heat rising in my cheeks, a burning wave. I had spent hours wishing I could escape to her world, only to find out she was stuck in the exact same miserable town, mocking my gullibility the entire time.

The ceiling leaked a steady drip of murky water onto Elias’s shoulder, but his eyes remained glued to the forum moderator’s latest post. 'SilverFox' had just uploaded a photo of his new mechanical keyboard. Elias zoomed in on the shiny keys. Reflected in the glossy monitor bezel behind the keyboard was a very specific, gaudy stained-glass window. It was the window from the leasing office downstairs. 'SilverFox', the compassionate moderator who always gave Elias advice on tenant rights, was Mr. Henderson. His own landlord. The same landlord who had ignored Elias’s maintenance requests for the leaking roof for six months. Elias’s breathing grew heavy, his chest rising and falling in sharp, jagged movements. He gripped the edge of his laptop screen, his thumbs pressing hard enough to distort the pixels. He abruptly stood up, his chair scraping violently against the floorboards.

The notification lit up my dark room: MrH_History started following you. I stared at the screen until the edges of my vision blurred. My thumb hovered over the block button, trembling so hard I almost dropped the phone. He was the one who lectured us about digital footprints yesterday, preaching about professional boundaries. Now he was digitally creeping into my weekend life? I grabbed my pillow and twisted the fabric until my knuckles turned white, my chest heaving with sharp, uneven breaths. How dare he intrude on the one place I didn't have to raise my hand to speak. I slammed the phone face-down on my nightstand, the loud clack echoing in the quiet room. I wanted to march into first period tomorrow and sweep every neatly stacked paper off his stupid oak desk. Instead, I jabbed the screen, hitting 'Block', my jaw aching from how hard I was grinding my teeth.

Chloe’s fingernails dug crescent moons into her palms as she stared at the Instagram notification from Mrs. Gable. The audacity burned in her chest like swallowed hot coals. Just yesterday, Gable gave her a low grade on a privacy essay, claiming Chloe didn't understand real-world implications. Now, the woman’s profile picture smiled innocuously next to a request to view Chloe's private photos. Chloe shoved her chair back, the metal legs shrieking against the hardwood floor. She paced the length of her bedroom, her breathing shallow and fast. She pictured herself confronting Gable in the hallway, demanding to know what gave her the right to pry into a high schooler's weekend. Grabbing her notebook, Chloe ripped out the page with her essay draft, crumpling it into a tight, hard ball and hurling it with all her strength at the bedroom wall.

I almost choked on my coffee when I saw the handle. @CoachDavis_Track liked my beach photo. I crushed the disposable cup in my grip, brown liquid splashing over the rim onto my favorite jeans, but I didn't even care about the stain. My blood roared in my ears. This was my personal space, my escape from his relentless whistle and condescending remarks about my sprint times. I aggressively swiped through my followers list, my finger jabbing the screen as if trying to puncture the glass. He had bypassed my privacy settings somehow, or I had left it open by mistake, and now he was scrolling through my summer memories. I stood up so fast my knee slammed into the table. The cafe patrons turned to look, but I just glared right through them, marching out the door with my hands balled into tight, trembling fists at my sides.

Julian’s phone glowed in the library, illuminating the harsh lines of his face. Ms. Albright is now following you on TikTok. A hot flush crept up his neck and settled in his cheeks. He snatched his earbuds out, the cord catching and knocking his textbook to the floor with a heavy thud. He didn't pick it up. Instead, he stared at her perfectly curated profile picture. She had just given him detention for whispering, citing his lack of boundaries. And yet, here she was, invading his space, watching the silly lip-sync videos he made with his little sister. His chest tightened, a heavy pressure building behind his sternum. He typed out a venomous direct message, his thumbs flying across the keyboard with punishing force, before deleting it all with a sharp exhale. He slammed his laptop shut, the crack echoing loudly through the silent study hall.

The little blue bird icon mocked me. Mr. Henderson followed you. I felt a sudden, intense heat radiate from the back of my neck. I immediately locked my phone and tossed it onto the passenger seat, gripping the steering wheel until the leather creaked under my hands. My breath came out in short, forceful puffs. I use that app to vent about my grueling AP Chemistry assignments and his unfair grading curve. Did he search for my name? Was he actively monitoring my complaints? The thought made my stomach twist into hard knots. I slammed my palm against the horn, the loud blare startling a flock of pigeons resting on the nearby power line. I grabbed the phone again, jabbing the screen with brutal force to permanently restrict his account, my jaw set so firmly my teeth ached.

Marcus didn't blink as he stared at the screen. The notification from his biology teacher sat at the top of his feed. A low, rumbling growl vibrated in his throat as he pushed away from his desk. He kicked the wastebasket, sending it skittering across the room and spilling crumpled papers over the rug. "Unbelievable," he muttered, his voice shaking. He paced back and forth, dragging a heavy hand down his face. Mr. Vance was notoriously strict about personal space in the classroom, refusing even to allow small talk before the bell rang. Now, the man was digitally peering into Marcus's weekend skateboard videos. Marcus picked up his favorite pen from the desk and snapped it cleanly in half, the plastic splintering into his palm. He threw the broken pieces at the wall, wishing it was Vance’s smug face, his chest rising and falling in rapid, jagged motions.

My eyes darted between the name on my screen and the framed debate team photo on my dresser. Mrs. Collins has requested to follow you. A bitter taste flooded my mouth. I dropped the phone as if it burned me. She was the one who constantly reminded us to "separate our personal and professional lives" during club meetings. My hands began to shake, a restless energy coursing through my veins that demanded I break something. I grabbed a throw pillow and hurled it at the closet door. It wasn't enough. I needed to yell, to demand why a fifty-year-old woman felt entitled to observe my late-night meme scrolling. My breathing grew loud in the quiet bedroom. I snatched the phone back up, glaring at her smiling profile icon, and aggressively tapped the 'Decline' button, wishing I could physically push her out of my room.

The phone buzzed in Maya’s palm, vibrating against her skin. New Follower: Senorita_Gomez. Maya’s eyes widened, and a dark, heavy flush crept up her face. She bit the inside of her cheek until she tasted copper. Gomez had spent the entire Spanish period today lecturing Maya about distraction and focus. Now, at nine on a Saturday night, the teacher was browsing Maya’s photography page. Maya shoved her phone into her pocket, marching out of the kitchen and letting the screen door slam shut behind her with a violent bang. She kicked a loose rock off the porch, watching it ricochet off the garden fence. The hypocrisy tasted sour in her mouth. She crossed her arms tightly over her chest, her nails digging deeply into the fabric of her sleeves as she glared out into the dark yard, wishing she could shout into the night sky.

I stared at the Twitch chat, the words blurring together. User MathWhiz_Peters just subscribed to your channel. Mr. Peters. My calculus teacher. My heart hammered against my ribs, loud and fast. I immediately muted my microphone, thankful my webcam was already off. He knew this was my safe haven, the place I talked about my anxiety and played games to escape the pressure of his pop quizzes. I gripped the edges of my desk so hard my fingers cramped. A hot prickling sensation washed over my scalp. I wanted to rip the power cord out of the wall. Instead, I forcefully typed commands to ban the username, slamming my fingers onto the mechanical keys. Each loud clack of the keyboard felt like a tiny release of the immense pressure expanding rapidly in my chest. I shut down the stream instantly without a single word to my regular viewers.

A sharp breath hitched in Liam’s throat as he recognized the profile photo. The drama teacher, Mr. Harrison, had just viewed his Instagram story. Liam’s jaw clenched so tight a dull ache radiated up to his temples. He tossed his phone onto the mattress and began pacing the narrow space between his bed and wardrobe. Just yesterday, Harrison had berated him in front of the entire cast for "lacking authenticity." Now, the man was silently watching Liam's private videos from a family dinner. Liam snatched his jacket off a chair, violently yanking the zipper up until it jammed. He pulled at the stuck metal tabs, his breathing shallow and erratic, until the teeth broke off in his hand. He threw the broken zipper piece across the room, glaring at his phone as if it were a venomous snake resting on his bedsheets.

The notification flashed across my smartwatch during dinner. Ms. Taylor accepted your follow request. But I never requested her. I tapped the screen, realizing she had a public profile and had just followed me back. I dropped my fork onto the porcelain plate with a loud clatter. My mom asked what was wrong, but my teeth were locked together. I pushed my chair back, the wood scraping harshly against the tile, and excused myself through gritted teeth. Once in the hallway, I punched the wall just hard enough to sting my knuckles. She always preaches about safe digital spaces in homeroom, and here she was, linking my private thoughts to her feed. I stood in the dark bathroom, splashing freezing water on my burning face, gripping the edges of the porcelain sink while glaring at my reflection, trying to slow my racing heart.

Samira’s thumbs stopped hovering over her phone screen. A notification popped up: Coach Miller tagged you in a post. It was a candid photo from the weekend track meet, posted on his personal account, heavily filtered. Samira’s nostrils flared. She pressed her lips together into a thin, bloodless line. She had explicitly opted out of the school's social media release form for a reason. Her hands shook as she navigated to his profile, the screen briefly blurring through her narrowed eyes. She hit the 'Remove Tag' button with a violent jab of her index finger. She stood up, her pulse pounding in her ears like a war drum. Without thinking, she grabbed her gym bag and kicked her closet door shut with a deafening thud. She wanted to march straight to his office right now, regardless of the hour, and scream until her vocal cords gave out.

I stared at the blinking cursor on the dean’s monitor, my fingernails digging crescents into my palms. The name on the official award letter read 'Marcus T. Vance,' not 'Marcus J. Vance.' The administrator offered a tight, apologetic smile, adjusting her glasses as she slid the misdirected acceptance letter across the desk. I snatched the paper, the crisp edges crumpling under my grip. Four months of pulling double shifts at the diner, skipping sleep, and pouring my soul into that essay, only to be told it was a clerical error. "We'll need the dispersed funds returned by Friday," she murmured. My jaw locked so tight my teeth ached. I shoved the chair back, the metal legs shrieking against the linoleum, and marched toward the glass doors. I didn't look back as the heavy oak slammed shut behind me, the glass rattling in its frame.

Elena stared at the email on her phone until the letters blurred. "We deeply regret to inform you that due to a system glitch, the Merit Endowment was awarded in error." She dropped the phone onto her desk. It landed with a sharp crack against her laptop. Her chest heaved, pulling in jagged, shallow breaths that offered no oxygen. Across the room, her roommate's cheerful congratulatory banner mocked her in bright glitter paint. Elena grabbed the banner by its edge and tore it down, the tape ripping paint from the drywall. She crushed the thick cardstock into a massive, jagged ball, the glitter cutting into her skin. They expected her to just pack up and leave? After she had already turned down her backup school? She kicked her laundry basket, sending clothes flying across the cramped dorm room, her vision narrowing to a pinpoint.

The official letterhead felt like sandpaper between my fingers. "Dear Ms. Carter, we apologize, but the STEM fellowship belongs to Aaron Carter." I read the sentence three times. My pulse throbbed in my temples, a rhythmic hammering that drowned out the chatter of the crowded hallway. A laugh echoed from the corner—Aaron himself, showing off his new campus ID to his buddies. He hadn’t even applied until the deadline extension. I crushed the letter into my jacket pocket, my breathing loud and ragged in my own ears. Blood rushed to my cheeks, hot and prickly. I marched straight past his group, deliberately clipping his shoulder with mine. He stumbled, his coffee spilling over his crisp white sneakers. "Watch it!" he snapped. I didn't say a word, just kept walking, my boots striking the tile floor like a gavel slamming down on wood.

Julian sat at the kitchen table, the glowing screen of his laptop casting long shadows across his rigid face. The university's portal showed a negative balance of twenty thousand dollars. The "Correction of Award Recipient" notice blinked mockingly at the top of the page. He gripped his ceramic coffee mug, his knuckles turning stark white. The coffee inside rippled with the tremors shaking his arms. His mother walked in, humming a soft tune, carrying the celebratory cake she had baked yesterday. "Should we cut it now?" she asked. Julian’s gaze shifted from the screen to the cake. The frosting read 'Future Architect'. He stood up so fast his knee knocked the table, making the plates clatter. Without a word, he grabbed his keys from the counter, his grip so tight the metal bit into his skin, and walked out into the freezing rain.

I was wiping down the espresso machine when my phone buzzed with an email from the bursar. "Clerical error. Immediate revocation of the Harrison Arts Grant." I stopped wiping. The damp rag in my hand began to drip lukewarm water onto the floor. My throat tightened, a thick knot forming that made it impossible to swallow. I thought of the canvas supplies I had just bought, the loans I had just declined. "Hey, I need a latte over here!" a customer barked from the counter. I looked up, my eyes burning. The espresso machine hissed, releasing a cloud of steam that matched the boiling pressure inside my chest. I threw the dirty rag directly into the trash bin with a violent thud. "Make it yourself," I whispered under my breath, untying my apron with sharp, jerky motions and throwing it onto the counter.

Priya stood perfectly still in Professor Lin’s office. The scent of old paper and peppermint tea suddenly made her nauseous. "It was meant for a local high school student with a similar ID number," Lin explained, refusing to meet her eyes. Priya’s jaw clenched, the muscles ticking visibly beneath her skin. She had spent three weeks sleeping in the library for that portfolio. "I see," she said, her voice dropping an octave, clipped and sharp as glass. She picked up her portfolio, her fingers digging into the black leather cover until it warped. Professor Lin started to offer a platitude about other financial aid options, but Priya spun on her heel. She shoved the heavy oak door open with both hands, letting it slam against the wall with a deafening crack that rattled the framed degrees, ignoring the startled gasps from the hallway.

I sat in the driver’s seat of my beat-up Honda, the engine off, staring at the brick facade of the admissions building. The dean’s words echoed in the confined space: 'An unfortunate database merge.' I gripped the steering wheel at ten and two. My chest rose and fell in rapid, shallow jerks. The leather cover squeaked under my tightening hands. I pressed my foot down on the brake pedal as hard as I could, wishing it was something else. A scream clawed its way up my throat, tearing out of me—a raw, guttural sound that filled the tiny car. I slammed my palms against the wheel, once, twice, three times, the horn blaring a jarring, dissonant note across the empty parking lot. My breathing was ragged, my face flushed with a heat that felt like a sunburn, as I glared at the university logo.

David crumpled the printout of the revoked scholarship letter, squeezing it until his hands shook. The paper ball wasn't enough. He threw it at the base of the campus statue, but the wind just lazily pushed it away. He began pacing the brick courtyard, his strides long and aggressive, his heavy boots striking the ground like he wanted to crack the masonry. His roommate called his name, jogging over with a concerned look. "Hey man, I heard about the funding mix-up." David stopped dead. His eyes narrowed into dark, unforgiving slits. He didn't look at his friend; he just stared right through him, his nostrils flaring with every heavy exhale. "Don't," David snapped, his tone laced with venom. He pushed past the boy, his shoulder deliberately colliding with the other student's chest, leaving his roommate standing in stunned silence as David stormed toward the gates.

I threw my textbooks into the cardboard box, ignoring the loud rip of my biology tome. "We require you to vacate the honors dorm by Sunday." The letter sat on my bed, a mocking little square of white doom. My blood pounded in my ears, a frantic drumbeat demanding release. I grabbed the framed acceptance photo from my nightstand—me, smiling like an idiot under the university arch. I hurled it at the trash can. It missed, striking the radiator. The glass shattered, exploding into dozens of glittering shards across the hardwood floor. Good. Let them clean it up. I kicked the empty suitcase across the room, watching it careen into the wall and leave a dark scuff mark on the pristine paint. My chest heaved, my fingernails biting half-moons into my palms.

Sarah stared at the glowing computer screen in the hushed library. The email subject line read: "Urgent: Scholarship Disbursement Reversal." As she read the words 'awarded to a student with an identical surname in error', her vision tunneled. A low, vibrating hum started in her ears. She pressed her lips together until they turned white. At the next table, a group of freshmen giggled loudly over a shared video. Sarah stood up abruptly, her chair scraping violently against the silence rule of the reading room. She walked over to their table, leaning down so her face was inches from the closest girl. Her eyes were wide, unblinking, and blazing with a terrifying intensity. "Shut. Up," Sarah hissed, her voice shaking with a barely restrained tremor. She didn't wait for their shocked reactions, sweeping her laptop and notes off her desk and marching out the double doors.

"What do you mean, an administrative oversight?" I gripped my phone tightly, pacing the narrow hallway outside the lecture hall. My boots squeaked sharply with every pivot. The voice on the line stammered something about a mixed-up social security digit and a different applicant. A hot prickling sensation crawled up the back of my neck. I stopped pacing and pressed my free hand against the cold cinderblock wall, my fingers curling into tight claws. "I already signed a lease," I said, my voice dangerously low and steady, lacking any of its usual warmth. The administrator muttered another hollow apology. I didn't say goodbye. I pulled the phone away from my ear and slammed the 'end call' button with my thumb. Without thinking, I threw the device down the hall. It skidded across the linoleum, the screen cracking in a spiderweb pattern against the baseboard.

Marcus stood in the financial aid queue for an hour, the misdirected award letter burning a hole in his pocket. When he finally reached the counter, the clerk barely glanced at his file before saying, "Oh, the glitch. Yes, that belongs to Marcus V. Smith, not Marcus B. Smith." Marcus placed his hands flat on the counter. His chest expanded, his breathing turning into loud, forceful exhales through his nose. He stared at the clerk's nametag, his jaw set so firmly his teeth ground together audibly. "Fix it," he said, the words biting and cold. "Sir, I can't—" the clerk started. Marcus brought his fist down on the laminate counter with a deafening bang that made the clerk flinch and the entire line fall dead silent. "I said, fix it," he repeated, his eyes locked onto the clerk like a predator cornering its prey.

I stared at the red circled zero on the top of my thesis. Professor Vance was still talking, his monotone voice droning on about academic integrity, but I only heard a high-pitched ringing in my ears. My nails dug so deeply into my thighs that I knew there would be crescent-moon bruises tomorrow. "I wrote every single word," I forced the statement out through a locked jaw, my voice shaking. He slid a printout across the desk, tapping a highlighted section. I snatched the paper from his desk, tearing the edge in my haste. Four months. Four months of late nights in the library, skipping meals, bleeding onto the keyboard, and he sat there behind his mahogany desk, casually erasing my existence with a stroke of his pen. I stood up so fast my chair tipped backward and crashed against the bookshelf. Let it stay there.

Marcus paced the narrow corridor, his boots striking the linoleum with heavy, rhythmic thuds. He stopped abruptly, pressing his forehead against the cool cinderblock wall, closing his eyes as a hot flush crept up his neck. Inside that frosted glass door, they were dismantling his future because an algorithm flagged his history essay. He spun around and kicked the metal baseboard. The loud clang echoed down the hall, turning the heads of passing freshmen, but Marcus didn't care. He pictured the sneer on the Dean's face, the condescending tone implying he wasn't smart enough to synthesize the French Revolution on his own. His hands curled into tight fists at his sides, the knuckles turning completely white. When the secretary finally called his name, he marched through the door, his chest heaving, ready to demand they run the damn file again while he watched.

The subject line read "Notice of Academic Misconduct." I read the sentence three times before the meaning actually penetrated my skull. A sudden, intense heat bloomed in my chest and rushed straight to my face. I slammed my laptop shut so hard the plastic casing cracked. "You have got to be kidding me," I muttered to the empty room. My breathing turned shallow and fast. I grabbed the nearest object—a half-empty water bottle—and hurled it across the room. It exploded against the closet door, soaking my favorite jacket, but the loud crack only fueled the fire in my veins. I had cited every single source. I had the rough drafts, the time stamps, the search history. The audacity of this teaching assistant to sit in her ivory tower and accuse me of stealing someone else’s code made a fierce, suffocating heat radiate through my entire body.

Chloe’s face burned hot on the webcam as the academic board laid out their evidence. She muted her microphone, breathing heavily through her nose like a cornered bull. On the screen, Dr. Aris pointed to two paragraphs of her sociology paper, claiming they mirrored a published journal too closely to be coincidence. Chloe’s knee bounced violently under her desk, sending tremors through her entire workstation. She unmuted herself, cutting off the department head mid-sentence. "Check the publication date of that journal," she snapped, her tone sharp enough to cut glass. "Then check the date I submitted my initial prospectus." Her eyes narrowed at the screen, staring down the grid of academics who dared to question her integrity. She gripped the edge of her desk, her knuckles aching under the pressure, waiting for them to realize they were the ones who had made the colossal mistake.

"They think I copied it," I said, my voice dropping to a harsh whisper. I stirred my coffee so violently that the dark liquid sloshed over the rim, scalding my fingers, but I barely felt the burn. Sarah gasped, but I just grabbed a handful of napkins and crushed them into a tight ball. "An AI detector," I scoffed, a bitter, grating sound tearing from my throat. "A stupid machine decides my style is too robotic, and suddenly I'm a cheat." I pushed the mug away, sending it sliding dangerously close to the edge of the table. The urge to flip the entire table was overwhelming. My chest felt tight, a caged animal throwing itself against my ribs. I had sacrificed my entire weekend, missing my sister's birthday, to polish that literature review. Now, I was supposed to sit back and politely defend my own words.

The classroom emptied, leaving Julian standing alone before Mrs. Gable's desk. The red 'See Me' on his poetry assignment glared up at him. "Julian, this level of maturity... it doesn't match your previous work," she said gently, sliding a printed internet link across the wood. Julian’s jaw locked. A pulse hammered fiercely at his temple. "Are you saying I couldn't have written it?" he demanded, his voice raising a full octave. "Because I'm usually a quiet C-student, I can't write a poem about my own grandfather?" He leaned over the desk, invading her space, his breathing ragged. He snatched the poem back, crumpling the heavy cardstock in his fist until it was a ruined, jagged ball. He didn't wait for her to formulate an excuse. He spun on his heel, his heavy backpack swinging wildly, and kicked the heavy wooden door open with his foot.

The critique was going well until Professor Higgins pointed at my canvas and casually mentioned the striking, impossible resemblance to a piece he’d seen in a Berlin gallery. My brush snapped in my hands. The sharp splinter of wood pierced my palm, but the sting was nothing compared to the roaring in my ears. "A resemblance?" I interrupted, the words tumbling out like jagged stones. "I mixed every single pigment. I stretched this canvas myself." I stepped forward, my chest practically touching his tweed jacket. I wanted to scream, to tear the canvas off the easel and shove it into his hands. I stared at the surrounding students, daring anyone to nod in agreement with him. My entire body vibrated with a tense, electric energy. I threw the broken halves of my favorite brush onto the paint-splattered floor and marched out, the studio door slamming behind me.

When the email notification popped up, Elena was halfway through her calculus homework. She opened the message from the honor council, read the accusation regarding her midterm essay, and went completely still. Then, very deliberately, she took her mechanical pencil and snapped it clean in half. The plastic shards scattered across her open textbook. Her breathing grew heavy, the sound loud in the dead-silent study room. She grabbed her notebook, the one containing fifty pages of handwritten research, and hurled it against the brick wall. The spine cracked, sending loose, painstakingly written pages fluttering to the carpet like dead leaves. She pressed the heels of her hands hard into her eyes until bursts of color exploded in her vision. The absolute nerve. She shoved her chair back with a harsh screech that echoed through the quiet stacks, grabbing her coat and storming toward the exit.

The rain plastered my hair to my forehead, but I didn't bother pulling up my hood. I needed the freezing water to cool the blistering heat radiating from my skin. The disciplinary committee had actually suspended me. Because a paragraph in my chemistry lab matched a senior's paper from three years ago. I stomped through a deep puddle, sending muddy water splashing up my jeans. I gritted my teeth so hard my jaw ached. "I didn't even know him," I yelled to the empty street. I kicked a metal garbage can, sending it toppling over with a satisfying crash, spilling trash across the wet pavement. My hands were balled so tightly inside my pockets that my fingernails were cutting into my skin. I wanted to march back, grab the dean by his silk tie, and make him read my raw data until he choked on his own accusation.

The silence in the rehearsal room was suffocating. Maestro Rossi held Liam’s original composition, tapping the sheet music. "The bridge is remarkably similar to a forgotten movement by Clementi," the old man murmured. Liam’s face flushed a deep, violent crimson. He stood up from the piano bench, the wooden legs screeching loudly against the hardwood floor. "Similar?" Liam spat the word like poison. "I spent six weeks writing that. I didn't sleep for three days to perfect the transition." His chest heaved rapidly. He snatched the sheet music from Rossi's delicate hands, tearing the thick parchment right down the middle. He threw the pieces into the air, letting the notes rain down around them. He stared at the maestro, his nostrils flaring, chest tight enough to burst. Without another word, Liam grabbed his coat and kicked the doorframe on his way out, leaving the maestro in silence.

I crumpled the official university letterhead into a tight ball, squeezing it until my knuckles ached. Plagiarism. The word echoed in my skull, lighting a match to my short fuse. I stood in the middle of the crowded student union, deaf to the chatter and the clinking of coffee mugs. "Hey, you okay?" my roommate asked, reaching out. I slapped his hand away. "Don't," I snapped, my voice sounding like gravel. I started pacing, my heavy boots striking the tile floor like hammer blows. My vision tunneled, focusing only on the administration building visible through the glass doors. I had worked three part-time jobs to pay for this tuition, bleeding for every grade, and they dared to claim I bought my capstone project online. I shoved the double doors open, ignoring the cold wind, marching straight across the quad with my jaw set like stone.

Maya sat rigidly in the wooden chair facing the honor council, her posture unnaturally straight. When the student prosecutor claimed her marketing proposal was lifted from a corporate brochure, Maya’s hands gripped the armrests. Her knuckles turned stark white. She took a sharp, jagged breath, her nostrils flaring as she locked eyes with her accuser. "Show me the brochure," she demanded, her voice a low, vibrating growl that silenced the room. The prosecutor shifted uncomfortably. "I have my rough drafts right here," she continued, standing up abruptly. She unzipped her backpack with so much force the zipper broke, spilling highlighters and flash drives across the polished table. She slammed a stack of handwritten notebooks onto the desk. The loud smack echoed against the high ceiling. She leaned over the table, staring directly at the council president, daring him to utter another word against her integrity.

I stared at the bolded words on my screen: "We regret to inform you." My jaw locked so tight I heard a faint popping sound in my ears. I had spent four months polishing that essay, missing weekend trips and skipping out on family dinners to perfect every single sentence. The library was dead silent, but a roaring static filled my head. My fingers hovered over the keyboard, trembling slightly. I wanted to pick up the heavy oak chair I was sitting on and launch it through the nearest stained-glass window. Instead, I grabbed the mechanical pencil lying next to my notebook and snapped it in half with one clean break. A piece of the graphite flew off and hit the screen right above the signature of the admissions committee. I slammed the laptop shut, the sharp crack echoing through the aisles.

Elias stood at the end of his driveway, the thin white envelope trembling in his grip. The words "Selection Committee" were printed in the corner, but it was far too thin to contain an acceptance packet. He tore the top off, his eyes darting over the polite dismissal. His chest began to rise and fall in rapid, jagged hitches. Without reading the second paragraph, he ripped the paper down the middle. Then he ripped it again, and again, until the pieces were nothing more than confetti. He threw the scraps into the gravel, grinding his worn-out sneaker over them until the white paper turned brown with dirt. Marching back toward the house, his footsteps landed heavy and hard against the pavement. He grabbed the handle of the screen door, yanking it open with such force that the hinges shrieked in protest.

"I'm sorry, Maya, but the foundation went with another candidate," Mr. Henderson said softly from behind his massive oak desk. My fingernails dug deep into the palms of my hands, leaving crescent-shaped indentations. I stared at the glossy brochure for the university he had deliberately placed in front of me. "Right," I forced the word through my teeth. They didn't even read my portfolio; I knew they didn't, because the tracker still showed zero views on my digital gallery. The heat rushed up my neck and settled in my cheeks, a burning flush that made the room feel unbearably small. I stood up so quickly that my wooden chair tipped backward, hitting the floor with a deafening clatter. Mr. Henderson flinched, opening his mouth to speak, but I was already out the door, my heavy boots stomping down the linoleum hallway.

The notification pinged on Clara’s phone just as she finished wiping down the espresso machine. "Application Status Updated." She swiped the screen with a damp thumb. Denied. A high-pitched ringing started in her ears. She looked around the crowded cafe, at the line of students wearing the sweatshirts of the exact university she could no longer afford. Her coworker bumped her shoulder, asking for a grande latte. Clara didn't move. Her heart hammered against her ribs in heavy, violent thuds. She grabbed a plastic tray of freshly washed ceramic mugs and shoved it onto the counter. The tray slid too far, teetering over the edge before crashing onto the tile floor. A dozen mugs shattered into jagged shards, sending patrons jumping back in surprise. Clara merely stared at the mess, her chest heaving, wishing she could sweep the rest of the counter onto the floor too.

I sat in the driver’s seat of my rusted Honda, parked in an empty lot behind the grocery store. The university’s portal gleamed on my phone screen, the word 'unsuccessful' burning into my retinas. I tossed the phone onto the passenger seat. My breathing quickened, pulling in the stale air of the car as my vision narrowed to the dashboard. Three jobs. I worked three jobs while maintaining a perfect GPA, and they gave the funding to someone else. I gripped the steering wheel, my knuckles turning stark white under the pale streetlights. A primal scream tore from my throat, raw and deafening, bouncing off the windshield and filling the cramped space. I slammed the base of my palm against the horn. The blaring sound pierced the quiet night, and I hit it again, and again, until my hand bruised.

Julian lay on his top bunk, staring at the ceiling as the email glowed from his tablet in the dark room. "While your academic record is impressive..." He didn't need to read the rest. His jaw clenched so tight his teeth ached. Below him, his roommate laughed loudly at a video game. The carefree sound grated against Julian’s ears like scraping metal. He closed his eyes, but the rejection text danced behind his eyelids. His hands began to shake. Without a word, he grabbed the thick hardcover biology textbook he had spent his last fifty dollars on, reared his arm back, and hurled it across the room. It smashed into the drywall with a massive crunch, leaving a dent the size of an apple. "Dude, what is your problem?" his roommate yelled. Julian stayed silent, glaring at the wall, his nostrils flaring with every sharp breath.

"Did you hear back from the merit board yet?" Dad asked, passing the bowl of mashed potatoes across the dining table. I pulled my phone from my pocket, loading the page. The little red 'X' next to my name appeared instantly. My stomach plummeted, immediately replaced by a scalding heat rising in my chest. "No," I lied, my voice tight and strained. I picked up my steak knife. The roasted chicken on my plate became the sole focus of my existence. I sawed into the meat, pressing the serrated edge against the ceramic plate so hard it created a screeching noise. Mom covered her ears. "Honey, please," she winced. I ignored her, slicing the chicken into smaller and smaller pieces, my elbow jerking in rigid, sharp motions. I threw the knife down, shoved my chair back from the table, and stormed upstairs without another word.

The chemistry lab was quiet except for the bubbling of beakers and scratched notes. Chloe slipped her phone under the black soapstone desk to check the time, only to see the banner notification from the dean's office. She clicked it. The word 'Declined' sat at the bottom of the message. Chloe’s vision blurred. She looked up at her lab partner, who was casually texting on his own phone, completely unbothered by the experiment they were supposed to be monitoring. Her hands formed tight fists, her fingernails biting into her skin. She grabbed her heavy protective goggles off the desk and twisted the thick plastic frames until they snapped loudly in her hands. The sharp edge sliced the side of her thumb. She didn't flinch. She just stared at the red drop welling up on her skin, breathing in quick, ragged gasps.

The rain soaked through my thin jacket, but I barely felt the cold. I stood on the sidewalk, the glow of my screen illuminating the puddles at my feet. The athletic committee had passed on me. Four years of waking up at dawn, running until I vomited, pushing through a torn ligament—all for a standard rejection email generated by an automated server. I crushed the phone in my palm, glaring up at the gray sky. A passing car drove through a puddle, splashing dirty water onto my jeans. I let out a guttural yell, kicking the metal trash can next to the bus stop. It tipped over, spilling soda cups and wrappers across the wet concrete. I kicked it again, the metal denting under my heavy boot, the loud clang doing nothing to quiet the roaring tempest inside my head.

Inside the quiet art studio, Leo stood perfectly still in front of his easel. In one hand, he held his finest brush. In the other, he held the crumpled letter from the arts conservatory. Denied. The word echoed in his skull. He looked at the magnificent oil painting he had spent six months perfecting, the very piece he had submitted in his portfolio. The colors suddenly looked grotesque to him. The brush trembled in his grip. His teeth ground together with a horrible scraping noise. He dropped the brush onto the floor and grabbed a palette knife from the wooden table. With a sudden, violent lunge, Leo drove the metal blade straight through the center of the canvas. He ripped it downward, tearing the fabric of his masterpiece into two jagged halves, standing over the ruined art with a rapidly heaving chest.

Coach tossed the sealed envelope onto my duffel bag before heading out to the field. "Open it," he said over his shoulder. I ripped the seal, pulling out the single sheet of paper. The first sentence was enough. I balled the paper into a tight fist, the sharp corners digging into my palm. My pulse pounded in my ears, a rhythmic, deafening thud. I looked at the pristine, freshly painted white lines of the football field. I was the one who painted them. I was the one who stayed late every single night. I grabbed my helmet by the facemask and swung it like a wrecking ball into the concrete wall of the locker room. The fiberglass cracked with a terrible snap, a giant fissure splitting down the center. I stood there, panting, glaring at the broken pieces scattered on the floor.

The kitchen was dark, save for the blue light of the laptop illuminating Sarah’s face. She hit the refresh button one last time. The portal updated: "Scholarship Denied." Sarah stopped blinking. She sat in the wooden chair, completely paralyzed as a hot, prickling sensation crawled up her neck. On the table sat a towering stack of prep books, application essays, and financial aid forms. Months of her life, piled high in neat, organized folders. Her lips pulled back into a tight, humorless smile. She stood up, planted her hands firmly on the edge of the kitchen table, and shoved forward with all her weight. The table screeched across the linoleum before flipping completely over. Books, papers, and pens exploded across the kitchen floor in a chaotic storm. Sarah stood amidst the wreckage, her hands curled into shaking fists at her sides.

Maya stared at the forwarded email, her grip tightening on the edge of the lab bench until her knuckles turned bone-white. Three years. Three years of running assays at 2:00 AM, sacrificing weekends, and meticulously following Dr. Aris’s rigid protocols. "I've accepted a position in Boston," the screen read. Maya grabbed the nearest rack of empty test tubes and shoved it aside, listening to the sharp clatter of plastic hitting the floor. She had deferred a lucrative industry job to stay under his mentorship. Now, he was simply packing up and abandoning their grant halfway through the funding cycle. Her jaw clicked as she ground her teeth together. She typed out a reply, her fingers striking the keys with such force that the keyboard rattled against the desk. "Congratulations," she wrote, backspacing fiercely to erase the typo caused by her shaking hands.

The ceramic mug shattered in my hands, hot coffee pooling across the table and dripping onto my jeans. I barely felt the burn. Across the booth, Sarah kept talking about Professor Lin’s sudden move to Oxford, oblivious to the roaring sound rushing through my ears. Lin had promised to co-author my latest paper. She had smiled directly into my eyes yesterday and told me my defense would be a breeze. And she was leaving next week? Without a single word to me? I grabbed a fistful of paper napkins and crushed them into the spreading brown stain, pressing down until my wrists ached. "He'll figure it out," Sarah was saying. I squeezed my eyes shut, my breathing coming in short, sharp bursts. I shoved away from the table, the wooden chair screeching violently against the tile floor, and stormed out into the biting winter air.

David stood outside Room 402, staring at the freshly printed paper taped to the door: All advising appointments canceled. Please contact the department head. A red pen was still clutched in his hand. Before he could stop himself, he snapped it in half. Ink splattered across his thumb, dripping like dark blood onto the linoleum floor. Dr. Kensington had signed his dissertation proposal just two days ago. He had known. He had sat there, drinking his chamomile tea, nodding at David’s timeline, completely aware he wouldn't be around to read a single chapter. David kicked the bottom of the heavy oak door, the thud echoing down the empty humanities hallway. His chest heaved as he pictured Kensington already packing his tweed jackets. David turned on his heel, leaving dirty ink smudges on the brass doorknob as he marched toward the dean’s office.

My phone buzzed with the department newsletter just as I found the perfect dusty alcove in the archives. Farewell to Dr. Vance. I read the headline three times, my vision narrowing until the words blurred into meaningless black lines. The antique book in my lap slipped, hitting the floor with a heavy thud, but I didn't reach down to retrieve it. Five chapters. I had written five chapters of my thesis based entirely on his exclusive fieldwork in Peru. Fieldwork he was now taking with him to a private institute. I dug my fingernails into my palms, leaving deep crescent-moon indentations in the skin. The quiet murmurs of the library felt like sandpaper scraping against my eardrums. I gathered my notes into a haphazard pile, crumpling the edges, and shoved them roughly into my leather satchel, breaking the zipper in my frantic haste.

Elena played the final chord of the sonata, but her hands came down on the grand piano keys with the subtlety of falling bricks. The dissonant crash reverberated violently through the empty practice room. Maestro Silva’s resignation letter sat crumpled in a tight ball next to her metronome. He was the only reason she had auditioned for this conservatory. He had promised to guide her through the international competition circuit this spring. Instead, he was leaving for Vienna, taking his prized prodigy—who wasn't her—along. Her chest rose and fell in rapid, shallow jerks. She snatched the sheet music off the stand and tore it straight down the middle, the sharp ripping sound cutting through the lingering echoes of the piano. She threw the torn halves to the floor and stomped on them, her breath hissing sharply through her teeth as she glared at the door.

The pixelated faces of my cohort stared back at me in stunned silence. Dr. Zhao was smiling, adjusting his glasses as he explained the wonderful opportunity awaiting him at a rival tech institute. I muted my microphone. "You coward," I spat at the screen, my voice vibrating with a harsh, raspy edge. My hands hovered over the keyboard, shaking so badly I couldn't command the mouse. I had turned down two fully funded internships because he insisted we were on the verge of a breakthrough in our machine learning model. A breakthrough he would now claim under a different university's banner. The heat in my face felt explosive. I abruptly slammed my laptop shut, the sudden plastic crack echoing in the quiet apartment. I stood up and paced the small room, kicking my laundry basket so hard it collided with the far wall, scattering clothes everywhere.

Marcus stood in the middle of the Nevada desert, the blazing sun beating down on his neck. His hands gripped the handle of his geological hammer so tightly that his forearms cramped. The message from the university administration had just reached his satellite phone. Dr. Henderson was relocating to Australia. Effective immediately. Marcus stared at the half-excavated rock face. Henderson had left him out here. Three hundred miles from civilization, leading a crew of undergraduates, with zero authority to approve the remaining budget. Marcus swung the hammer blindly at the nearest boulder. The metal struck stone with a deafening crack, sending a spray of sharp gray chips flying into the dry air. He swung again, harder this time, a guttural yell tearing from his throat. The rock splintered beneath his relentless assault, but the heavy, burning knot in his chest refused to break.

The neon sign of the campus dive bar flickered red across my face. I stared at the condensation rolling down my pint glass, tracing the water droplets with a rigid finger. "It's just a transition phase," the bartender offered gently, having overheard my rant. I shot him a glare so sharp he immediately turned his back to wipe the counter. A transition phase? Professor Gallagher had strung me along for four years, dangling the promise of a tenure-track recommendation letter. Now he was retiring to a beach in Florida and passing my dissertation off to an adjunct who didn't even study medieval history. I gripped the thick glass of my pint, feeling a desperate urge to hurl it at the mirror behind the bar. Instead, I slammed my fist onto the sticky wooden counter, making the coaster jump and the remaining beer slosh over the rim.

Chloe’s exacto knife sliced through the balsa wood, slipping past the safety ruler and gouging a deep, jagged line directly into her cutting mat. She didn't flinch. Her eyes were fixed on the corkboard where Professor Wright’s departure announcement was pinned. He was taking a position in Dubai. He was the sole reason she had spent eight months designing this sustainable housing prototype, tailoring every structural nuance to his specific theoretical framework. She grabbed her meticulously crafted scale model—the one that had consumed her entire winter break—and squeezed it. The fragile wood splintered and snapped under her grip, the delicate roof collapsing inward with a sickening crunch. She threw the ruined structure into the metal trash can. It hit the bottom with a loud clang, but the sound did nothing to loosen the tight, suffocating band constricting her throat.

I stood in the humid air of the research greenhouse, staring at the rare orchids Dr. Vance and I had cultivated together. The department secretary had just cheerfully informed me over the phone that Vance was leaving for a private agro-corp. He wasn't even staying until the end of the semester. I snatched a pair of heavy pruning shears from the metal cart. My breathing was loud in the enclosed glass space, echoing like a trapped animal. I looked at the fragile white blooms, the result of two years of my unpaid overtime, all of which would now be credited to his new corporate portfolio. My jaw locked tight, grinding until pain shot up my temples. I slammed the shears down onto the metal cart, the clash of steel ringing out sharply, and turned my back on the flowers, marching toward the exit without bothering to shut off the irrigation valves.

Paint dripped onto the floorboards from the brush gripped fiercely in Julian's hand. The scarlet pigment looked like fresh wounds against the pale wood. Professor Alarie’s goodbye email glowed brightly on his phone screen. She was moving to a prestigious academy in Paris, effectively canceling the senior exhibition she had promised to curate for him. Julian’s chest heaved. He stared at his nearly finished canvas, a portrait they had spent weeks discussing. His pulse thrummed violently in his ears, drowning out the ambient noise of the city outside. With a sudden, harsh movement, he slashed the loaded brush diagonally across the canvas, destroying the delicate facial features with a thick, jagged red scar. His breathing came in ragged gasps as he snapped the wooden handle of the paintbrush over his knee, tossing the jagged pieces onto the floor before kicking his stool across the room.

The fluorescent lights of the hospital corridor buzzed incessantly above me, a sound that grated against my skull. I clutched the patient chart to my chest, my fingernails digging into the hard plastic clipboard. Chief Resident Torres had just breezed past, casually mentioning that Dr. Patel was transferring to Johns Hopkins. Patel. The man who held my fellowship recommendation in his hands, who had told me yesterday to keep up the good work. I pushed through the heavy double doors into the stairwell, letting them slam shut behind me. The harsh echo bounced off the concrete walls. I let out a guttural scream, the sound tearing at the back of my throat. I kicked the steel handrail, my shoe connecting with a loud, ringing crash that sent a shockwave of pain up my leg. I welcomed the sting, letting it ground the rushing heat burning behind my eyes.

Leo stared at the red circled 'C-' on his canvas. His grip on the charcoal stick tightened until it snapped into black dust against his palm. Forty hours. He had missed his sister's birthday and barely slept for three days to perfect the shading on the portrait. The professor’s note read, "Lacks depth." Leo’s jaw locked. He snatched the canvas off the easel, the wooden frame protesting under his rigid fingers, and shoved it face-down onto the concrete floor. The sharp crack of the wood didn't offer enough release. He paced the cramped studio, his chest rising and falling in rapid, shallow hitches. "Lacks depth," he muttered, the words burning the back of his throat. He kicked the metal stool, sending it clattering violently against the metal lockers.

I hit the refresh button on the student portal for the fifth time, convinced a glitch was displaying someone else's transcript. But the glaring '62' next to Constitutional Law remained burned into the screen. My blood pounded behind my ears like a war drum. I had memorized every precedent, outlined every case, and led the study group for six weeks. I shoved my laptop away; it skidded across the desk and slammed into my coffee mug, spilling cold brew over my pristine notes. I didn't care. I grabbed the syllabus, staring at the professor's bolded grading rubric. Participation: 20%. I was the only one who answered his hypothetical questions. I pressed the heels of my hands into my eyes, my breathing coming out in hot, jagged bursts, imagining the sound of the dean's door splintering off its hinges as I demanded a recount.

Maya stared at the top right corner of her lab report. The red ink was so thick it had bled through the cheap lined paper. 45/100. Her teeth ground together so hard a sharp ache radiated up to her temples. She looked up at Mr. Harrison, who was calmly sipping from his 'World's Best Teacher' mug. Her hands began to tremble. Slowly, deliberately, she folded the report in half, then into quarters, her knuckles turning bone-white. The paper crinkled loudly in the silent classroom. She pressed her fingernails into her palms, leaving deep crescent-shaped indentations. Months of tutoring, skipping weekend movies, flashcards until 2 AM—all reduced to a failing grade by a man who couldn't even bother to grade the final page. She shoved her chair back, the metal legs shrieking against the linoleum, and marched toward his desk, her vision narrowing to a tunnel.

The evaluation sheet fluttered onto my music stand, light as a feather but hitting me with the force of an anvil. "Technically proficient, but emotionally stagnant. Grade: D." I read the words three times, the heat rising in my cheeks until my face felt like it was hovering over an open flame. I had bled onto these cello strings. My calluses had calluses. I looked at the jury panel packing up their briefcases, chatting about their lunch plans as if they hadn't just dismissed my entire existence. I grabbed my bow, my grip so tight the wood began to bend dangerously. A harsh, bitter laugh forced its way up my throat. I wanted to smash the polished mahogany of my instrument into a thousand splinters right at their feet, just to show them exactly what my supposed emotional stagnation looked like.

Julian’s eyes flicked between the solution manual on the projector and the blue examination book in his hands. A harsh red '58' glared back at him. He checked the steps. His methodology was identical to the professor’s. His only error was dropping a negative sign on line fourteen, but Dr. Aris had crossed out the entire page with a singular, dismissive diagonal slash. Zero points for partial credit.
