Julian’s chest tightened, his breath whistling sharply through his nose. He grabbed his pen and dug the ballpoint into the desk so fiercely the tip bent. The injustice sat like a lead weight in his stomach, quickly heating into a roaring furnace. Without a word, he ripped the blue book perfectly down the middle, the tearing sound echoing in the lecture hall, before dropping the shredded remains directly into the recycling bin on his way out the door.

"A bit derivative," the comment bubble on my document read, attached to a 'C-'. I stared at the glowing screen until the letters blurred. Derivative? I had poured my grandmother's real-life escape from the war into this narrative. I typed a reply to the professor, my fingers hammering the keys with such force that the keyboard clattered violently in the quiet library. Backspace. Backspace. I slammed the laptop shut. The sudden loud smack caused the girl across from me to jump, but I couldn't bring myself to apologize. My pulse throbbed in my neck. I snatched my bag from the floor, the strap biting into my shoulder. Let him write a hundred original pieces. Let him mine his own family trauma for a grade. I stormed past the turnstiles, shoving the heavy glass doors outward with both hands, letting the cold winter air hit my flushed skin.

The critique sheet rested beside Elias’s pristine workstation. "Grade: 6/10. Soufflé lacks adequate rise." Elias stared at the numbers, his jaw muscles jumping beneath his skin. Chef Gerard had kept him waiting for forty-five minutes before coming over to evaluate the dish. Of course it had fallen; gravity was a law of physics, not a culinary flaw. Elias picked up his favorite paring knife, his fingers wrapping around the handle with a white-knuckled vice grip. He stared at his reflection in the stainless-steel prep table. He wanted to scream until his vocal cords frayed. Instead, he drove the blade completely through his leftover stack of printed recipes, pinning the thick paper into the wooden cutting board with a dull, heavy thud. He left the knife standing perfectly upright, untied his pristine white apron with quick, violent tugs, and walked out of the kitchen without a backward glance.

I flipped to the final page of my thesis on the French Revolution. "Off-topic. 65%." The paper slipped from my trembling hands, scattering across the dorm room floor. I had cleared the topic with Professor Vance three times. Three separate office hours, all documented in my notebook. My blood rushed like a freight train in my ears. I stood up so quickly my desk chair tipped backward, crashing into the closet door. I didn't bother to pick it up. I paced the length of the tiny room, my hands balling into fists inside my pockets, my nails digging half-moons into my palms. I grabbed my phone, dialing my study partner, almost shattering the screen with how hard I tapped his name. When he answered, my voice came out in a low, shaking hiss that I barely recognized. "You won't believe what that absolute hypocrite just did."

The automated email arrived at precisely midnight. "Capstone Project: FAIL." Sarah’s eyes narrowed into tiny slits as she read the feedback. The automated grader had marked her entire application invalid because of a deprecated library—a library the instructor explicitly told them to use yesterday. Her jaw set so hard her teeth squeaked. She shoved her rolling chair back, sending it slamming into the wall behind her. The dull thud reverberated through the silent apartment. She picked up her stress ball, squeezing the foam until it ripped down the seam, white stuffing bursting out over her desk. It wasn’t enough. She grabbed the heavy textbook on algorithms, marched over to the open window, and hurled the thousand-page volume into the rain-soaked dumpster three stories below, watching the pages flutter wildly before hitting the trash with a satisfying crash.

The casting board was finally up. Next to my name was a 70 and 'Chorus Member 4'. I traced the numbers with a shaking finger. I had booked the lead in every community play for the last three years. The girl who got a 98 and the lead role was the director's daughter, who had spent half her audition staring at her script. A hot prickling sensation washed over my scalp. I bit the inside of my cheek until I tasted the sharp tang of copper. When the director walked by, flashing me a patronizing smile and offering a "Good job, kiddo," I couldn't speak. I just glared at him, my breathing shallow and fast, feeling the intense urge to rip the paper off the corkboard, tear it into confetti, and scatter it over his shiny, bald head. I turned on my heel and stomped toward the exit.

Marcus looked at the rubric returned by the TA. Team Grade: 50%. Beneath the score was a note about missing financial projections. Marcus slowly turned his head to look at Kevin, who was currently watching a gaming stream on his phone in the back row. Kevin was supposed to do the financials. Marcus's vision literally swam with red for a second. His face burned as if he had stepped into a sauna. He grabbed his heavy hardcover textbook and slammed it flat onto Kevin’s desk. The resulting bang silenced the entire lecture hall. Kevin jumped, dropping his phone. Marcus leaned in, his voice dropping to a low, gravelly whisper that vibrated with suppressed energy. "You told me you submitted the spreadsheet," he said, each word punched out through tightly gritted teeth, his hands gripping the edge of Kevin's desk so hard the wood groaned.

The tag attached to my balsa wood model read 'C+'. The critique cited a "lack of structural ambition." I stared at the towering, cantilevered suspension design that had consumed my weekends for two straight months. My hands shook so violently I had to jam them deep into my jacket pockets. The professor walked past, casually sipping a latte, completely oblivious to the fact that he had just torched my GPA. The heat radiating from my skin felt suffocating. I stepped closer to my model. A dark, intrusive impulse surged up my spine. Without breaking eye contact with the professor's retreating back, I raised my heavy steel ruler and brought it down across the center beam. The delicate wood splintered and collapsed into a chaotic heap of useless sticks, the loud crunch echoing through the studio. If it lacked ambition, it didn't deserve to stand.

The glossy hardcover arrived on Mr. Harrison’s desk during third period. He tore away the brown paper, his jaw tightening as he read the title. It was Marcus Vance’s debut novel. The dedication page fluttered open: "To Mr. Harrison, who said I’d never write a single original sentence." Harrison’s breath hitched, hot and shallow in his chest. This was the boy who had copied every essay, manipulated the administration when caught, and skated by with a warning. Now, Marcus was a bestselling author rubbing his success in Harrison’s face. The teacher’s fingers dug into the book’s pristine cover. The cardboard groaned, then cracked under the immense pressure of his thumbs. He stared at the smirking author photo on the back flap, a heavy, dark heat rising up his neck. With a sharp exhale, he hurled the heavy volume straight into the overflowing recycling bin.

The courier required a signature for the velvet box. I ripped the ribbon off, my hands trembling so violently I nearly dropped it. Nestled inside was a solid gold Rolex. The card read, "No hard feelings about the expulsion hearing! - Trent." My vision tunneled. Trent’s father had threatened the school board, dragged my name through the local papers, and ultimately cost me my pension just because I refused to change his son’s failing grade. My teeth ground together with a sickening crunch. The audacity to send this gaudy trinket after destroying my twenty-year career. I grabbed the heavy gold watch, the cold metal biting into my sweaty palm. I marched to the window overlooking the concrete alleyway behind my apartment building. I didn't even pause before I pitched it as hard as I could, waiting for the satisfying shatter below.

An ornate wooden box awaited Clara in the faculty lounge. Inside lay a crystal apple, polished to a blinding shine, accompanied by a letterhead from the Governor’s office. "Thanks for the early lessons in debate. - Senator Hayes." Clara’s chest heaved. She remembered Hayes perfectly—a silver-tongued teenager who had gleefully bullied the special needs students, always twisting the rules to avoid detention. Just yesterday, Hayes had voted to slash the state’s special education budget by thirty percent, citing "frivolous spending." The crystal apple felt like a block of ice in her hands. Her face flushed a deep crimson, and the veins in her neck pulsed against her collar. She slammed the box shut, the hinges snapping under the force. Marching over to the industrial trash compactor, she tossed the crystal apple inside and slammed her palm onto the crush button.

I stared at the pristine white envelope resting on my lectern. The embossed logo of the prestigious biotech firm mocked me. Inside was a handwritten note from Elena, thanking me for "laying the groundwork" for her new patented sequence, along with a gift card to a coffee shop. My knuckles turned stark white as I gripped the edges of the wooden podium. She hadn't just used my groundwork; she had copied my private laboratory files during her senior project, locked me out of the data, and published the findings under her own name. A high-pitched ringing echoed in my ears. I squeezed the plastic gift card between my thumb and forefinger until it snapped. Breathing in ragged gasps, I struck a match from my desk drawer, held the flame to her elegant stationary, and watched it turn to ash in the metal wastebasket.

A bouquet of black roses sat on the auditorium stage, right where the lead actress was supposed to stand. Mr. Davis picked up the attached card. "Break a leg tonight! - Leo." Davis’s jaw locked so tightly his teeth ached. Five years ago, Leo had intentionally dropped a sandbag from the catwalk during opening night, shattering a young girl’s collarbone just for a laugh. The school swept it under the rug, calling it an accident, and Leo had walked away without a scratch. Now, on the anniversary of that night, this arrived. Davis crushed the card in his fist, his breathing loud and erratic in the empty theater. He grabbed the bouquet, ignoring the thorns slicing into his bare palms. He marched to the prop room, hurled the roses onto the concrete floor, and ground his heavy boots over them until nothing remained but a smear of dark, bruised petals.

The glossy photograph slid out of the envelope and landed on my grading pile. It was a picture of Jason leaning against a cherry-red Ferrari, holding a custom license plate that read DROPOUT. A sticky note was attached: "Told you I wouldn't need calculus." I stared at the photo, a hot prickling sensation spreading across my scalp. I had spent countless unpaid hours tutoring Jason, fighting the administration to keep him enrolled, only for him to mock my salary on his way out the door to join his father's hedge fund. I grabbed my red grading pen and pressed the tip directly into Jason’s smug face. I dragged the pen down, carving a deep, jagged canyon through the glossy paper, tearing it into ribbons. I swept the shreds off my desk, my chest rising and falling in violent staccatos.

The cream-colored wedding invitation featured delicate gold foil and a silk ribbon. Ms. Albright read the names: Samantha & David. The note inside fluttered out: "I’d love for my favorite teacher to be there!" Ms. Albright’s hands began to shake uncontrollably. Samantha had orchestrated a malicious rumor campaign that Ms. Albright was drinking on the job, sparking a humiliating six-month district investigation. She had been cleared, but the stress had caused her hair to fall out. The sheer gall of this invitation was suffocating. A sour taste flooded her mouth. She stood up abruptly, her chair screeching against the linoleum. She marched straight to the faculty breakroom paper shredder and forced the thick cardstock into the blades, listening to the screech of the machine as it choked on the silk ribbon.

A blinding heat rushed behind my eyes. Ten years ago, my seniors spent six months painting a breathtaking mural in the courtyard. Tyler spray-painted obscenities over it the night before graduation because I gave him a C in ceramics, destroying hundreds of hours of passionate work. Now, a package was waiting outside my classroom door. I tore through the brown paper to find a cheap, plastic set of watercolors and a note: "Sorry about the mural. Here’s a replacement! - Tyler." I squeezed the brittle plastic case until it shattered in my hands, sending cheap, chalky discs of color clattering across the hallway floor. My jaw locked. I dug the heel of my boot into the red paint disc, grinding it into a fine powder, desperate to wipe the memory of his smirk from my brain.

Professor Higgins stared down at the mug sitting on his lectern. It declared "World's Most Tolerable Lecturer" in bold, obnoxious font. A folded card leaned against it: "Thanks for putting up with my debates! - Kevin." Higgins felt a vein throb steadily at his right temple. Kevin had never debated; he had merely interrupted, talked over female classmates, and derailed complex lectures with crude internet conspiracies. For two semesters, Higgins was forced by the dean to tolerate the disruptive behavior because of his family’s donor status. Higgins picked up the ceramic mug. His grip was so tight his knuckles resembled polished marble. He didn't say a word to the arriving freshmen. He simply extended his arm over the heavy cast-iron radiator and released his fingers. The mug exploded into sharp white fragments. Higgins stepped over them.

The athletic department forwarded my mail. Inside the box sat a gleaming football signed by a newly drafted NFL rookie, Tommy Carver. The note read, "Glad you couldn't keep me off the field." The blood drained from my face, rushing straight to my clenched fists. Tommy had viciously assaulted a classmate in my biology lab. I reported it, but the football coach and principal buried the report to keep their star quarterback eligible for the championship. I had resigned in protest. I stared at his scrawled signature, my breathing growing fast and loud. I grabbed heavy fabric shears from my desk, jammed the sharp metal tip directly into the leather laces, and ripped the football open. The internal bladder hissed, deflating into a useless shell.

Inside the courier box was a high-resolution replica of an Ivy League diploma. A sticky note on the glass read: "Proof that your failing grade didn't matter. - Sarah." Mrs. Gable’s eyes narrowed into sharp slits. Sarah had stolen the final exam answer key from Gable’s locked desk. When caught, Sarah’s wealthy parents threatened a massive defamation lawsuit, forcing the school to magically change her grade to an A. Gable’s breath pushed through her teeth in a sharp, hissing sound. Her entire body went rigid. She grabbed the heavy oak frame with both hands, lifted it high above her head, and brought it down violently against the edge of her metal desk. The glass shattered in an explosion of jagged shards, slicing a thin red line across her cheek. She didn't even flinch.

Inside the envelope on my windshield was a fifty-dollar gift card for an auto glass repair shop and a poorly spelled note: "My bad about your car back in 09. - Derek." My vision swam, red hot and pulsing. In 2009, Derek had taken a baseball bat to my vintage Mustang simply because I had assigned him weekend detention for skipping class. I had spent two years restoring that vehicle, and he had treated it like a junkyard piñata. Now, fifteen years later, he thought a measly fifty bucks would settle the score. My jaw clamped down so hard a sharp pain shot through my temples. I marched back into the school building, shoved my way into the staff kitchen, and jammed the plastic card into the microwave. I hit start, watching the plastic bubble, spark, and melt into a black puddle.

The crumpled yellow paper lay on the kitchen island, its edges sharp against the polished marble Elias had installed himself. He stared at the typed words—Notice to Vacate—until the letters blurred into a meaningless black smear. His jaw locked so tight his teeth ground together with a faint, chalky squeak. Three years of never missing a payment, three years of fixing the leaky pipes the landlord ignored, and this was the thanks he got? Elias snatched his coffee mug from the counter and hurled it into the stainless steel sink. It shattered with a violent, satisfying crash, ceramic shards ricocheting against the metal. He leaned over the basin, his breath coming in hot, ragged bursts, gripping the counter's edge until his knuckles turned completely white beneath the harsh fluorescent lights. Let them try to drag him out. He wasn't leaving without a fight.

I read the letter three times before my brain actually processed the formal, sterile language. Thirty days. I shoved the paper into my pocket, the crinkling sound grating against my eardrums. My heart hammered against my ribs like a trapped bird trying to break free. I marched down the hallway, my boots stomping against the threadbare carpet, straight toward the manager’s office. Every step amplified the burning sensation rising in my chest. I slammed my palm against the frosted glass of her door, the heavy thud rattling the frame. "Open up, Sheila!" I barked, my voice cracking at the edges. I could see her silhouette freeze inside. She thought she could just price me out of my home of ten years to build her luxury condos? My hands shook violently as I waited, my fingernails digging sharp crescent moons into my palms.

The eviction notice was taped to the door with cheap, peeling masking tape. Clara ripped it off, taking a chip of the fading green paint with it. She stood in the damp hallway, staring at the thirty-day deadline. A hot flush crept up her neck, spreading across her cheeks and burning behind her eyes. She crumpled the cheap paper into a tight ball, squeezing it until her joints ached. After all the delays on the heating repairs this winter, after she had frozen through January, Mr. Henderson had the absolute audacity to kick her out. She kicked the baseboard, her heavy work boot leaving a deep scuff mark on the wood. The sting in her toes barely registered. She dialed his number, pacing the short span of the corridor. When it went straight to voicemail, she let out a guttural scream that echoed off the peeling wallpaper.

The neat, typed font felt like a personal insult. Please vacate the premises by the 15th. I stared at the paper, my vision narrowing to a tunnel. I grabbed my keys off the hook and threw them at the wall; they hit the plaster with a sharp smack and clattered to the floor, leaving a small dent. I’ve paid on time every month since 2019, even during the layoffs. Now, because a greedy corporation bought the building, I’m out on the street? A sudden, intense heat radiated from my core. I paced the length of my tiny living room, my breath whistling through my nose. Every object I looked at—the sofa I moved in, the curtains I sewed—felt tainted. I wanted to rip the wallpaper down in strips. Let them renovate a shell. I grabbed the notice and shredded it into tiny pieces.

Marcus sat on the porch steps, the eviction notice trembling in his left hand. His right hand was curled into a fist, resting heavily on his knee. He stared out at the overgrown lawn he had mowed just yesterday, a bitter taste flooding the back of his throat. The new owners hadn't even bothered to call; they just slapped a cold legal document on his mailbox. He stood up abruptly, the wooden stair groaning under his sudden weight. He marched over to the mailbox, grabbed the wooden post, and gave it a violent shake. It rattled loosely in the dry dirt. He wanted to uproot it entirely, to smash the rusted metal box against the pavement until it was nothing but jagged shards. Instead, he kicked his heavy work boot into the dirt, sending a cloud of dry dust billowing into the sweltering afternoon air.

I found the letter slipped under my door like a coward's whisper. As my eyes scanned the black ink, my vision swam. Termination of lease. The paper snapped between my rigid fingers. For five years, I tolerated the mold in the bathroom and the upstairs neighbor who practiced tap dancing at midnight. I kept quiet. I played by the rules. I marched into the kitchen, grabbed the heavy iron skillet off the stove, and slammed it down onto the stovetop. The metal-on-metal clang rang in my ears, but it wasn't loud enough to drown out the rush of blood roaring in my head. My chest heaved. I spun around, glaring at the peeling paint on the ceiling. I dialed the management office, my finger stabbing the keypad so hard my nail bent. "Put the owner on the phone," I snarled into the receiver. "Now."

The bold red lettering on the envelope caught Jin’s eye immediately. Inside lay the formal demand to leave. He dropped his briefcase to the floor with a heavy thud, oblivious to the fact that it toppled over. His jaw set like stone as he read the words. He had practically rebuilt the deck out back with his own money, and now they were tossing him aside to flip the property. He tore the notice in half, the crisp tearing sound echoing in the silent apartment. He tore it again, and again, until it was nothing but jagged flakes, and hurled them violently into the air like toxic snow. His pulse pounded in his temples, a relentless drumbeat. He stormed into the bedroom, grabbed an empty cardboard box from the closet, and hurled it forcefully against the windowpanes, praying the glass would shatter and match the chaos inside him.

The official seal on the document mocked me from the kitchen table. Eviction. The word tasted like bile in my mouth. I braced my hands against the wooden edge of the table, leaning my weight over it as if trying to crush the furniture beneath me. A hot prickling sensation crawled up my neck. They were converting the lofts into tech offices. After we artists revitalized this entire block, making it desirable, the developers swoop in to harvest the crop we sowed. I grabbed a thick black marker from the cup holder, uncapped it with my teeth, and pressed the tip onto the landlord’s pristine letter. I slashed a thick, dark line diagonally across the page, the ink bleeding through the cheap paper and staining the wood beneath. I didn't care about the table anymore. I didn't care about anything except making them pay.

Maya’s breath hitched, but not from sadness. The document in her hand felt like a lit match, and the fire was rapidly spreading up her arm. Notice to Quit. She glared at the signature of the property manager—the same man who had smiled to her face yesterday and complimented her window garden. Her teeth ground together, producing a sharp ache in her jaw. Without thinking, she grabbed the nearest terracotta pot from the windowsill. She hoisted it high above her head and brought it crashing down onto the hardwood floor. Soil exploded in every direction, splattering against the baseboards, while jagged pieces of orange clay skittered across the room. Her breathing came fast and shallow, her chest rising and falling in sharp jerks. She stomped her heel into the largest piece of clay, crushing it to dust under her full weight.

The bright pink slip of paper was wedged into my doorframe. It caught the afternoon sun, almost glowing with its toxic message. Fourteen days to vacate. I ripped it free, taking a splinter of wood with it. My blood temperature seemed to spike instantly, bringing a flush of heat to my face. I walked straight down the driveway, my strides long and aggressive, zeroing in on the landlord's shiny new Mercedes parked at the curb. The vehicle he bought with our exorbitant rent. My hand closed tightly around my metal keychain, the jagged edge of my house key pressing painfully into my skin. I stopped inches from the glossy black paint job, my chest heaving. The reflection staring back at me had narrowed eyes and lips pressed into a bloodless, thin line. I raised my fist, the key protruding sharply between my knuckles, ready to strike.

Arthur stood perfectly still in the center of his living room, the court-ordered eviction summons held loosely in one hand. The silence of the house was deafening, save for the rapid, heavy thudding of his own heart. The corporate stamp at the bottom of the page was practically a sneer. A vein throbbed visibly at his temple. He slowly walked over to the antique grandfather clock, an heirloom the landlord had repeatedly offered to buy for a fraction of its worth. Arthur’s grip tightened around the heavy brass candlestick on the mantle. His knuckles drained of color. With a sudden, explosive burst of motion, he swung the candlestick laterally, sweeping every framed photo and decorative plate off the mantle. The resulting clatter of breaking glass and splintering wood filled the room, but Arthur didn't flinch. He just stood there, breathing heavily through his nose, jaw locked tightly.

I stared at the letter on my phone screen, the email from the management company glaring back at me. Lease termination. I gripped the phone so tightly I was surprised the screen didn't crack under my thumbs. A sharp, burning sensation lodged tight in my throat. I stood up from my desk chair so fast it tipped backward and crashed onto the floor. I didn't bother picking it up. I paced the length of the room, my footsteps heavy, thudding with enough force to make the floorboards groan. How dare they? After the plumbing disaster I paid for out of pocket? I let out a sharp, humorless bark of laughter that echoed off the walls. I grabbed the edge of my desk, my muscles trembling, wanting nothing more than to flip the heavy wood over and watch my monitor shatter into a million jagged pieces.

Marcus squeezed the flimsy paper of his boarding pass until his knuckles turned white. The glowing red "DELAYED: 4 HOURS" on the terminal monitor mocked him from above. By the time he landed, Sarah would already be walking down the aisle, her brother's designated seat conspicuously empty in the front row. He ground his teeth together so hard a sharp ache bloomed in his jaw. A laughing couple bumped into his shoulder, and Marcus spun around, his mouth opening to snap a vicious reprimand, but they had already moved on. He directed his glare back toward the empty tarmac, feeling a hot prickle climb up his neck. He jammed his hands deep into his pockets to stop the tremors in his fingers, visualizing the satisfying crunch of kicking his leather suitcase straight through the reinforced glass window.

I stared at the departure board until the yellow pixels blurred. "Delayed. Equipment failure." My chest tightened, a heavy pressure building behind my ribs like trapped steam. My final interview at the firm was in exactly three hours. It had taken six months of back-to-back screenings to get this sit-down, and now I was going to miss it because a bolt was loose on an aluminum wing. I paced a tight circle around my carry-on, my boots striking the carpeted floor with heavy, deliberate thuds. A chipper announcement apologized for the inconvenience over the PA system. I barked a harsh, humorless laugh, drawing nervous glances from the businessmen nearby. I dug my nails into my palms, feeling a pulse hammering relentlessly at my temples. I wanted to scream until my throat gave out, to rip the overhead monitors straight from the ceiling.

Elena stood at the gate counter, her posture rigid as steel. "You don't understand," she said, her voice dropping to a dangerous, vibrating whisper. "My daughter walks across the stage to get her diploma in two hours." The gate agent offered another practiced, hollow apology about weather patterns over Chicago. Elena’s face flushed violently. She grabbed her leather purse off the counter, her manicured nails digging deep into the expensive material. She spun away from the desk, her chest heaving with short, jagged breaths. She threw herself into a plastic waiting chair, crossing her arms so tightly it hurt. The little graduation gift box in her tote bag felt like a physical weight dragging her down. She glared at the stationary Boeing 737 through the window, wishing she could melt its engines with the sheer intensity of her gaze.

The red font on my phone screen confirmed what the garbled intercom had just announced: a five-hour delay. I jabbed the power button, plunging the screen into darkness, and shoved the device into my pocket with enough force to bruise my thigh. Today was the day. The only day the venture capitalists had agreed to sit in a room with me and hear my pitch. I marched over to the nearest coffee kiosk, my jaw set so firmly my teeth squeaked against each other. "Black coffee," I told the barista, my tone clipped and sharp enough to cut glass. When she handed me the cup, I gripped the thin cardboard sleeve, feeling the scalding heat seep into my skin. I didn't care. I squeezed the cup tighter, watching the dark liquid tremble near the brim, matching the erratic, violent thumping of my heart.

David sat completely still, staring at the text from his sister: "He’s fading. Please hurry." He looked up at the departure screen, which had just pushed his flight back another ninety minutes due to a missing flight attendant. A dark, suffocating heat rose from his stomach, flooding his chest and flushing his cheeks. He closed his eyes, his breathing sounding unnaturally loud in his own ears—harsh, ragged intakes of air through his nostrils. The man next to him was loudly chewing on potato chips, smacking his lips with every bite. David’s eyes snapped open. He turned his head slowly, locking onto the stranger with a stare so icy and intense that the man immediately stopped chewing and scooted his bag a few inches away. David swallowed hard, tasting copper, his hands curled into white-knuckled fists resting heavily on his knees.

I had not seen him in eight months. I had booked the reservation at our favorite restaurant three weeks ago. Now, I was trapped in Terminal B, watching the rain hammer relentlessly against the glass. "Due to air traffic control restrictions," the automated voice droned. I unzipped my jacket with a sharp, forceful tug, feeling a sudden, stifling heat prickling across my skin. I began to pace the length of the waiting area, my strides long and aggressive, pivoting sharply at the end of the row. I pulled out my phone to text him the news, but my thumbs were trembling so much I kept hitting the wrong keys. With a sharp hiss of breath, I locked the screen and tossed the phone roughly onto my duffel bag. It bounced and clattered to the floor, but I didn't bother picking it up.

Chloe’s heel tapped a frantic, staccato rhythm against the linoleum. Tap-tap-tap-tap-tap. The judge had been clear: 9:00 AM sharp for the final adoption decree, or they would have to reschedule for next quarter. The pilot had just announced a mechanical issue requiring a new plane. Chloe stood abruptly, her chair screeching in protest. She marched toward the window, her lips pressed into a thin, bloodless line. She crossed her arms, her fingers digging deeply into her own biceps. Every time a maintenance worker ambled casually past the nose of the plane, a fresh wave of heat flared in her chest. How could they move so slowly? She wanted to march out onto the tarmac, grab them by their neon vests, and shake them. She bit the inside of her cheek until she tasted the sharp, metallic tang of blood.

Three years of writing, recasting, and begging for funding, and I was going to miss opening night. The curtain would rise in New York, and I would be stuck in a plastic chair in O'Hare. I stared at the gate agent who had just delivered the news of the staffing shortage. "Are you kidding me?" My voice echoed louder than I intended, sharp and grating. The agent blinked, offering a flimsy voucher. I didn't reach for it. I turned on my heel and stalked toward the far end of the concourse, the muscles in my neck pulled taut like piano wires. I found a secluded corner near the restrooms and kicked the base of a concrete pillar with the toe of my boot. Pain shot up my leg, but I welcomed it. It gave the churning, explosive energy in my chest somewhere to go.

Sam stared down at the crumpled program in his hands. His son’s name was printed in bold: First Recital. The announcement over the intercom about a sudden air traffic control hold was still echoing through the concourse. Sam shoved the crinkled paper into his briefcase, yanking the zipper closed with a vicious jerk that snagged the fabric. He let out a loud, guttural groan, tilting his head back to glare at the ceiling tiles. A woman beside him bumped his elbow with her oversized tote bag, offering a breezy, indifferent apology. Sam’s jaw clenched so tightly a muscle ticked visibly in his cheek. He didn't say a word, just turned to her, his nostrils flared, breathing heavily through his nose. He grabbed his briefcase handle, his knuckles popping, and stormed off down the corridor without looking back.

I had planned my best friend’s surprise thirtieth birthday party down to the last confetti cannon. Now, I was stuck on the tarmac in Atlanta, waiting for a gate to open up, missing my connection entirely. The seatbelt sign glowed a mocking neon orange. I gripped the armrests of my seat, digging my fingernails into the worn upholstery. The man next to me cleared his throat and asked if I was alright. I whipped my head toward him, my eyes narrowed to slits. "I'm perfectly fine," I snapped, the words clipping off my tongue like snapping twigs. He visibly recoiled, sinking deeper into his own chair. I turned back to face the seat in front of me, glaring a hole into the woven fabric, my heart hammering a rapid, violent rhythm against my ribs as heat flooded my face and neck.

The closing agent had explicitly stated that both signatures were needed by 3:00 PM today, or the sellers were pulling out. The departure board blinked, updating the delay from one hour to three. Arthur stopped dead in his tracks. His briefcase slipped from his grasp, hitting the floor with a heavy thud. He stood completely rigid, staring at the board as the blood roared loudly in his ears. The terminal around him felt like it was closing in. He squeezed his eyes shut, exhaling a long, trembling breath through his teeth that sounded remarkably like a hiss. He bent down, snatching the handle of his bag, and hauled it up with unnecessary force. Without a word to his traveling companion, Arthur marched toward the airport bar, his footsteps echoing like hammer strikes against the polished stone floor.

My wife was running the Boston Marathon, and I was supposed to be at the finish line holding our daughter. Instead, a snow squall had grounded every flight out of Denver. I stood by the massive floor-to-ceiling windows, watching the snowflakes lazily drift down onto the wings of our stationary jet. "Unbelievable," I muttered, my voice tight and strained. I gripped my phone, pressing my thumb against the screen so hard the LCD colors warped around my fingerprint. I wanted to hurl the device into the reinforced glass. I wanted to tear the departure screens from their mounts. I paced back to my seat, my chest rising and falling in shallow, rapid breaths. When the flight attendant passed by offering complementary water, I shot her a glare so blistering she actually took a half-step backward before hurrying down the aisle.

I dragged the last cardboard box into the room still plastered with glow-in-the-dark stars. Before I could even drop it, Mom was at the doorway. "You should unpack the sweaters first, sweetie, or they'll wrinkle." My jaw locked instantly. I squeezed the box cutter in my hand until the plastic casing dug sharply into my palm. "I know how to unpack my own clothes," I said, my voice coming out in a clipped, flat monotone. She fluttered around, adjusting the curtains I had literally just closed. The heat climbed up my neck, settling right behind my eyes. I dropped the box. It hit the hardwood floor with a loud, reverberating thud that made her jump. "I'll do it later," I muttered, pushing past her into the narrow hallway and letting the bedroom door shut behind me with a solid, echoing crack.

Elias dragged his suitcase up the porch steps, the wheels catching on every wooden slat. "Well, look who finally decided the real world was too tough," his father said from the porch swing, not looking up from his tablet. Elias stopped. The handle of the suitcase groaned under his white-knuckled grip. A thick, heavy pulse hammered loudly in his ears. "I lost my job, Dad. The whole department got downsized," Elias said, each syllable snapping off his tongue like brittle twigs. His father simply hummed, finally turning a page on his screen. Elias felt the muscles in his back pull taut, hard as steel cables. He stared at the back of his father’s thinning head, his breathing growing shallow and fast. Without another word, he kicked the front door open, the heavy wood rebounding off the wall with a thunderous strike.

The kitchen smelled like pot roast, a scent that immediately made my stomach churn with claustrophobia. I placed the specialty groceries I’d bought on the counter, turning my back for just a moment to wash my hands. When I looked back, Mom was already sorting through the canvas bags, sliding my expensive oat milk into the back of the pantry and pulling out her whole milk. "You don't need this diet nonsense here," she chirped. I gripped the edge of the granite sink, the cold stone digging under my fingernails. My teeth ground together so hard my temples ached. "Leave my things alone," I hissed, snatching the carton from her hands with enough force to slosh the liquid inside. I shoved past her, taking the stairs two at a time, my heavy footsteps shaking the framed family portraits on the wall.

Maya sat at the small kitchen table, staring at the mail spread out before her. The envelope from her credit card company had a jagged tear across the top. "It was an accident," her mother offered lightly from the stove, stirring a pot of soup. "I thought it was mine." Maya’s chest rose and fell in rapid, jerky motions. She pressed her lips together into a thin, bloodless line. She picked up the torn envelope, her hands shaking so severely the paper vibrated. "My name is in bold letters right on the front," Maya stated, her voice dropping an octave. She crumpled the envelope into a tight ball, the sound of crinkling paper deafening in the quiet room. Before her mother could offer another flimsy excuse, Maya threw the crushed paper hard against the refrigerator door and marched out of the room.

"Are you going out dressed like that?" Dad asked, blocking the front hallway. I paused with my hand hovering over the doorknob. I was thirty-two years old, wearing a standard button-down and jeans, yet I felt twelve all over again. A sudden, searing heat bloomed in my chest. I balled my free hand into a fist, pressing it firmly against my thigh to keep it from trembling. "I'm meeting friends," I replied through gritted teeth. "Just be back by eleven," he said, adjusting his glasses. "We lock the deadbolt at eleven." I closed my eyes for a fraction of a second, drawing in a breath that flared my nostrils. Instead of arguing, I spun the deadbolt loudly, wrenched the front door open, and pulled it shut behind me with a jarring slam that rattled the porch light glass.

The drone of the vacuum cleaner directly outside his bedroom door began at exactly seven in the morning. David stared at the ceiling, the familiar floral wallpaper mocking his return. The machine banged deliberately against the baseboards—thud, thud, thud. He threw his blankets off, swinging his legs over the side of the twin mattress. His jaw clicked as he clamped his mouth shut. Striding to the door, he yanked it open, ripping it from his mother's grasp as she tried to vacuum the threshold. She blinked at him innocently. "Oh, did I wake you?" David didn't answer. He reached down, grabbed the power cord from the wall outlet, and yanked it out with a sharp snap. The vacuum died with a pathetic whine. He retreated into his room, throwing his heavy body back onto the bed and shoving a pillow over his face.

I set up my dual monitors on the tiny desk crammed into the corner of the living room. It was the only place with decent Wi-Fi. Just as I unmuted myself to speak on the conference call, the television blared to life with the deafening theme song of a daytime game show. I whipped my head around. My dad was settling into his recliner, remote in hand. I muted my microphone, my fingers striking the keyboard with enough force to rattle the monitors. "Dad, I told you I have a presentation at noon," I whispered harshly, my neck burning. "It's my house, and it's my TV time," he replied, turning the volume up another notch. I dug my nails into my palms until crescent-shaped indentations formed in the skin. Snapping my laptop shut, I grabbed it and marched out to the garage.

Chloe dumped her laundry basket on the linoleum floor of the utility room. When she reached for the detergent, she found her mother already pulling Chloe's dark clothes from the washer. "I'm doing these on hot, they smell like that city smog," her mother said. Chloe froze. "Those are delicates. They’ll shrink," she said, her voice tight and constrained. "Nonsense, I've been doing laundry since before you were born." Chloe’s shoulders hiked up toward her ears. Her breathing grew audible, harsh and ragged in the small space. Without warning, she lunged forward, sweeping her arm across the folding table. A stack of neatly folded towels tumbled to the floor, followed by a plastic spray bottle that bounced and clattered. Chloe stared hard at the mess, chest heaving, then turned on her heel, leaving her mother standing in stunned silence.

I walked into my old bedroom to find that my mattress had been pushed against the wall to make room for a massive, bulky treadmill. "We didn't think you'd be coming back," Mom said from the hallway, offering a tight smile. I dropped my duffel bag. It hit the floor with a heavy thud. I stared at the treadmill, a monstrous hunk of black plastic and metal sitting right where my desk used to be. A hot prickling sensation crawled over my scalp. My hands formed tight fists at my sides. "Where am I supposed to put my things?" I asked, my voice dangerously quiet. "Oh, you can use the closet in the guest room," she waved dismissively. I stepped forward and delivered a swift, brutal kick to the treadmill's heavy base. Pain shot up my foot, but I welcomed the sharp distraction.

Marcus sat at the dining table, staring at the single scoop of mashed potatoes his mother had deposited onto his plate. "You need to watch your portions now that you aren't playing college sports," she noted casually. Marcus gripped his fork. He pressed the tines into the ceramic plate, the metal screeching against the surface. His father looked up, frowning, but Marcus didn't stop. He pressed harder, the fork bending slightly under the pressure. A vein throbbed visibly at his temple. He pushed his chair back abruptly, the wooden legs loudly scraping against the tile floor. "I’ll buy my own dinner," he said, each word punched out from the back of his throat. He tossed the fork onto the plate with a loud clatter, grabbed his car keys from the counter, and marched out into the freezing night air.

The lease was broken, my bank account was drained, and now I was staring at the floral wallpaper of my childhood home. I was trying to fit my king-sized sheets onto a squeaky twin bed when Dad walked in holding a clipboard. "I've drafted a chore schedule," he announced, tapping a pen against the metal clip. "Since you're living rent-free." I stopped pulling the fitted sheet. My heart drummed a rapid, violent rhythm against my ribs. I snatched the clipboard from his hand, my grip so tight my knuckles turned a stark, bony white. I didn't even look at the paper. I just stared directly into his eyes, my jaw clamped shut so intensely that my teeth ached. I ripped the paper from the metal clip, tore it straight down the middle, and let the pieces flutter onto the bare mattress.

Sarah found her vintage armoire entirely cleared out, her carefully curated wardrobe shoved into cardboard boxes in the hallway. "I needed the space for my sewing supplies," her mother called from the living room. Sarah stood completely still in the center of the room. Her breathing stopped entirely for a few seconds before releasing in a long, shaky hiss. She walked over to the nearest box and stared at her silk blouses crumpled thoughtlessly under heavy denim jeans. Her vision narrowed. She grabbed the edge of the box, her fingernails biting into the corrugated cardboard. With a sudden, explosive heave, she upended the entire box in the hallway. Clothes spilled everywhere in a chaotic heap. She didn't bother looking at the mess. She just stepped deliberately over a tangled silk blouse, her heavy boots crushing the delicate fabric as she walked out.

I stared at the barista’s forearm as he handed me my latte. There it was—my charcoal owl, down to the skewed feather on the left wing. The piece that took me eighty hours to perfect, the piece I poured my late grandmother's memory into, now permanently etched onto a stranger making minimum wage. My fingernails dug so deeply into my palms that they broke the skin. "Nice ink," I managed to choke out, the words tasting like battery acid. "Thanks," he grinned. "Found it on Pinterest. Cool, right?" I snatched the cup from his hand, the hot liquid sloshing over the plastic lid and scalding my knuckles. I didn't care about the burn. My heart pounded a deafening rhythm against my ribs as I crushed the cardboard sleeve, turned on my heel, and marched out, leaving the door to slam violently against its chimes.

Elias paced the convention floor, his jaw locked so tight his teeth ached. A crowd gathered around Booth 44, admiring a rising star. Elias shoved past a tall man to see the display. Front and center was a photograph of a back piece: Elias’s custom geometric wolf. His breath hitched, coming out in a sharp hiss. He grabbed the edge of the display table, his knuckles turning stark white. The needle buzzed nearby, a mocking, high-pitched whine. "Did you design this?" Elias asked, his voice dropping an octave, cold and razor-edged. The artist looked up, wiping ink from a gloved hand. "Yeah, custom flash." Elias’s vision narrowed to a tunnel. He swept his arm across the table, sending heavy plastic ink bottles clattering across the concrete floor, before turning and stalking toward the exit, his blood roaring in his ears.

The sun beat down on the sand, but I felt utterly cold as the woman laid out her towel next to mine. Across her shoulder blade rested my mural. The exact sweeping koi fish I painted on the side of the downtown community center. The one I wasn't paid for. I sat up abruptly, sending a spray of sand over my beach bag. My chest heaved, pulling in jagged, shallow breaths. "Where did you get that?" I demanded, my shadow falling over her face. She blinked behind oversized sunglasses. "A guy in Miami. Do you mind? You're blocking my sun." I gritted my teeth, a violent heat rushing up my neck. I wanted to grab the nearest bottle of sunscreen and hurl it into the ocean. Instead, I violently shoved my belongings into my tote, snapping the handle, and kicked up sand as I stormed away.

Clara stared at the glowing monitor, the blue light reflecting in her widened eyes. The Instagram post had fifty thousand likes. The influencer was posing in a mirror, showing off her new rib tattoo. It was Clara’s deeply personal sketch of her childhood home, vines and all. A high, sharp ringing echoed in Clara’s ears. She pressed the heels of her hands against her temples, squeezing her eyes shut as her pulse hammered against her skull. She snatched her phone off the desk, her thumb jabbing the screen with brutal force to draft a message, then deleting it just as viciously. Her breath rasped in the quiet studio. With a sudden, explosive motion, she grabbed her sketchpad from the desk and hurled it against the brick wall. The spine cracked, scattering pages across the floor like dead leaves, while Clara stood trembling in the center of the room.

I clung to the overhead rail on the crowded L train, staring at the back of the neck of the man sitting directly in front of me. My stomach twisted into a tight, sickening knot. Tattooed right beneath his hairline was the exact emblem I had designed for my sister’s gravestone. The intertwining lotus and crescent moon. A deeply private tribute, stolen. My jaw clamped down hard enough to send a shooting pain through my temples. I leaned forward, my breathing heavy, hot air hitting the stranger's collar. I wanted to reach out and claw the skin right off his neck. My fingers twitched, curling into rigid claws by my sides. When the train screeched to a halt, I deliberately dropped my heavy steel toe boot onto the man's pristine sneaker, stepping down with all my weight before shoving my way through the sliding doors.

The gallery opening was supposed to be Julian’s triumph. Then the art collector walked in, wearing a sleeveless evening gown. Displayed on her bicep was a perfect, permanent replica of Julian's centerpiece painting—the very painting hanging ten feet away. Julian's champagne flute snapped in his grip, the delicate crystal shattering. A shard sliced his thumb, but he didn't feel it. A dark, suffocating heat rose in his chest, flushing his cheeks crimson. He grabbed a cloth napkin, wrapping his bleeding hand in tight, punishing binds. The collector spotted him and waved enthusiastically, pointing proudly at her arm. Julian’s eyes narrowed into dark slits. He strode directly past her, intentionally clipping her shoulder with enough force to make her stumble, and walked straight out the front doors into the freezing rain, leaving his own exhibition behind without a backward glance.

The steam in the locker room felt suffocating, but it was nothing compared to the fire burning in my veins. The guy pulling off his shirt two benches down was sporting a massive chest piece. It was the comic book character I created, the intellectual property I was currently fighting a massive corporation for in a grueling lawsuit. He was parading it around like a cheap novelty. I slammed my locker door shut with a deafening metal crash that echoed off the damp tiles. The guy flinched, looking over at me. "Problem, man?" he asked. I took a step toward him, my hands balled into fists so tight my forearms cramped. Every muscle in my body was coiled like a spring ready to snap. "Take it off," I hissed, the words slipping through gritted teeth. I didn't care that my demand made absolutely no sense.

Maya’s date rolled up his sleeves as the appetizer arrived, revealing an intricate sleeve of watercolor flora. Maya stopped chewing. She swallowed hard, the bread suddenly tasting like ash. The weeping willow on his forearm was unmistakable. It was the exact commission piece she had done for her ex-boyfriend, the man who had ruined her life three years ago. Her date tapped the ink. "My buddy does these. Cool, huh?" Maya stared at the willow branches. Her chest rose and fell in rapid, shallow jerks. She gripped her butter knife, pressing the dull edge into her napkin until the fabric tore. The ambient chatter of the restaurant faded into a high-pitched buzz in her ears. She stood up abruptly, her chair screeching violently against the hardwood floor. "I have to go," she clipped out, tossing a twenty onto the table and marching out into the night.

I handed back the midterms, pausing at Jeremy’s desk. As he reached for the paper, his cuff slipped up. There, etched in sloppy black lines, was the exact linocut print I had debuted at the faculty show last month. The one I sold exclusive rights to. My breath stopped dead in my throat. I stared at his wrist, a hot prickling sensation spreading across my scalp. "Like it, professor?" Jeremy smirked. "Got it done at a house party for twenty bucks." The stack of remaining exams crumpled in my hands as my fingers spasmed. I wanted to flip his desk over. I wanted to scream until my vocal cords shredded. Instead, I leaned over him, my face inches from his, my voice a dangerous, trembling whisper. "Get out of my classroom." I pointed at the heavy oak door, my arm rigid and shaking. "Now."

The bass thumped through the floorboards of the dive bar, but Liam couldn't hear the music. His gaze was locked on the lead singer of the local opener. Stamped proudly on the frontman's neck was a vividly colored geometric raven. Liam’s original digital art. The piece he sold prints of to pay his rent. Liam pushed through the sweaty crowd, his elbows jabbing into ribs without apology. The heat in his chest was a living, breathing monster threatening to claw its way up his throat. He reached the edge of the stage just as the song ended. He grabbed the microphone stand, violently yanking it toward him, bringing the singer to his knees in surprise. "Where did you steal that?" Liam roared over the feedback, his face flushed dark red, a vein pulsing wildly in his temple as security guards rushed from the wings.

My cousin pulled down the collar of her shirt to show my aunt her new ink. I sat on the couch, my tea frozen halfway to my mouth. It was my mother's portrait. The abstract cubist sketch I drew the night she passed away. I hadn’t shared it with anyone except the family group chat. The porcelain cup shattered as my grip crushed it, spilling scalding liquid over my jeans. I didn't brush it away. I stood up, my legs moving mechanically. "Oh, do you like it?" she asked, oblivious. "I thought it was just a cool abstract face!" My ears roared. I grabbed my car keys from the bowl, hurling them against the front door where they left a deep gouge in the wood. I stormed past my terrified relatives, slamming the door so hard the living room windows rattled in their frames.

Dr. Evans rolled up his sleeve to check his watch, and Chloe’s heart slammed into her ribs. Wrapping around his forearm was her precise, stippled illustration of an anatomical heart intertwined with barbed wire. It was the centerpiece of her senior thesis, unpublished anywhere except her locked portfolio site. Her pulse throbbed behind her eyes. She stood up from the examination table, the paper tearing harshly beneath her. "Is something wrong?" the doctor asked. Chloe’s hands trembled so violently she had to shove them deep into her jacket pockets. Her face burned hot, and a bitter, metallic taste flooded her mouth from biting the inside of her cheek. She snatched her purse from the chair, kicking the metal trash can across the small room with a vicious clatter, and marched into the hallway, leaving the bewildered physician staring at her dust.

Elias stared up at the glowing billboard overlooking the highway, his fingernails digging crescent moons into his palms. High above the traffic, his private digital painting—a deeply personal piece he had created during a severe depressive episode—beamed down as an advertisement for a wellness app. He hadn't posted it anywhere but his locked, anonymous blog. His breathing grew shallow and rapid, each exhale a sharp hiss escaping his clenched teeth. The hot blood rushed to his ears, drowning out the honking cars. He dropped his coffee cup, letting the hot liquid splatter across his boots without blinking. His jaw set so hard it ached, Elias pulled his phone from his pocket, his thumb jabbing the screen with enough force to crack the glass as he dialed his lawyer's number, his eyes never leaving the stolen strokes of his own suffering.

The bell above the gallery door chimed a cheerful note that felt like a slap to my face. Sitting right in the center of the window display was my unfinished clay torso. I had left it covered under a damp towel in the shared studio just last night. My chest tightened until it felt like my ribs might snap. I marched toward the pedestal, my heavy boots thudding against the hardwood floor in a harsh rhythm. The gallery owner emerged from the back, offering a polite smile that made my stomach churn with acid. "Beautiful piece, isn't it?" she asked. I planted my feet, my muscles pulled taut as bowstrings. My voice came out as a low, dangerous gravel that I barely recognized as my own. "Take it down," I hissed, staring a hole right through her pleasant expression. "Right now."

Mia’s grip on the damp party flyer was so tight her knuckles were completely white. Pinned to the community bulletin board was her face—a raw, vulnerable self-portrait she had taken entirely for herself, now overlaid with neon text advertising a frat basement rave. Someone had lifted it straight off her password-protected hard drive. A hot prickling sensation crawled up the back of her neck. She ripped the paper from the corkboard, leaving a torn corner pinned behind. The harsh fluorescent lights of the hallway seemed to pulse with the hammering rhythm of her heartbeat. She crumpled the glossy paper into a tight, jagged ball, squeezing it until her joints throbbed. She turned on her heel, her boots slamming against the linoleum as she headed straight for the fraternity house, her eyes narrowed into sharp, dark slits.

I sat frozen in the front row of the fashion show, my jaw locked so tight my teeth ground together with an audible scrape. Down the runway walked a model wearing a jacket adorned with the exact intricate, asymmetrical embroidery I had spent three months designing in my private sketchbook—the same sketchbook that had gone missing from the staff breakroom last week. The lead designer stepped out to take his bow, beaming at the thunderous applause. A roaring heat climbed up my throat. I stood up abruptly, knocking my folding chair backward. It clattered loudly against the concrete floor, drawing a few startled glances, but I didn't care. My hands shook violently as I pushed my way through the crowd of clapping socialites, marching directly toward the backstage entrance with a single, burning focus.

Julian stared through the glass of the rival bakery, his chest heaving with sharp, uneven breaths. Sitting proudly on the top tier of the display fridge was his exact wedding cake design: cascading sugar orchids with a unique geometric gold-leaf base he had spent months perfecting. A small handwritten placard read, "Chef Armand's Original Creation." Julian’s face flushed a deep, mottled red. He pushed open the heavy glass door with enough force that the hinges groaned in protest. The sweet smell of vanilla and buttercream hit his nose, but it only made the sour taste in his mouth worse. Armand looked up from the counter, his smile faltering as Julian closed the distance between them in three long, heavy strides. Julian slammed his open palms flat against the glass counter, making the display plates rattle violently.

The university library was supposed to be my sanctuary, but the blood pounding behind my eyes made the quiet room spin. Framed beautifully on the "Student Spotlight" wall were three pages torn directly out of my leather-bound journal. My most intimate, painful poems about grief were now public exhibits. My breath hitched in my throat, coming out in ragged, harsh bursts. I reached out, my fingers trembling so much I could barely grasp the wooden frame. Without a second thought, I yanked it off the wall. The wire snapped, and the heavy frame crashed onto a reading table, shattering the glass front. A librarian gasped, rushing over with widened eyes, but I just stood there, glaring at the broken glass, my chest rising and falling rapidly as I waited for whoever had done this to show their face.

Trey stopped dead in his tracks in the middle of the crowded mall. Displayed prominently on a rack of cheap, mass-produced t-shirts was his signature tag—the complex, sprawling mural he had spent ten hours painting under the bridge, scrubbed of its brick background and printed on neon cotton. The kiosk vendor was actively handing one to a teenage customer. Trey’s jaw shifted, the muscles in his face twitching. He marched over, ignoring the shoppers he bumped into along the way. His breathing sounded like a freight train in his own ears. Without a word, he grabbed the display shirt by the collar and yanked it off the mannequin, the plastic snapping loudly. The vendor shouted in protest, but Trey leaned over the counter, his eyes burning into the man’s face, holding the stolen fabric in a white-knuckled fist.

The champagne turned to ash in my mouth. Projected onto the massive screen at the front of the ballroom were the blueprints for the new eco-center. My blueprints. The ones the senior partner had explicitly told me were "too ambitious" and "unusable" just last month. Now, he was standing at the podium, graciously accepting a thunderous round of applause for his "visionary genius." My grip tightened around the stem of my crystal flute. The thin glass let out a sharp crack, snapping completely and slicing into my thumb, but I barely registered the sting. Drops of blood and spilled champagne dripped onto the pristine white tablecloth. I dropped the broken pieces, my gaze locked onto the smiling man on the stage. I pushed my chair back, the legs screeching against the tile, and walked purposefully toward the microphone.

Elena’s breath caught as she turned the corner toward the diner’s restrooms. Hanging crookedly above a scuffed wainscoting was her oil canvas. It was the portrait of her late mother, the one she had left drying in her landlord's basement. Now, it was being used to cover a hole in the plaster, right next to the kitchen door. The smell of stale grease seemed to coat the back of her throat. Her hands balled into tight fists, her carefully manicured nails digging deep into her palms. She stared at the splatters of ketchup staining the bottom left corner of her mother’s painted cheek. Her vision narrowed to a pinpoint. Elena spun around, storming back into the main dining area. She marched straight past the startled waitresses, heading directly for the manager's office with a heavy, stomping gait.

I stood frozen in the middle of the school gymnasium, staring at the blue ribbon pinned next to the charcoal sketch. It was the drawing I had made of the old lighthouse, the one I had hidden in my portfolio because it wasn't ready. Below it, in neat, bubbly letters, was the artist's name: my younger sister. A suffocating heat flared in my chest, radiating outward until my skin felt entirely too tight. My teeth ground together so forcefully I heard a distinct pop in my jaw. I whipped my head around, scanning the crowd of parents and students until I spotted her standing by the punch bowl, accepting congratulations with a wide grin. My breathing grew ragged. I crossed the gym floor in a blind blur, my boots hitting the polished wood like strikes on an anvil.

Marcus sat in the dim light of his bedroom, the glow of his tablet illuminating his flushed face. He had clicked a banner ad on a whim, only to find his original webcomic characters crudely animated, begging players to buy gems in a sleazy mobile game. His breath exited his nose in a sharp, sustained rush. He threw his stylus across the room; it ricocheted off the wall with a loud clatter. He stood up, knocking his rolling chair backward into his bookshelf. He began to pace the narrow strip of floorboard between his bed and desk, his hands threading roughly through his own hair, pulling at the roots. The more he looked at the screen, the harder his heart hammered against his ribs. He slammed the laptop shut, the metallic crack echoing through the silent apartment.

The blare of the television normally faded into background noise, but a specific cello melody cut through the air, freezing me in my tracks. I turned slowly. There, playing beneath a cheesy voiceover for a detergent commercial, was the symphony I had spent two years composing. The one I had only submitted to one private fellowship program. A strange, vibrating heat flooded my veins. My chest he heave up and down as I stared at the dancing cartoon soap bubbles completely trivializing my life's work. I grabbed the remote control from the coffee table, squeezing the black plastic until it groaned under the pressure. With a harsh, guttural sound tearing from my throat, I hurled the remote at the wall. It shattered into a dozen pieces, batteries rolling across the floor, but the stolen music just kept playing.

I stared at the printed roster taped to the locker room door, my eyes scanning the alphabetized list three times. My name wasn't there. A hot prickle started at the base of my neck, spreading rapidly across my shoulders. I grabbed the edge of my heavy canvas duffel bag, my knuckles turning white, and yanked it off the bench. "Hey, man, maybe next season," Coach Miller started to say, putting a hand on my shoulder. I violently shrugged off his grip, the sudden movement causing a stray puck to skitter across the linoleum. Without a word, I spun around, my cleats biting harshly into the rubber mats, and marched out into the freezing arena hallway. The heavy metal exit door slammed shut behind me with a deafening crack that echoed through the empty bleachers.

Maya’s phone screen lit up with the official email from the National Training Center. She read the single sentence thanking her for her time, her jaw tightening until her teeth ached. She tossed the phone onto her bed, but a second later, she snatched it back up and hurled it against the opposite wall. The screen splintered into a spiderweb of jagged lines. She stood in the center of her bedroom, her chest heaving as she stared at the row of glittering medals hanging from her mirror. With a sharp, sudden motion, she swept her arm across her dresser, sending water bottles, chalk blocks, and framed photographs crashing to the hardwood floor. Her breathing came in short, jagged gasps, the blood roaring so loudly in her ears that she couldn't even hear her mother knocking tentatively on the bedroom door.

The words "We decided to go in a different direction" kept replaying in my head. I gripped the leather steering wheel of my parked car until my hands cramped. I had spent six hours a day in that sweaty, windowless gym, sacrificing my entire summer while the guys who actually made the roster were out partying. A sudden, intense heat flooded my cheeks. I slammed my palm against the horn, the blaring sound slicing through the quiet parking lot. When a couple of freshmen turned to look, I locked eyes with them, glaring until they quickly looked away. I cranked the ignition, throwing the gearshift into reverse with a violent jerk. The tires screeched as I peeled out of the spot, leaving a thick, dark skid mark across the pavement of the athletic center I swore I'd never step foot in again.

Marcus stared at the Olympic Trials qualification list. His time was a fraction of a second too slow. He stood perfectly rigid at the edge of the rubber track, his spikes digging deep into the red surface. When his training partner patted his back, Marcus recoiled as if burned. He unlaced his expensive custom running shoes, the knots pulling so tight under his rough hands that the laces snapped. He didn't care. He ripped them off his feet and hurled them, one after the other, deep into the empty grassy infield. "It’s politics! Complete garbage!" he shouted to no one in particular, his voice cracking violently. He kicked the starting block out of his lane, the heavy metal apparatus clattering loudly against the concrete curb. His chest rose and fell in rapid, sharp movements as he glared at the finish line.

My goggles snapped in half between my hands. I hadn't even realized I was bending them until the hard plastic cracked, digging sharply into my palm. I sat dripping on the edge of the tiled pool deck, staring at the clipboard resting on the official's folding table. The elite squad had taken five swimmers, and I was exactly sixth. The chlorine suddenly burned my nose and throat. I stood up abruptly, knocking my water bottle into the gutter. When the head coach walked by holding a stopwatch and offered a tight-lipped nod of sympathy, I turned my back to him, staring fiercely at the lane lines. My jaw locked. I grabbed my towel, dragging it roughly across my face, and stormed toward the locker room, my wet bare feet slapping the slick tiles with a heavy, deliberate force that echoed off the high ceiling.

Leo read the text message from the academy director three times. 'Not selected for the traveling squad.' A thick, hot knot formed in his throat. He threw his shin guards onto the locker room floor, the hard plastic echoing loudly in the quiet space. He paced back and forth in front of the benches, his breathing shallow and rapid. Whenever a teammate tried to catch his eye, Leo stared straight through them, his brow heavily furrowed, his lips pressed into a thin, bloodless line. He grabbed his brand-new jersey from his locker, gripping the fabric so tightly his fingernails dug into his palms. With a sharp, guttural sound, he ripped the locker door shut. It bounced back, so he kicked it with the heel of his boot, leaving a prominent dent in the gray metal before marching out into the rain.

The minor league call-ups were posted on the bulletin board. I scanned the sheet, my heartbeat hammering violently against my ribs. Nothing. Four years in this dusty farm system, and they took the rookie who couldn't even hit a curveball. The clubhouse felt unbearably hot, the air suffocating. I grabbed my favorite ash wood bat from the rack. I didn't bother heading to the batting cage. I walked straight to the concrete pillar near the showers, raised the bat high above my shoulder, and swung with every ounce of force in my body. The wood shattered into sharp splinters with an earsplitting crack, sending pieces flying across the damp floor. The room went completely silent. I dropped the broken handle, ignoring the stinging vibration radiating up my forearms, and grabbed my keys, letting the heavy door slam behind me.

Elena stood perfectly still as the varsity roster was read aloud in the gymnasium. When the final name echoed through the microphone, her teeth ground together so hard her temples throbbed. She didn't stay for the coach's wrap-up speech. She spun on her heel and marched straight to the equipment closet. Her hands shook violently as she grabbed a practice ball. Instead of putting it in the mesh bag, she hurled it directly at the cinderblock wall. It bounced back with a sharp smack, and she caught it, winding up to throw it again, harder this time. "Elena, stop!" the assistant coach called out. She ignored the voice. She spiked the ball into the hardwood floor with a vicious strike, the echoing boom ringing out just as the rest of the girls walked in. She shouldered past them without a single glance.

The crisp morning air usually calmed me, but today, the boathouse felt like a cage. The First Eight boat had just launched, and I was left standing on the wooden dock, assigned to the reserves. I watched their perfectly synchronized oars slice through the water, a bitter taste flooding my mouth. I kicked a stray lifejacket off the edge of the dock, watching it bob uselessly in the freezing river. My fists were clenched so tightly at my sides that my nails left half-moon indentations in my palms. When the junior coach offered me an oar for the secondary boat, I simply stared at his outstretched hand. My face flushed with a blazing heat. I swatted the oar away, the heavy composite material clattering against the wooden planks, and turned on my heel, marching back up the gravel path to the parking lot.

The judges' scores flashed on the overhead monitor, confirming Julian had missed the national team by a mere point. He sat in the kiss-and-cry area, his face completely rigid. When his coach attempted to wrap a consoling arm around his shoulders, Julian abruptly stood up, shrugging the jacket to the floor. He marched past the media zone, ignoring the flashing cameras and thrust microphones. In the privacy of the dressing room, he yanked at the laces of his custom skates, his hands trembling so violently he could barely undo the knots. He ripped the right boot off and hurled it directly at the mirrored wall. The heavy steel blade struck the glass, creating a massive, jagged starburst of cracks. He stood amidst the falling shards, his chest heaving, his eyes burning as he glared at his fractured reflection.

The sponsor’s email was brief, informing me that the final spot on the tour had gone to someone five years younger. I read it while sitting in my garage, surrounded by thousands of dollars of gear. A hot, prickling sensation crawled up the back of my neck. I grabbed the carbon-fiber frame of my primary race bike, lifting it completely off the ground. For a second, I imagined smashing it onto the concrete. Instead, I forcefully threw it onto the nearest workbench, sending tools and oil cans crashing to the ground. I paced the length of the garage, kicking a pile of empty water bottles across the floor. My jaw was locked so tight it ached, my breathing coming in sharp, forceful bursts. I grabbed a wrench, gripping the cold metal until my knuckles turned stark white, staring blankly at the wall.

Chloe watched the club president pin the final tournament bracket to the clubhouse corkboard. Her name was relegated to the alternate list. Her nostrils flared as she drew in a sharp, hissing breath. She marched back to the clay courts where her expensive gear bag sat on a bench. Without unzipping it, she grabbed her favorite racket by the grip. She walked straight to the metal net post and swung the racket like a baseball bat. The composite frame cracked loudly upon impact, the high-tension strings snapping and curling like dead spiders. Not satisfied, she struck the post again, and again, until the head of the racket hung loosely by a few broken fibers. A few club members stopped to stare, their mouths open. Chloe dropped the mangled remains onto the red clay, grabbed her bag, and stomped toward the exit gates.

Coach Miller tapped the whiteboard, sliding the magnet with 'Kessler' on it from the crease to the blue line. Marcus Kessler’s hockey stick snapped in half under the sudden, crushing weight of his heavy boots. The fiberglass splintered across the rubber locker room floor. "Defense? After I carried this team to the playoffs with a .940 save percentage?" Marcus spat, his chest heaving under his pads. The vein on the side of his neck throbbed rhythmically. Coach started to explain about team needs, but Marcus had already unbuckled his chest protector, throwing it so hard against the metal lockers that the clang echoed through the damp room. He ground his jaw until his teeth squeaked, staring daggers at the blue line magnet. Six years between the pipes. Six years. He shoved past the assistant coach, kicking a water bottle across the room.

"We need you distributing from the midfield," Coach Reyes said, clapping my shoulder. I didn't say a word. I just stared straight ahead at the rain-soaked pitch, feeling the heat rise in my cheeks despite the freezing drizzle. My cleats dug so deeply into the turf I ripped up a massive chunk of grass. Seventy-two goals. I held the school scoring record. And now I was supposed to sit back and feed passes to a freshman who tripped over his own shoelaces? I bit the inside of my cheek until I tasted copper. "Sure, Coach," I managed to say, the syllables grinding out like gravel in an engine. I turned my back to him, marching to the equipment shed. Once inside, I grabbed a bag of practice balls and kicked them one by one into the concrete wall with everything I had.

The whistle blew, and Coach blew a bubble with her gum. "Chloe, slide over to the two. Let Harper run the point." Chloe’s basketball hit the hardwood with a deafening crack. She didn't pick it up, watching it bounce away toward the bleachers. She had run this offense since she was ten years old. She knew the plays before they were even drawn up. Harper didn't even know the difference between a pick-and-roll and a pick-and-pop. Chloe’s hands balled into tight fists, her fingernails digging crescent moons into her palms. Her chest rose and fell in short, sharp hitches. "My court," she muttered under her breath, glaring at Harper who was happily dribbling up the court. Chloe crossed her arms tightly over her chest, refusing to move from the center circle, her jaw locked like a vault door.

I stared at the new lineup card taped to the dugout wall. Right Field. The words burned into my retinas. My name belonged at the top, next to Starting Pitcher. I tore the paper off the tape, crumpled it into a tight ball, and threw it into the dirt. "My shoulder is fine!" I shouted at the manager's back as he walked toward the umpire. He didn't turn around. I kicked the water cooler, sending a spray of ice and Gatorade over the wooden bench. Three months of rehab, pitching off a mound in a freezing warehouse at 5 AM every morning, just to be shoved into the outfield where the washouts go to hide. I grabbed my favorite pitcher’s glove from my bag and slammed it into the trash can. Let them lose. Let them see exactly what happens without me on the mound.

The gym was silent except for the squeak of Maya’s sneakers as she paced back and forth behind the service line. The coach had just told her to trade her contrasting jersey for a regular one; she was setting today. Maya grabbed a volleyball, her knuckles turning bone-white against the synthetic leather. She threw the ball straight up and spiked it into the net, the nylon mesh tearing slightly under the violent impact. She was the best defensive specialist in the state. She practically bled on the floor digging out impossible spikes. To put her at setter was an absolute insult to her reflexes. The head coach blew his whistle to start drills. Maya stood frozen, glaring through the net at the opposing side, her breath escaping her nose in hard, visible huffs in the chilly gym, refusing to set her hands.

"You've got the size for tight end, son," Coach grunted, not looking up from his clipboard. "We're going with the transfer under center." I felt a sudden, intense roaring in my ears. I unstrapped my helmet and hurled it at the turf, watching it take a wild bounce. "I've been the quarterback here for three seasons!" I roared, veins bulging in my forehead. The field went dead silent. Players pretended to stretch. The transfer kid had the audacity to look sorry for me. I lunged forward, grabbing my playbook from the bench, and ripped the spiral binding clean off, scattering the laminated sheets into the wind. Tight end. He wanted me blocking for a guy who couldn't throw a ten-yard out route. I turned on my heel and marched straight for the parking lot, kicking over the chalk bucket.

Elena’s hands gripped the carbon-fiber oar until her calluses threatened to split open. The coxswain had just directed her to the bow seat, giving the stroke seat—her seat—to a novice.
