My idol hadn't written a single original word in a decade. I pushed my chair back so forcefully it toppled over with a loud crash. I paced the length of my small apartment, my hands balling into fists at my sides, my fingernails biting into my palms. I marched over to the bookshelf that held my complete, color-coordinated collection of his works. I grabbed the first book and threw it against the wall. Then the second. Then the third. I hurled them one by one, the spines cracking and pages fluttering like dying birds, until the shelves were completely bare and I was standing breathless amidst a sea of stolen words.

The English department lounge was completely silent as Professor Higgins read the literary journal's feature piece. He had championed this author, built entire syllabi around her so-called genius, only to discover she had copied essays from her own graduate students. Higgins’s face darkened to a deep plum. The teacup in his hand rattled against its saucer. He abruptly stood, knocking his knees against the low coffee table, and stormed down the hall to his office. He grabbed his syllabus for the upcoming semester and ripped it cleanly down the middle, then ripped it again. He logged into the university portal, his fingers striking the keyboard like hammers, deleting every lecture, every slide, and every assignment bearing her name. He slammed the laptop lid shut with a deafening crack.

I sat in the front row of the auditorium, waiting for the keynote speech to begin. I had been her biggest defender online when the rumors started, but the undeniable proof had just leaked an hour ago. She walked onto the stage, waving elegantly to the crowd, soaking in the applause. I felt a tight knot form in my stomach, hot and heavy. The air in the room suddenly felt too thick to breathe. While everyone else clapped, I stood up. I kept my arms rigidly by my sides. When she made eye contact with me, flashing a brilliant smile, I didn't smile back. I held her gaze, turned my back to the stage, and walked heavily up the aisle. I let the heavy wooden doors slam shut behind me, the sound echoing through the lobby.

My thumb hovered over the glowing notification on my screen. Marcus Vance wants to connect. The name tasted like dirt in my mouth. My grip tightened on the ceramic mug until my knuckles turned stark white, the lukewarm coffee inside rippling with the slight tremor in my hand. I stared at his smiling profile picture, a manicured family man holding a golden retriever. My jaw clamped shut so hard my teeth ached. Suddenly, the memory of being shoved into a rusty locker—the metallic clang, the suffocating darkness, the mocking laughter—flooded my chest like boiling water. How dare he? How absolutely dare he reach out now, twenty years later, as if those middle school years were just a pleasant shared nostalgia? I slammed my phone face-down on my mahogany desk, the sharp crack making my assistant jump in the next room.

Elena stared at the friend request, her breath catching in her throat before releasing in short, sharp exhales. Chloe Davis. The screen displayed a perfectly curated photo of the woman who used to pour spoiled milk into Elena’s backpack every Tuesday. Elena’s fingernails bit into the soft meat of her palms, leaving deep crescent-moon indentations. The bustling noise of the coffee shop faded into a distant hum, replaced by the roaring rush of blood pounding in her ears. She pressed her lips together until they were a thin, bloodless line. With a sudden, jerky movement, Elena shoved the laptop away. It slid across the table and knocked over her iced matcha latte, but she didn’t even glance at the spreading green puddle. Her eyes remained locked on the wall, her chest heaving as she mentally incinerated that smiling digital face.

The chime of my phone interrupted the quiet hum of the evening news. I casually swiped down, expecting a message from my wife. Instead, the screen read: Friend Request: Thomas Kessler. The air evaporated from my lungs. My heart immediately launched into a frantic, hammering rhythm against my ribs. Thomas Kessler. The boy who made me eat a handful of gravel behind the bleachers while his friends cheered. I squeezed the phone, half-expecting the glass to shatter under the sudden, immense pressure of my grip. A hot, prickly sensation spread across my neck and face. I stood up abruptly, kicking the coffee table so hard the heavy glass top shifted with a screeching scrape against the wood. "Everything okay?" Sarah called from the kitchen. I couldn't answer. My throat felt thick with a burning heat, my vision narrowing to that single, audacious name.

Julian was mid-stride on the treadmill when the notification flashed on his smartwatch. Jason Buckley added you. Julian missed his step. His foot slapped awkwardly against the moving belt, and he had to grab the side rails to keep from eating rubber. He stopped the machine with a violent slap to the red button. Jason. The guy who used to wait by the bus stop just to trip him into the muddy ditch. Julian stepped off the treadmill, his chest expanding and contracting in erratic, jagged intervals. He grabbed his water bottle and hurled it into the canvas laundry bin across the room; it hit the metal frame with a deafening crack. A few gym-goers turned to look, but Julian just glared a hole through the tiled floor, his jaw working back and forth as a familiar, scalding heat radiated from his stomach.

Riding the subway home, I opened my social app to pass the time. A red badge sat on the bell icon. Request from Amelia Stone. I stopped breathing. Amelia. The architect of every miserable rumor that destroyed my high school reputation. My thumb hovered over the 'Accept' and 'Decline' buttons, trembling so violently I had to press my wrist against my thigh to steady it. The nerve. The absolute, unfiltered audacity. Did she think time had just erased the crying in bathroom stalls? I glared at her sun-kissed vacation photo, a sour taste rising in the back of my throat. I dug my teeth into my lower lip until I tasted the sharp, metallic tang of copper. I wanted to throw my phone onto the tracks. Instead, I forcefully jabbed the 'Block' button, my chest tight and burning long after the screen went black.

Sitting in the quiet archives, Professor Higgins scrolled through his neglected personal email. A notification caught his eye: Greg Miller wants to connect. Higgins froze. His shoulders stiffened into rigid peaks, drawing up toward his ears. Greg Miller. The varsity brute who used to hold Higgins down and spit on his glasses. Higgins gripped the edge of his oak desk, the wood groaning slightly under his sudden, immense weight. His cheeks flushed a deep, mottled crimson, and the vein at his temple began to throb in a rapid, relentless tempo. He stared at the screen, his breathing growing shallow and loud in the silent room. With a sudden, explosive motion, Higgins slammed his fist down onto the desk. A stack of rare manuscripts toppled over, scattering across the floor, but Higgins just sat there, glaring at the digital phantom of his childhood tormentor.

I was chopping onions for dinner when the phone on the counter buzzed. Wiping a tear from my eye, I tapped the screen. Friend Suggestion: Eric Thorne. No, not a suggestion. A direct request. The chef’s knife in my right hand suddenly felt very heavy. Eric Thorne. The kid who locked me in the gym closet overnight. My grip on the handle tightened until the metal bit painfully into my palm. I stared at his profile—a picture of him holding a giant fish, grinning like he owned the world. A sudden rush of heat flooded my chest, radiating out to my fingertips. I slammed the knife down onto the wooden cutting board with a resounding thwack, embedding the blade an inch deep into the timber. The chopped onions scattered across the granite counter. I left the kitchen, my hands shaking uncontrollably by my sides.

Maya was enjoying the crisp autumn air on a park bench until her phone vibrated. Samantha Hayes wants to be your friend. Maya’s posture immediately snapped perfectly straight. Samantha. The girl who organized the entire eighth grade to give Maya the silent treatment for a month. Maya’s lips parted, but no sound came out. She locked her phone, the screen going black, but the name was already burned into her retinas. She began to aggressively tear a fallen oak leaf into tiny, microscopic shreds, letting the pieces fall into her lap. Her breathing came faster, her nostrils flaring with every sharp intake of cold air. She grabbed her leather purse, yanked the zipper shut with a vicious tug, and stood up. She marched down the paved path, her heels striking the concrete with heavy, punishing steps that echoed loudly through the quiet park.

I lay in the dark, doing my nightly scroll, when a notification popped down from the top of the screen. Vince Rossi sent you a friend request. The warm comfort of my bed instantly evaporated. My body went completely rigid, the muscles in my back locking up like stone. Vince Rossi. The boy who broke my science fair project and laughed while I tried to tape the pieces back together. A hot prickling started behind my eyes. I threw the covers off, suddenly feeling like the room was entirely too small and entirely too hot. I paced the length of my bedroom, my bare feet slapping heavily against the hardwood. I muttered a string of harsh curses to the empty room, my hands balling into tight fists and releasing, over and over, as a fiery heat crawled up my neck and settled in my jaw.

Arthur was comparing cereal boxes in aisle four when his pocket buzzed. He pulled out his phone and squinted at the screen. Derek Vance has requested to follow you. Arthur’s eyes widened, then immediately narrowed into sharp, dark slits. Derek Vance. The bully who used to steal his lunch money and push him into the snowbanks. Arthur’s grip crushed the cardboard cereal box he was holding, denting the corners and popping the glued seam open. Cereal spilled onto the linoleum floor with a dry rattle. Arthur didn't look down. His face felt as though he had stepped out of the air-conditioned store and directly into a furnace. He forcefully shoved the ruined box back onto the shelf, knocking three other boxes to the ground in the process. He abandoned his shopping cart right there in the aisle and stormed out of the sliding glass doors.

I was idling at a red light when my phone chimed from the passenger seat. I glanced over. Friend Request: Brittany Cole. The engine's low hum suddenly sounded like a roar inside my head. Brittany Cole. The girl who publicly read my diary to the cafeteria. I grabbed the steering wheel with both hands, squeezing the leather cover so fiercely my forearms cramped. The light turned green, and the car behind me honked, but my foot stayed cemented to the brake pedal. I stared at the name, a suffocating, fiery weight pressing down firmly on my chest. My jaw clamped tight, grinding my molars together until a sharp pain shot up into my temples. The honking behind me grew frantic. I finally stomped on the gas pedal, the tires screeching loudly against the asphalt as I peeled away, my breathing heavy and ragged.

Clara sat in the dentist's waiting room, flipping idly through social media. A notification popped up: Brad Higgins requested to be your friend. Clara stopped breathing. The cheesy waiting room music seemed to warp into an unbearable, high-pitched ringing. Brad Higgins. The terror who used to lock her inside the playground tunnel. Clara’s thumb hovered over the screen, vibrating violently. She bit the inside of her cheek until the metallic taste of blood flooded her tongue. Her face flushed a deep, blotchy red, and she aggressively shoved the phone deep into her coat pocket. She crossed her arms tightly over her chest, digging her fingernails into her own forearms. When the hygienist called her name, Clara stood up so abruptly she knocked her chair backward into the wall, the loud thud doing absolutely nothing to release the burning pressure expanding inside her ribcage.

Marcus stared at the oversized brown box blocking his front door. The name "Amanda Higgins" stared back at him, tauntingly printed in bold black ink. He kicked the side of the corrugated cardboard, his boot leaving a dent. Five months. Amanda had moved out five months ago, yet her Amazon Prime addiction somehow remained his daily problem. He snatched his phone from his pocket, pressing the screen so hard his thumb joint cracked. He dialed the landlord’s number, pacing the length of the porch with heavy, thudding steps. "Listen to me," he bit out the moment the line connected, not waiting for a greeting. "If I trip over one more of Higgins’s deliveries, I’m dumping them straight into the storm drain. I’m not running a free storage facility." He slammed his thumb against the 'end call' button, his breath coming in short, hot bursts.

I jammed my key into the tiny metal lock of mailbox 4B, twisting it with a sharp jerk that threatened to snap the brass. Out spilled a cascade of junk mail and a soft, padded envelope. I snatched it up, my eyes narrowing at the label. Gregory Vance. My jaw tightened until my teeth ground together. Gregory hadn't lived here in two years. I crumpled the padded envelope in my fist, the bubble wrap popping like miniature gunshots in the echoing mailroom. Why did I have to spend my Thursday evening playing secretary to a ghost? I hurled the package into the "Return to Sender" bin with enough force that it bounced off the plastic rim and hit the tiled floor. Let the postal service figure it out. I stomped toward the elevator, jabbing the up button three times in rapid succession, my face burning.

Elena’s grip on the rusted letter opener turned her knuckles a stark, bloodless white. On the battered kitchen table sat a heavy, tape-wrapped parcel addressed to Jonathan Reed. He had sold her this farmhouse last spring, neglected and filled with rot. Now, his junk was being delivered to her sanctuary. She drove the metal opener into the center of the packing tape, slicing downward with a harsh, tearing screech. She didn't care what was inside; she just wanted it gone. Her chest rose and fell in jagged, rapid movements. "I told the post office," she muttered to the empty kitchen, her voice tight and clipped. "I told them to stop bringing his trash here." She shoved the heavy box off the edge of the table. It hit the floorboards with a satisfying, deafening thud, spilling packing peanuts across the worn wood.

The doorman held out a slender, elegant box, smiling politely. I snatched it from his hands, immediately zeroing in on the recipient name: Chloe Sinclair. I squeezed the rigid cardboard edges until my palms stung. Chloe. The woman who had left an unpaid electricity bill and a stained rug for me to inherit. "This isn't mine," I told the doorman, my voice dropping an octave, carrying a sharp edge that made his smile vanish. "You know my name is David. You buzz me every day." I shoved the box back into his chest, forcing him to grab it. "Return it. Burn it. I don't care. Do not hand me another piece of Sinclair's mail, or I'll start deducting courier fees from my HOA dues." I spun on my heel, marching toward the glass doors with my heart hammering violently against my ribs.

The cardboard was soggy from the downpour, but Sam grabbed it anyway, his jaw locked so tightly his temples throbbed. To: The Peterson Family. He had lived in this duplex for eight months. The Petersons were long gone, yet their wine club delivery still arrived on his doorstep. He marched to the edge of the driveway, rain soaking his bare shoulders. He only felt the hot rushing in his ears. With a guttural grunt, Sam hoisted the heavy box over his head and hurled it into the overflowing recycling bin. The sound of shattering glass and sloshing burgundy brought a fleeting surge of satisfaction, quickly replaced by the intense heat radiating off his neck. He turned back to the house, slamming the heavy oak door hard enough to rattle the front windows.

I dumped my heavy backpack onto the floor and glared at the neon green parcel resting on my bed. My roommate wasn't here, which meant the housing office had let someone in to drop this off. I picked it up, my eyes darting to the label. Sarah Jenkins. My predecessor. The same Sarah who left rotting food in the mini-fridge. I squeezed the squishy green plastic, my fingernails digging sharp half-moons into my palms. I marched out into the hallway, my boots stomping heavily against the thin carpet. Reaching the RA’s door, I hammered my fist against the wood three times in quick, bruising succession. "Open up," I barked, not bothering to lower my voice despite the quiet hours. "I am not Sarah's personal mail carrier, and if housing puts one more of her stupid packages on my pillow, I’m taking it to the dean."

Dust swirled around Wade’s boots as he stood by the communal mailbox. A heavy, metal crate sat on the gravel, bearing the name Hank Roster. Wade kicked the rusted metal leg of the mailbox stand, the vibration shooting painfully up his shin, but he welcomed the sting. Hank owed Wade three hundred dollars and had skipped town in the dead of night. Now, his rusted motorcycle parts were getting dropped off at lot 42. Wade grabbed the heavy crate, his breathing turning into sharp, raspy hisses. He lugged it toward the center of the park's dried-up fire pit. "Keep sending him stuff!" Wade yelled into the empty, wind-swept desert, his voice raw and cracking. He grabbed a rusted crowbar from his truck bed and swung it down onto the crate with a deafening clang, shattering the wooden lid into jagged splinters.

The sleek silver tube arrived by drone courier, hovering gently before dropping onto my balcony. I snatched it before the drone could even ascend, checking the digital e-ink display on the side. Deliver to: Felix Vance. I felt a familiar heat rising up my neck, settling right behind my eyes. Felix had been fired a month ago for stealing my code, and now I was receiving his severance prototype deliveries. I gripped the smooth metal tube, imagining it was his smug neck. The drone buzzed happily above me, waiting for a confirmation tap. Instead, I swatted at the machine with the tube itself. "Go away!" I yelled, throwing the silver package with all my strength over the glass balcony rail. I watched it plummet forty stories into the bustling traffic below, my chest heaving, a tight, harsh smile stretching across my face.

The delivery truck tires crunched against the fresh snow, retreating down the mountain path. Clara looked down at the wooden crate left on her snowy stoop. The stenciled black lettering read Property of M. Vance. She ground her teeth together until a sharp ache bloomed in her jaw. Vance. The idiot who had nearly burned the cabin down before selling it to her. She shoved her bare hands into her pockets, her face flushed with a burning heat that defied the sub-zero air. She kicked the crate. Her toe throbbed, but she kicked it again, harder this time, sending it tumbling down the icy wooden stairs. It cracked open at the bottom, spilling brightly colored climbing gear into the pristine white drift. Clara stood on the top step, breathing in harsh, ragged gasps, glaring at the spilled contents as if they had personally insulted her.

I dragged the massive, tape-covered box out of my bakery's doorway, my chest tight and my breathing shallow. The label proudly displayed Carla's Couture. Carla had gone bankrupt and moved out of this space a year ago. Now I had twenty pounds of what felt like mannequins blocking my morning customers. I grabbed a pair of industrial shears from the counter and stabbed them into the box’s thick cardboard flank, ripping a long, jagged gash down the side. A plastic arm tumbled out. "I don't have time for this!" I shouted at the wall. I grabbed the phone, mashing the keypad with my flour-covered fingers to dial the shipping company. As the hold music chimed in my ear, I paced furiously behind the counter, snapping a wooden stirring spoon cleanly in half between my white-knuckled hands.

Julian dragged the dripping cooler off his deck, his flip-flops slapping violently against the wet wood. The shipping label was half-peeled but clearly read: Troy Miller. Troy, the guy who had skipped out on the final two months of his lease. Julian’s face felt like it was sitting too close to an open flame. He grabbed the handle of the cooler, ripping it upward with a sudden, vicious yank that tore the plastic molding straight off the hinges. The lid popped off, revealing rows of premium fish bait on melted ice. Julian let out a guttural sound, somewhere between a growl and a shout. He tipped the cooler sideways, dumping the slimy bait and icy water directly into the sand. He kicked the empty plastic shell across the yard, his chest heaving as he glared at the dead fish baking in the sun.

The wax-sealed parcel sat on my antique console table like a poisonous toad. I didn't need to look at the elegant calligraphy to know it was for Beatrice. She had abandoned this townhouse, and me, without a backward glance last autumn. I stared at her name, a hot, prickly sensation crawling up the back of my neck. I snatched the parcel off the polished wood, my nails digging into the heavy parchment paper until it crinkled loudly in the quiet hall. I marched straight to the fireplace. The embers were still glowing a dull, menacing orange. Without a second thought, I hurled the package directly into the center of the grate. The wax seal hissed and melted instantly, the paper curling into black ash. I gripped the stone mantelpiece, my knuckles stark white, watching the flames consume her lingering presence with unblinking, burning eyes.

The letter arrives in a sleek envelope. I tear it open, and the handwriting is instantly recognizable. He writes "I'm sorry" after five years. My grip tightens until the thick paper crumples, my knuckles turning stark white against my skin. How dare he? Five years of my life rearranging the pieces he shattered, and he thinks expensive stationery and black ink can patch it up. I strike a match, watching the small flame lick the edges of his perfect calligraphy. Heat crawls up my neck, flushing my cheeks, but the fire isn't half as hot as the blood pounding in my ears. I drop the burning page into the sink, gripping the porcelain edge so hard my fingers ache, wishing it were his throat beneath my hands.

Julian stared at the email attachment. Ten years. Ten years since Marcus took the credit, took the promotion, and took Julian’s career trajectory. Now, a multi-paragraph document outlining Marcus's "deepest regrets" sat on the screen, prompted by some twelve-step program. Julian’s jaw locked. The muscles in his cheeks twitched rhythmically as he ground his molars together. He slammed his coffee mug onto the coaster, the dark liquid splashing over the rim and staining the quarterly reports. "Regrets," Julian hissed to the empty room. He typed a single keystroke, deleting the message, then shoved his chair back so violently it crashed into the filing cabinet. He paced the small office, his chest heaving, wishing the delete button had actually erased Marcus from existence.

The return address was a slap to the face. Seattle. She had the nerve to write to me from Seattle. I ripped the seal, scanning the looping cursive that talked about ‘growth’ and ‘forgiveness’ regarding the night of our high school graduation. My vision blurred, a sharp ringing amplifying in my head. I laughed, a harsh, jagged sound that startled the stray cat on my porch. She wants absolution after ruining my reputation and skipping town? I marched straight to the recycling bin, shoving the scented paper deep beneath yesterday’s coffee grounds and eggshells. My breath came in short, jagged gasps. I scrubbed my hands together, trying to rub away the lingering scent of her jasmine perfume, my nails leaving deep red crescents in my palms.

Clara found the envelope tucked inside a box of her late mother’s things. It was from her sister, dated seven years ago. "I apologize for not being there." Clara’s eyes darted over the words. Her chest constricted, a sudden, suffocating tightness gripping her ribs. She stood up abruptly, knocking a stack of photo albums to the hardwood floor with a heavy thud. While Clara had spent months feeding, bathing, and holding their mother’s frail hand, her sister was touring Europe, too busy to answer the phone. Clara kicked the heavy wooden trunk, pain flaring up her toe, but it wasn't enough to distract her from the boiling heat rising in her chest. She tore the letter down the middle, then again, and again, until it was just confetti.

The red light cast a harsh glow across the dashboard where the opened letter lay. "I was foolish to let you go," the neat print read. Three years since he walked out of our apartment without a backward glance. My hands gripped the leather steering wheel, twisting it slightly even though the car was parked. The leather creaked in protest. My jaw felt like solid iron, teeth locked together. I shoved the gear shift into park and grabbed the thick parchment, crumpling it into a tight, dense ball. I hurled it at the passenger side window. It bounced harmlessly, a pathetic impact that only fueled the roaring heat in my chest. The light turned green. I slammed my foot on the accelerator, tires squealing against the damp asphalt.

The barista handed Elias his espresso just as he opened the direct message on his phone. It was his old bandmate, apologizing for stealing the song royalties back in 2018. Elias didn't touch his drink. He stared at the glowing screen, his breathing turning shallow and fast. The bustling noise of the coffee shop faded into a dull drone beneath the loud rushing of blood in his ears. His thumb hovered over the keyboard, but his hand was shaking too violently to type. He locked the screen and shoved the phone into his pocket. Grabbing his untouched espresso, he dumped the scalding liquid straight into the trash can. He stormed out into the street, shoving past a group of tourists, his fists balled so tightly his knuckles shone like bleached bone.

I sat on the wooden locker room bench, athletic tape unspooling in my hands as I stared at the note slipped into my bag. Coach was finally admitting he was wrong to bench me during the finals five seasons ago. The nerve. The sheer audacity of this wrinkled piece of notebook paper. A hot prickling sensation crawled up my neck and settled behind my eyes. I stood up, ripping the tape in half with a sharp tearing sound. Five years. I lost my scholarship because of his "tactical decision." I kicked the aluminum trash can across the room, the deafening clatter echoing off the tiled walls. It wasn't enough. I picked up my helmet and hurled it against the nearest locker, the metal denting with a satisfying, thunderous crunch.

Beatrice knelt in the soil, her trowel digging viciously into the earth. The letter from the city council lay on the patio table, a formal apology for seizing her grandfather’s land a decade ago due to a "clerical error." A clerical error that cost her family their farm. She drove the trowel down, severing a thick root with brutal force. Her breath hissed through her teeth. She hacked at the dirt, flinging clumps of soil onto the pristine walkway. The formal, stamped apology felt like a physical blow, a mocking reminder of years spent in cramped apartments. She threw the metal trowel; it spun through the air and embedded itself deep into the wooden fence. Beatrice stood panting, dirt beneath her fingernails, glaring at the fluttering white paper on the table.

The snow piled high against the cabin windowpane, but inside, I was burning up. I stared at the handwritten pages spread across the oak table. It was my father, claiming he was finally sober and deeply sorry for the ruined holidays, the broken promises, the empty bank accounts. Eighteen years too late. A bitter laugh escaped my throat, harsh and grating. I swept my arm across the table, sending the pages, the envelope, and my ceramic mug crashing to the floor. The hot tea pooled over the ink, blurring his desperate excuses. I paced the length of the rug, my boots leaving heavy indentations. My chest heaved, my fingernails digging into my palms. Apologies don't buy back childhoods. I kicked a stray log into the fireplace, sending sparks flying onto the hearth.

The bouquet of roses sat on the vanity, accompanied by a little card. "Sorry for how things ended. You were always the star." Signed, David. It had been four years since he stole her choreography and claimed it as his own on Broadway. Sofia stared at the red petals. The muscles in her neck pulled taut. She picked up the heavy crystal vase, the water sloshing over the sides. Her reflection in the mirror showed flared nostrils and a flushed, red chest. Without a word, she inverted the vase over the trash bin. The water, the stems, and the pristine blooms tumbled into the garbage. She took the little card, ripped it into tiny, jagged shreds, and threw them to the floor, grinding them into the carpet with her heel.

I squeezed the tube of cadmium red, watching the thick paint coil onto my palette. The courier had just delivered the package: my stolen sketchbook from college, accompanied by an apology note from my former roommate. "I found this and realized I should return it. Sorry for taking it." A low rumble started in my chest. I pressed the palette knife into the red paint, scraping it across the wood with unnecessary violence. Two years of my best concepts, gone when I needed them for my thesis. I grabbed a large brush, loaded it with the wet crimson, and slashed it across my blank canvas. My jaw ached from clenching it. I dragged the brush again and again, leaving heavy, slashing strokes until the canvas was utterly ruined, my breathing loud and ragged.

Professor Vance adjusted his spectacles, reading the handwritten letter from his former colleague. After fifteen years, Dr. Aris was apologizing for falsifying the data that got Vance ousted from the university. Vance’s fingers began to tremble. A dark flush crept up from his collar, turning the tips of his ears bright pink. He stood slowly, his joints stiff. He walked to the bookshelf, pulling out the volumes he had published in obscurity, while Aris had basked in stolen glory. Vance grabbed the edge of his heavy oak desk, his knuckles stark white against the dark wood. He breathed in through his nose, his nostrils flaring, and exhaled a hot, shaky breath. He picked up the expensive brass paperweight from his desk and hurled it at the window, the glass shattering outward into the courtyard.

Elias stared at the embossed card resting on his mahogany desk. Class of 2014. His jaw tightened so hard a dull ache radiated up to his temples. He snatched the thick cardstock, his knuckles turning white as he squeezed the edges. They actually had the nerve to ask for a "suggested donation" for the venue. After what they did to him at graduation? The memory of the laughter in the auditorium echoed in his ears, making his pulse hammer against his collarbone. He grabbed his heavy metal stapler and brought it down hard on the corner of the invitation, driving a staple right through the golden crest. Again and again, he hammered the metal device down, leaving a mangled, stapled ruin on his blotter. "I'll give you a donation," he muttered through gritted teeth, sweeping the shredded remains into his wastebasket with a violent flick of his wrist.

I opened the mailbox expecting bills, but found a glossy envelope instead. Ten-year reunion. I laughed, but the sound was sharp and scraped against my throat. My grip on the paper tightened until the glossy surface buckled and cracked under my thumbs. They wanted to see me now? After spending four years treating me like I was invisible, like I was something they stepped in on the way to the cafeteria? I marched into the kitchen, my boots hitting the linoleum with heavy, deliberate thuds. I turned on the gas stove, watching the blue flame hiss to life. I held the edge of the envelope to the burner. The fire crawled up the paper, turning the cheerful invitation into curling black ash. I dropped the burning remnants into the sink and watched them sizzle out, my chest heaving with deep, ragged breaths.

Maya’s brush snapped in half. She stared down at the jagged wood in her hands, her chest rising and falling in sharp, erratic jerks. The email notification still glowed on her laptop screen: Westfield High Reunion! A droplet of red paint fell from the broken brush, splattering like blood over her pristine canvas. She threw the pieces of wood across the studio, wincing as they clattered sharply against the brick wall. Her phone buzzed—a text from Sarah asking if she was going. Maya snatched the phone, her thumbs hitting the glass screen so hard it felt like it might crack. Why would I ever go back to a place that let Coach Miller get away with what he did? she typed, then deleted it. She threw the phone onto the couch, pacing the floorboards with heavy, stomping steps, tearing at her hair.

The digital display on my dashboard lit up with a calendar alert. Eastwood High Reunion. I hit the steering wheel with the heel of my hand. The horn blared, echoing through the empty parking garage, but it wasn't loud enough to drown out the rush of blood roaring in my ears. I shifted into drive, my jaw locked. They had a gall sending that to my personal email. The committee was run by the exact same group who had actively campaigned to get my scholarship revoked. I gripped the leather steering wheel, my nails biting into my palms, leaving deep crescent-moon indentations. The stoplight ahead turned yellow, and instead of slowing down, I slammed my foot onto the accelerator. The engine roared, pushing me back into my seat, my eyes burning as I glared straight ahead at the asphalt.

David adjusted his grip on the barbell, his breathing loud and nasal. His phone rested on the bench, displaying the digital flyer for the Oak Creek High alumni gathering. He hoisted the weights, bringing them down with a deafening crash against the rubber matting. The gym attendant shot him a look, but David ignored it. He grabbed a towel, twisting it between his hands as if wringing out water, though it was perfectly dry. They expected him to pay seventy-five dollars to eat stale chicken and pretend the bullying never happened. He could still feel the phantom sting of the locker room towel snaps. He kicked his gym bag, sending it skidding violently across the floor. "Hey man, watch it!" someone yelled. David just glared at the wall, his nostrils flaring, every muscle in his back coiled as tight as a steel spring.

The gold-lettered invitation slid out of my mother's care package and landed squarely in my spilled coffee. I didn't rush to save it. I sat perfectly still, my teeth grinding together so fiercely my jaw popped. Five years. It had been five years since the principal told me I wasn't "valedictorian material" because of my zip code, despite my perfect grades. I picked up my metal spoon and began stirring my coffee, the metal scraping harshly against the ceramic mug. Scrape. Scrape. Scrape. The barista glanced over, startled by the sharp, grating noise. I stared unblinking at the soggy invitation, watching the brown liquid seep into the expensive cardstock, blurring the smug faces of the reunion committee. I grabbed the soaking paper, crushed it into a tight, dripping ball, and threw it forcefully into the trash bin on my way out the door.

Sparks flew in an aggressive arc as Marcus ground the metal pipe against the sanding wheel. His phone vibrated in his breast pocket. Pulling it out with a grease-stained glove, he saw the Facebook event invite: Lincoln High Class of '14. His grip on the device turned rigid, the casing groaning under the pressure. The image of the school's crest made his vision swim. He threw the phone onto the workbench, scattering a pile of screws onto the concrete floor. He didn't bend to pick them up. Instead, he grabbed a heavy wrench and slammed it down onto the metal table. The deafening clang vibrated through his boots. They wanted a reunion? The same people who spray-painted his locker and slashed his tires? He picked up the wrench and struck the table again, his chest heaving, his face burning hot beneath the fluorescent lights.

I was walking the dog when I saw the banner hung over Main Street. Welcome Back, Tigers! Class of 2004. My pace stopped dead. The leash went taut as Buster pulled, but I stood planted on the pavement, my breath catching in a sharp hiss. Ten years later, and they still used the tiger mascot I had drawn, never once paying me or giving me credit after the principal claimed it as school property. My hands balled into tight fists inside my jacket pockets. I felt my fingernails digging into my palms. I spat on the sidewalk right below the banner, the bitter taste lingering in my mouth. I yanked the leash, perhaps a little too sharply. "Come on, Buster. We're going down Elm," I barked, my voice harsh and unrecognizable, refusing to spend another second standing in the shadow of that stolen artwork.

Chloe tore the envelope open with a swift, jagged motion. As she read the words Ten Year Reunion, her breathing accelerated into short, rapid intakes of air. She paced across her living room rug, her bare feet stomping heavily against the floorboards. She snatched the framed photograph from the mantel—the one of her and her former best friend, who was now listed as the reunion chairwoman. The same best friend who had spread the rumors that ruined her senior year. Chloe’s face flushed a deep crimson. She stared at the smiling faces in the frame, her eyes narrowed to thin slits. With a sudden, explosive movement, she hurled the picture frame into the fireplace. The glass shattered with a loud crash, sending shards scattering across the soot-stained hearth. She stood over the ruins, her hands shaking uncontrollably at her sides.

The ping of an incoming email interrupted my spreadsheet. Subject: Your 20th High School Reunion! I froze, the mouse slipping from my sudden, vice-like grip. A hot rush of blood rushed to my cheeks, making my ears burn. I aggressively hammered the backspace key, trying to delete a typo I’d just made, but my fingers were trembling so much I deleted half the paragraph. The screen blurred. Twenty years, and they thought an email could erase the fact that not a single one of them had showed up to my father's funeral our senior year. I pushed my rolling chair back so violently it slammed into the partition behind me. "Everything okay?" my cubicle neighbor asked. "Fine," I snapped, the word biting and sharp. I grabbed my mug and marched toward the breakroom, each step driving hard into the thin commercial carpet.

Flour puffed into the air as Julian slammed the dough onto the stainless steel counter. His sister had just dropped off his mail, leaving the thick, cream-colored alumni invitation sitting next to the cash register. He punched the dough, flattening it with unnecessary force. He punched it again, his knuckles sinking deep into the sticky mass. The alumni board. The same board that had tried to have his family's bakery condemned to build their new football stadium parking lot. Julian's jaw was locked so tight his teeth ached. He grabbed the heavy wooden rolling pin, gripping the handles until his knuckles blanched white. He rolled out the dough, pressing down with his entire body weight, his breath whistling sharply through his nose. He glared at the envelope out of the corner of his eye, wishing it were under the crushing weight of his rolling pin.

I was digging for my winter coat when I found it: the unopened reunion save-the-date card my mother had forwarded months ago. Just holding the heavy cardstock made my chest tighten, a familiar heat rising up my neck. I ripped the card precisely in half. Then in quarters. Then eighths. The tearing sound was loud in the quiet closet, a satisfying rasp that matched the heavy rhythm of my breathing. They wanted to celebrate the glory days. The days when I ate lunch in this exact kind of dark closet to avoid the varsity boys. I threw the confetti of torn paper onto the floor and ground it into the carpet with the heel of my boot, twisting my foot back and forth. My reflection in the mirror caught my eye—flared nostrils, a rigid posture, and a hard, icy stare that refused to blink.

The delivery boy dropped the massive bouquet of red roses onto Clara’s spotless desk, whistling a tune as he walked away. Clara didn't sign the receipt. She didn't have to. She stared at the velvet petals, her jaw locking so tightly her teeth groaned against each other. There was no card nestled in the baby’s breath, but she knew exactly whose cowardly apology this was supposed to be. A dozen roses to erase three years of lies? Her nails dug into the fleshy part of her palm, leaving deep crescent-moon indentations. Without a word, she grabbed the thick glass vase by its neck. The chilled water sloshed over her knuckles as she marched straight to the breakroom and upended the entire arrangement into the industrial trash bin, watching the pristine red blossoms sink beneath coffee grounds and damp paper towels.

I stared at the arrangement of yellow lilies left on my welcome mat, my chest rising and falling in sharp, jagged breaths. No card. Of course there was no card. My hands shook as I picked up the heavy vase, the sweet, cloying scent of the pollen making my nostrils flare. I had changed my locks, unlisted my number, and moved halfway across the city to escape this exact shadow, yet here these flowers sat, a quiet taunt mocking my false sense of security. I kicked my front door shut with the heel of my boot, the wood rattling in its frame. The glass vase slipped from my trembling grip, shattering into a hundred glittering shards across the entryway tiles. Water and crushed stems bled over the grout. Let them stay there. Let him see the mess if he came creeping around my windows tonight.

Marcus lay in the sterile hospital bed, the heavy plaster cast weighing down his shattered leg. When the nurse brought in the extravagant arrangement of white orchids, setting them cheerfully on the windowsill, Marcus felt a hot flush crawl up his neck. He scoured the cellophane for a note, but the plastic was perfectly bare. Only one person had the kind of money to afford orchids like that, and it was the same man who had run the red light in his silver sports car three nights ago. Marcus’s hands balled into tight fists atop the thin cotton blanket. His pulse hammered a brutal rhythm in his temples. A plastic apology delivered by a proxy. He pressed the call button repeatedly, jabbing the rim until his thumb ached, demanding she take the sickly-sweet blooms out of his room before he threw them out the window himself.

The dressing room mirror reflected my flushed cheeks and the rigid line of my shoulders. Sitting squarely on my makeup table was a bouquet of pink carnations. No card. I didn’t need one to recognize Chloe’s signature passive-aggressive theatricality. She had snatched the lead role right out from under me by cozying up to the director, leaving me with the understudy scraps, and now she was playing the gracious victor. My breathing grew shallow and fast. I grabbed the stiff green stems, squeezing them until the plant tissue crushed against my palms, and dragged the entire bunch across the table. Foundation bottles crashed to the floor. Lipsticks rolled under the chairs. I snapped the stalks one by one, tossing the decapitated flower heads into the vanity sink. I turned the hot water on full blast, watching the petals turn soggy under the scalding torrent.

The hostess handed Elena the extravagant bouquet of tulips right in the middle of the dinner rush. “A delivery guy just dropped these off for you,” she whispered. Elena searched the crinkling paper for a small envelope, but found nothing. Her grip tightened around the damp stems. Diego. He always thought grand gestures could pave over his constant betrayals. The nerve of him, sending these to her workplace where everyone could watch her reaction. Heat radiated from her face, prickling along her scalp. She didn't have time for this humiliating theater. Without breaking stride, she marched past the swinging doors of the kitchen, her jaw set like stone. She bypassed the water pitchers and headed straight for the industrial food disposal. With one swift, aggressive motion, she shoved the colorful arrangement down the steel chute and slammed the pulverizing switch, letting the roaring blades obliterate the insult.

The bridal suite was quiet except for the ragged sound of my own breathing. Sitting on the antique settee was a sprawling arrangement of black baccara roses. Dark, almost bruised in color. I tore through the wrapping, hunting for a note, a name, anything, but the sender remained hidden behind a cowardly silence. I knew exactly what they meant. The late-night texts he thought I hadn't seen. The perfume that lingered on his coats. She was letting me know she was still here, hiding in the margins of my wedding day. I picked up a pair of heavy fabric shears from the seamstress’s kit. My vision tunneled, focusing solely on the velvety blooms. I sliced through the thick stems, the metal blades gnashing together with a satisfying, violent crunch. Petals rained onto the pristine white carpet, bleeding their dark, vicious color into the fibers.

Standing before her brother’s headstone, Maya stared at the lavish wreath of white lilies leaning against the granite. She knelt in the damp grass, hastily flipping through the ribbons, searching for a card. Nothing. Her teeth ground together with a force that sent a dull ache shooting up to her temples. It was them. The company executives who had cut corners, ignored the safety protocols, and caused the collapse. They couldn't even put their names on the tribute, hiding behind corporate anonymity to assuage their guilt. Maya snatched the wreath by its wire frame, ignoring how the sharp metal scratched the skin of her knuckles. She marched to the edge of the cemetery, her boots slamming into the gravel path. With a sharp, guttural exhale, she hurled the entire arrangement over the wrought-iron fence, letting it tumble into the muddy ditch beside the busy highway.

I slammed my locker shut, nearly catching my fingers in the metal door, but my eyes were locked on the small bouquet of daisies resting on the vent. There was no tag, no note, nothing to explain the sudden delivery. But I had heard the snickers down the hall. I saw Jason and his friends huddled by the water fountain, watching me with predatory grins. It was a joke. Another prop in their endless campaign to make my life miserable. My cheeks burned so hot I thought they might spontaneously combust. I grabbed the flowers, my fingernails digging into the green stalks until my knuckles turned stark white. I didn't look at them. I kept my eyes fixed straight ahead, marching directly to the janitor's garbage bin, and shoved the entire bouquet deep into the half-eaten cafeteria trash, burying it beneath a pile of greasy milk cartons.

Detective Miller found the dozen black orchids sitting on his desk right next to the open case files. He tore through the dark tissue paper, checking the vase, the soil, every square inch of the delivery. No card. His chest tightened, a muscle jumping frantically along his jawline. It was the Nightshade killer’s signature, delivered right into the heart of the precinct. They were mocking him. Taunting his failure to close the net. Miller swept his arm across the desk, sending the heavy glass vase crashing into the cinderblock wall. Water and soil exploded across the crime scene photos pinned to his corkboard. He stood panting in the center of the cubicle, ignoring the sudden silence of the squad room. His hands shook as he stared at the ruined blossoms on the floor, imagining his hands wrapping around the throat of the phantom who sent them.

I wiped the espresso machine, my rag moving in quick, abrasive circles that threatened to scratch the stainless steel. On the counter sat a gaudy arrangement of cheap gas-station sunflowers. The delivery guy had bolted before I could refuse them. No card was attached, but the lingering scent of cheap cologne on the plastic wrapping told me everything. It was the guy from the corner table. The one who ignored my fake engagement ring, who kept insisting I owed him a smile. My jaw ached from clenching it for the past hour. I grabbed the bouquet, my pulse hammering a frantic rhythm in my ears. I didn't care that the manager was watching. I carried the flowers to the back alley, lifted the heavy lid of the dumpster, threw them into the rotting waste, and slammed the plastic lid down with a deafening crack.

The gallery was buzzing with critics, but Sophia was frozen in front of the pedestal where a massive arrangement of white calla lilies sat. She frantically turned the envelope-sized enclosure over in her hands. Empty. The blood drained from her face, only to return in a rush of searing heat. Those were Julian’s favorites. After stealing her techniques, discrediting her name, and trying to ruin her career, he dared to send these to her debut solo exhibition as some kind of territorial marker. Sophia’s fingernails bit into the soft, fleshy petals of the nearest lily, tearing it perfectly down the middle. Her breathing grew loud, echoing over the chatter of the room. She snatched the entire heavy vase off the pedestal and marched toward the back exit. She wouldn't let his silent poison ruin tonight. She hurled the glass into the alley brickwork, watching it shatter.

I stood on the porch in the freezing rain, staring down at the extravagant bundle of peonies left on the welcome mat. I didn't need to search for a card to know they were from David. He knew they were my favorite, and he knew I was allergic to cheap apologies. A hot, prickling sensation crawled up the back of my neck, completely at odds with the icy downpour. After what I had found on his phone last night, he thought a florist could fix it. I kicked the bundle with the steel toe of my work boot, sending the delicate pink blossoms scattering across the wet concrete. I kicked them again, and again, until the stems were broken and mangled, the petals mashed into a miserable, muddy paste against the driveway. I turned my back on the wreckage, marched inside, and threw the deadbolt.

I crushed the neon-orange eviction notice in my fist until my fingernails dug deep half-moons into my palm. The diesel engine of the excavator roared to life, a mechanical beast gearing up to tear through the porch where I learned to ride my bike. The foreman tipped his hard hat at me, offering a polite, empty smile that made my jaw lock so tight my teeth ached. "Just doing our job, sir," he called out over the rumbling machinery. I spat on the dusty ground right at the treads of his machine, my chest heaving with quick, shallow breaths. They called it urban renewal, slapping a shiny new strip mall over the chalk-drawn hopscotch squares of my youth. I shoved my hands into my jacket pockets to keep them from swinging at his smug, ignorant face, glaring at the wrecking ball swinging lazily against the morning sky.

Elias stood perfectly still on the cracked driveway, his knuckles white around the handle of the final moving box. Across the street, the property developer was pointing at the oak tree his grandfather planted, gesturing with a rolled-up set of blueprints in a chopping motion. A hot, prickling sensation crawled up Elias's neck. He dropped the box into the trunk of his sedan with a violent thud, making the suspension groan. "Careful," his sister murmured, but Elias didn't look at her. He marched toward the property line, his boots crunching heavily on the gravel, stopping just short of the temporary chain-link fence. The developer laughed at something on his phone. Elias’s breathing grew ragged, his vision narrowing strictly to the man's polished Italian loafers. He gripped the metal wire of the fence, pulling it so fiercely that the steel posts bowed inward with a metallic shriek.

The steering wheel leather squeaked under my death grip as I watched the yellow backhoe position itself on the overgrown lawn. This was the house my father built with his own bare hands, now draped in ugly yellow caution tape like a cheap crime scene. A city planner in a tailored suit stood on the sidewalk, sipping an iced latte and checking his watch. I slammed my palm against the horn, laying on it for three solid seconds. The man jumped, spilling coffee on his pristine tie. Good. I wanted his morning ruined. I wanted his whole week ruined. He wiped his shirt, entirely oblivious to the decades of family dinners and Christmas mornings he was authorizing to be pulverized into dust. My jaw trembled. I cranked the radio volume to the absolute maximum, desperately trying to drown out the sickening sound of the first timber frame splintering apart.

Maya kicked an empty paint can across the living room floor, watching it ricochet off the floral wallpaper she had picked out when she was twelve. The hollow clatter echoed through the empty house, doing absolutely nothing to quell the roaring in her ears. Tomorrow, this sanctuary would be a paved parking lot. She grabbed a loose strip of the wallpaper and yanked it violently, tearing it all the way down to the baseboards. Outside, a heavy commercial truck backed into the driveway, its reversing alarm beeping in a relentless, mocking rhythm. Maya picked up a stray wooden chair and hurled it straight at the brick fireplace. The brittle wood shattered into jagged splinters upon impact. Her chest rose and fell in sharp, uneven spikes. She glared at the rubble, wishing she could set the place ablaze herself just to deny the bank the satisfaction.

"It's just a building, Leo," my brother muttered, refusing to meet my eyes. He tapped his phone, calculating his share from the developers. I placed my coffee mug down, deliberately controlling my hands to avoid shattering the ceramic. "Just a building," I repeated, my voice a gravelly whisper. I leaned across the laminate table, bringing my face inches from his. The vein in my temple throbbed with a heavy beat. "That building is where Mom passed away." I stood up abruptly, knocking my knees against the booth and making the silverware clatter. I threw a crumpled ten-dollar bill onto his plate, directly into his eggs. "Enjoy your payout, David," I hissed through clenched teeth, spinning on my heel and storming out the door before I did something I'd regret.

Clara paced the length of the adjoining yard, her boots kicking up violent sprays of wet morning dew. The wrecking crew had just erected the chain-link barricade around her childhood Victorian home. A worker tossed a heavy chain over the intricate wrought-iron gate she used to swing on as a girl, securing it with a padlock. Clara’s fingernails bit deeply into her palms. She marched right up to the boundary line, her jaw locked so tight her ears rang. "Hey!" she yelled, her voice cracking like a whip. "Watch the hydrangeas! My grandmother planted those!" The worker didn't turn around, casually tossing a stray soda can right into the flowerbed. Clara's pulse hammered in her temples. She grabbed a fistful of wet earth and hurled it over the fence with everything she had, watching the mud splatter aggressively against the side of their pristine white company truck.

The lawyer’s mahogany desk felt cold under my sweating palms. "Eminent domain," he said smoothly, adjusting his gold-rimmed glasses. "There's nothing more we can do to stop the highway expansion." I stared at his perfectly polished shoes, my breathing growing shallow and fast. My childhood bedroom, the treehouse out back, the kitchen where I learned to bake—all paved over for a commuter bypass. I stood up so quickly my leather chair wheeled backward and slammed into the wall. The lawyer flinched. Good. I grabbed the glossy settlement folder he offered and ripped it squarely in half, the thick cardstock tearing loudly. I let the ripped pieces flutter down onto his pristine keyboard. "You didn't even try," I spat, my voice shaking with a heat that threatened to boil over. Without waiting for his pathetic excuses, I kicked the heavy oak door open and strode out.

Julian aggressively twisted the screwdriver, stripping the brass screw on the front door's knocker until the metal burred. The demolition crew was scheduled for dawn, and he refused to let them have the heirloom. His hand slipped, the flathead blade gouging a deep scratch into the varnished wood and slicing the side of his thumb. A line of crimson welled up, but Julian didn’t stop. He wiped his bleeding hand carelessly on his jeans, leaving a rusty streak, and switched to a heavy crowbar. He wedged the iron tool behind the brass plate, his face flushed and covered in a sheen of sweat. With a guttural grunt, he threw his entire body weight backward. The wood splintered with a loud crack, freeing the fixture. He held the heavy metal lion in his shaking, bloodied hands, glaring at the empty bulldozer parked ominously across the street.

"You have until noon to clear out the remaining salvage," the foreman barked, pointing a thick finger at my chest. I slapped his hand away before I could even think about the consequences. He took a surprised step back. My chest was a tight drum, every heartbeat echoing in my ears. I looked at the Victorian windows, their stained glass already cracked by careless workers moving equipment. "Don't you point at me," I said, my voice dangerously low and steady. "I know the schedule." I stepped into his personal space, forcing him to look me in the eye. I could feel the heat radiating off my own skin. I snatched the clipboard right out of his grasp, snapping his plastic pen in half between my fingers, and dropped the broken pieces into the dirt. "Stay off the porch until noon."

A local news reporter stood on the sidewalk, gesturing toward the crumbling brick façade of the old farmhouse. Marcus shoved a heavy tote into his pickup, letting the tailgate slam shut with an echoing, metallic bang. The reporter jumped, offering a microphone. "Sir, how does it feel to see this residence make way for progress?" Marcus’s jaw muscles twitched. He stared at the microphone like it was a venomous snake, his hands gripping the edge of his truck bed so fiercely his knuckles lost all color. He didn't speak. Instead, he took a slow step toward the camera crew, his dark eyes fixed in an unblinking glare. The cameraman nervously lowered the lens. Marcus spat onto the asphalt right by the reporter's expensive heels, climbed into his driver's seat, and peeled out, leaving a thick cloud of exhaust.

The flashlight beam shook in my grip as I swept it across the graffiti on my childhood living room wall. Intruders had drawn obscene shapes over the pencil height chart my parents had maintained on the doorframe for eighteen years. A sharp, burning sensation crawled up my throat. I kicked a shattered beer bottle, sending green glass skittering across the hardwood. The echo mocked me. The developers hadn't even bothered to board up the windows properly. I grabbed my heavy steel flashlight with both hands and swung it like a baseball bat into the only intact pane of glass on the bay window. It shattered with a violent crash, letting the cold night wind rush inside. I stood panting in the dark, my chest heaving, listening to the jagged shards tinkle onto the front porch where my mother used to read.

The liquidator handed Silas a meager stack of twenty-dollar bills, smiling as strangers carried out the antique dining table. "Everything must go before the wrecking ball hits on Monday," the man chirped, entirely tone-deaf. Silas felt his teeth grinding together so hard his jaw began to ache. He snatched the cash, crumpling the bills into a tight ball. A customer walked past carrying the custom birdhouse Silas had built with his grandfather, carelessly bumping it against the doorframe and chipping the painted wood. Silas surged forward, his boots stomping heavily on the floorboards, and ripped the birdhouse right out of the customer's hands. "Hey! I paid for that!" the man protested. Silas threw the wad of crumpled twenties directly into the man’s face. "Keep the change," Silas growled, storming off with the wooden house tucked tightly under his arm.

I stared at the refrigerator door, my vision narrowing to the single piece of construction paper pinned under a magnet. There he was. Barnaby. Complete with his crooked top hat and the missing left button on his waistcoast. My chest tightened until my ribs ached. I grabbed the edge of the paper, my knuckles turning bone-white as I crumpled the edge. "Who told you about him?" I demanded, my voice coming out in a sharp, clipped hiss. My five-year-old niece just kept coloring, humming a cheerful tune that grated against my eardrums like sandpaper. I snatched the purple crayon right out of her hand. "I asked you a question, Lily. Who told you?" The heat creeping up the back of my neck felt like a physical fire, my jaw locked tight enough to crack a molar. Barnaby was mine. Nobody else's.

Elias shoved the sketchbook across the glass coffee table, the heavy thud rattling the coasters. "Look at it, Sarah," he barked, pointing a stiff finger at the open page. His sister blinked at the crude crayon drawing of a blue dog with six legs. "It's just Maya's new doodle, Elias." He paced away, kicking a stray wooden block so hard it ricocheted off the baseboard with a sharp crack. "It's not a doodle! That's Pip! Down to the twisted collar!" He spun around, his chest heaving under his sweater. "You had no right to go digging through my childhood journals and feeding my private thoughts to your kid as a bedtime story." When Sarah swore she hadn't touched his things, Elias drove his fist into the doorframe, the sudden pain barely registering over the pounding blood roaring in his ears.

"Her name is Seraphina," Chloe whispered, tapping the wet watercolor paper. I stopped breathing. The winged girl on the page had the exact silver scar over her right eye that I had invented when I was seven. A hot, prickly sensation spread across my cheeks. I grabbed the water cup, my grip so tight the plastic buckled, splashing murky water onto the table. "Where did you hear that name?" I asked, my tone dropping an octave, razor-thin and flat. Chloe shrank back. "Nowhere. She visits me at night." I set the cup down with a harsh slam, ignoring the puddle seeping into the tablecloth. My hands shook as I grabbed the painting. I wanted to tear it into tiny, unrecognizable shreds. Seraphina abandoned me fifteen years ago, and now she had the nerve to show up in my brother's house?

Marcus stared at the chalkboard easel in the playroom. The chalk dust settled on the carpet, but he couldn't look away from the unmistakable silhouette of Captain Cuffs. His jaw muscles flexed rhythmically. He grabbed the felt eraser and scrubbed it across the slate, pressing so hard the wooden block screeched against the board. He obliterated the hat, the cape, the stupid little boots. "Uncle Marcus, what are you doing?" little Mia whined from the doorway. He dropped the eraser, breathing through his nose in short, forceful bursts. "We don't draw him," Marcus snapped, stepping toward her with rigid, heavy strides. He snatched the remaining chalk pieces from the tray and tossed them into the trash bin with unnecessary force. "Pick another character. He isn't welcome here." His hands were balled into tight fists at his sides, fingernails digging half-moons into his palms.

The moment my niece handed me the drawing, a sour taste flooded the back of my throat. I recognized the lopsided grin and the mismatched polka-dot tie immediately. Mr. Giggles. I crushed the corner of the paper between my thumb and forefinger. "Did your mother tell you about him?" I ground out, not taking my eyes off the crayon strokes. Sophie shook her head. "He told me himself. He says you used to be fun." A red-hot spike drove itself into my temples. I ripped the drawing right down the middle, the sound of tearing paper echoing loudly in the quiet living room. Sophie gasped, but I just dropped the torn halves onto the floor and stood up so fast my chair tipped backward and crashed onto the hardwood. I stormed out, slamming the door behind me hard enough to rattle the windows.

Jenna's breathing turned shallow and fast as she stared at the tablet screen. Her niece had used a drawing app to create a perfect replica of Zephyr, the cloud-dragon Jenna had confided in during her parents' divorce. Jenna snatched the stylus from the seven-year-old’s fingers. "Who gave you permission to draw this?" she demanded, her voice vibrating with a harsh edge. "Nobody, Aunt Jenna. He just came to play." Jenna’s face flushed crimson. She pressed the power button on the tablet, holding it down until the screen went completely black. She threw the stylus onto the kitchen island, watching it clatter and roll off the edge. Her shoulders were hiked up to her ears, rigid as stone. How dare this creature ignore her for two decades only to casually waltz into the mind of a child who had everything?

I found the sketch tucked inside Emma’s math workbook. It was a pencil drawing of a tall man with branches for arms. Woodsy. The very friend who promised to stay with me forever before vanishing when I turned ten. Blood rushed to my head, pounding a frantic rhythm against my eardrums. I grabbed my phone and dialed my sister's number, pressing the device against my ear so hard it bruised the cartilage. "You went through my attic boxes, didn't you?" I spat the moment she answered. "Excuse me?" she said. "The sketchbooks! You took my old sketchbooks and showed them to Emma!" I yelled, pacing the length of my kitchen. I kicked the base of the cabinets with the toe of my boot. "Tell her to leave my things alone!" I hit the end call button and hurled the phone onto the sofa.

Leo sat frozen at the patio table. His eight-year-old niece proudly held up a finger-painting of a glowing green tortoise wearing a top hat. "His name is Barnacles," she beamed. Leo’s jaw clamped shut. He dug his nails into the wooden armrests of his chair, a sudden, searing heat radiating from his chest. He stood up abruptly, knocking his knees against the underside of the table. The glasses of lemonade rattled dangerously. "Leo?" his brother asked, startled. Leo didn't answer. He glared at the painting, his lips pressed into a thin, bloodless line. He snatched his jacket off the back of the chair, his movements sharp and jerky. Without a single word to his family, he marched down the patio steps, his heavy boots crushing the blooming marigolds bordering the walkway as he strode straight toward his car.

"Look at my fairy, Auntie!" Evie cheered, pushing the glittery paper into my lap. I looked down and my stomach violently contracted. It wasn't just a fairy. It was Trixie, complete with the asymmetrical violet wings and the tiny silver crown I had spent hours detailing in my own mind. My teeth ground together with an audible squeak. I grabbed the bottle of craft glue from the table and hurled it directly into the trash can. "We are done with arts and crafts for today," I announced, my voice entirely devoid of warmth. I started swiping the loose beads and markers into their plastic bins with frantic, sweeping motions. Evie started to cry, but I ignored her, aggressively scrubbing a stray mark off the table until the sponge began to shred under my grip. Trixie had no right to be here.

The crayons snapped under David’s heavy boots. He didn't care. He stared at the giant mural his niece had taped to the basement wall. The multi-colored goblin grinning back at him was Bogart. David’s nostrils flared. He grabbed the edge of the butcher paper and yanked it downward. The tape tore away, taking chunks of drywall paint with it, but David didn't stop. He balled the massive sheet of paper into a tight, crumpled mess, his chest heaving with every ragged breath. He threw the wad of paper against the concrete wall. "You left me!" David shouted to the empty room, his voice echoing off the exposed pipes. He kicked a plastic toy chest, sending it skidding across the linoleum floor. He stood in the center of the room, fists clenched at his sides, glaring at the empty space on the wall.

I stared blindly at the notebook. The stick figure had a triangle for a head and three squiggly lines for a tail. "Triangula," my niece piped up, pointing at her masterpiece. "She said you used to cry a lot." A roaring noise filled my ears, drowning out the background hum of the television. I gripped the spiral binding of the notebook, the metal wire biting deeply into my thumb. I ripped the page out in one vicious, jagged motion. "Hey!" she protested. I crumpled the paper into a tight ball, squeezing it until my hand cramped. I didn't say a word. I just turned my back on her and stomped out of the room, my heels striking the floorboards with heavy, deliberate thuds. I went straight to the kitchen, shoved the paper ball into the garbage disposal, and aggressively slammed the switch.

Hannah’s eyes narrowed into dark, dangerous slits. The sketch on the dining table depicted a raccoon with a monocle—Professor Paws. Her sister emerged from the kitchen holding a tray of snacks. "Isn't Lily's imagination amazing?" her sister chirped. Hannah picked up the drawing, her fingers trembling slightly. "Did you read my diary?" Hannah asked, her voice dangerously quiet, vibrating with a tense energy. "What? No, of course not," her sister laughed. Hannah tore the drawing perfectly in half. Then in quarters. "Hannah! What is your problem?" Hannah let the confetti-sized pieces flutter onto the tray, landing squarely in the spinach dip. She leaned across the table, her face inches from her sister’s. "If you ever go through my childhood room again, I will burn this house to the ground," she hissed through gritted teeth, before spinning on her heel and storming out.

Mark stared at the glass walls of the conference room, watching Sarah nod and smile at the director. They were discussing the new VP opening, the exact role Mark had sacrificed his last three vacations to secure. His jaw muscles locked, grinding his molars together until a dull ache radiated up to his temples. He picked up his favorite fountain pen, gripping it so tightly the polished resin squeaked. When Sarah walked out, flashing him a sympathetic, overly sweet smile, Mark didn’t smile back. He just stared at the spreadsheet on his monitor, his vision swimming, his fingers hovering stiffly over the keyboard. A hot, prickling sensation crawled up the back of his neck. With a sudden, sharp motion, he swept his coffee mug off the desk, letting it shatter against the carpeted floor.

The email hit my inbox at exactly four-thirty, just as I was finalizing the quarterly projections. Dave had replied-all to the executive board, subtly taking credit for the cost-saving initiative I had pitched last month—the exact initiative our boss said would determine who got the Senior Analyst title. I read the words three times, the blood roaring in my ears like a freight train. My chest felt tight, expanding and contracting with short, jagged breaths that didn't provide enough oxygen. I shoved my rolling chair back with such force it crashed into the filing cabinet. Getting up, I paced the cramped length of my cubicle, dragging my hands down my face. I wanted to march over to Dave’s desk and flip his dual monitors onto the floor. Instead, I just stood there, digging my fingernails into my palms until the skin yielded.

In the sweltering heat of the prep kitchen, Elena brought her chef’s knife down on the cutting board with the force of a guillotine. She was supposed to be mincing garlic, but the cloves were practically pulverized beneath the relentless thud of the steel blade. Across the line, Julian was leaning against the stainless-steel counter, laughing loudly at a joke the restaurant owner had just made. They were discussing the Executive Chef vacancy, a role Elena had earned through ten years of sweat and burns. Julian had been here six months. Elena’s face flushed a deep, mottled crimson beneath her hairnet. She scooped the obliterated garlic into a pan, the metal scraping against the board with a high-pitched shriek. When Julian caught her eye and offered a smug little wink, she slammed the heavy iron skillet onto the stovetop, making the entire line jump.

I sat rigidly in the polished leather chair, staring a hole into the mahogany boardroom table. Beside me, Richard was smoothly walking the partners through the merger logistics. This was my account. I had spent eight weekends flying to Dallas to secure these numbers, knowing it was my golden ticket to Junior Partner. Yet here was Richard, utilizing my slide deck, casually dropping my statistics as if they were his own spontaneous brilliant insights. A suffocating heat radiated from my sternum. I pressed my lips together so firmly I tasted blood. Every time Richard paused for dramatic effect, my foot tapped a frantic, staccato rhythm against the carpet. I gripped the armrests of my chair, my knuckles stark white against my dark skin, silently imagining what would happen if I just stood up, grabbed his laser pointer, and snapped it cleanly in half.

Greg watched the elevator doors slide shut, cutting off his view of Chloe and the managing director as they headed out for a casual lunch. The Senior Associate position was down to the two of them, and Chloe was currently schmoozing her way straight to the corner office. Greg returned to his desk, his breathing shallow and rapid. He snatched up the six-hundred-page brief he had stayed up until four in the morning to proofread and threw it hard against the wall. The heavy binder burst open on impact, sending hundreds of crisp white pages fluttering to the floor like snow. He didn’t bother picking them up. He just braced his hands on his desk, leaning forward, glaring at his blank computer screen as a single, pulsing vein throbbed visibly at his temple. The absolute audacity of her smile made him want to scream.

I dragged the heavy boxes of inventory off the pallet, slamming each one onto the stockroom floor. It was eleven at night. The store had closed two hours ago, but the district manager wanted the seasonal display perfect before deciding who would take over the Store Manager role. Through the swinging doors, I could hear Kyle out on the sales floor, chatting on his phone and casually wiping down the same glass register counter he’d been cleaning for forty minutes. My chest heaved as I ripped the packing tape off a box, the harsh tearing sound masking the heavy thumping of my heart. I had covered his shifts, fixed his scheduling errors, and trained him. I kicked an empty cardboard box across the room, watching it bounce off the cinderblock wall. My jaw felt locked in place, tight and aching with an unspeakable, scalding heat.

The harsh fluorescent lights of the ICU seemed to pulse in time with the hammering in Sarah’s head. She stood by the nurses' station, her hands shoved deep into her scrub pockets, fingers curled into rigid fists. Ten feet away, Marcus was handing the Chief of Nursing a coffee, laughing easily, his charting completely abandoned. They were both up for Head Nurse, and Marcus was playing the political game while Sarah managed three critical patients on her own. She marched over to the crash cart, her footsteps heavy and deliberate against the linoleum. When a junior nurse asked her a question, Sarah spun around, her eyes wide and dark, her lips drawn back in a tight, humorless line. She didn't speak. She just pointed a trembling finger toward the patient rooms, shoved the heavy rolling cart forward, and aggressively pushed through the double doors.

The notification popped up in the upper right corner of my screen: Meeting invite: Engineering Lead Transition. I clicked it open, seeing Brian's name listed right under the new title. I stared at the glowing pixels until they blurred into a bright, meaningless streak. The office was quiet, save for the click-clack of mechanical keyboards, but a roaring noise filled my head. I slowly lowered my hands to my lap, my fingers twitching. I had built the entire backend architecture while Brian played ping-pong in the breakroom and made jokes with the investors. A sudden, searing heat bloomed in my chest, climbing up my throat and making my face burn. Without thinking, I grabbed my ergonomic mouse and whipped it against the plaster wall beside my desk. The plastic shattered into a dozen pieces, the loud crack echoing through the suddenly silent open-plan office.

Maya stood in the back of the drafting room, her arms crossed so tightly across her chest that her fingernails left crescent-shaped indentations in her sleeves. The senior partners had just announced that Arthur would be taking over as Principal Architect. Arthur, who had completely miscalculated the load-bearing requirements on the downtown plaza project—a mistake Maya had quietly fixed to save the firm from a lawsuit. She watched him accept a glass of champagne, his posture relaxed, a modest smile playing on his lips. Maya’s breathing turned sharp and ragged. She turned on her heel, marching back to her drafting table. She grabbed the meticulously detailed blueprints she had drawn up for their upcoming joint pitch, her hands shaking uncontrollably. With one swift, decisive motion, she tore the heavy vellum paper straight down the middle, the ripping sound loud and immensely satisfying in her ears.

The faculty lounge smelled like stale coffee and dry-erase markers, but all I could focus on was the sound of Lisa’s voice bragging about her new promotion to Department Chair. I stood perfectly still by the microwave, gripping my ceramic mug. She was telling the new history teacher about her innovative curriculum overhaul. My curriculum overhaul. The one I spent six weeks developing in my dining room while she vacationed in Cabo. I bit the inside of my cheek until a sharp metallic taste flooded my mouth. I didn't congratulate her. I couldn't even look at her. I just stared straight ahead at the spinning plate in the microwave, my vision tunneling. When the timer beeped, I took my mug, dumped the scalding hot coffee directly into the sink, and slammed the ceramic down on the counter with enough force to crack the base.

The regional sales metrics were projected on the massive whiteboard, and Jake’s numbers were undeniably higher. Yet, the Regional Director had just pulled Brett into his office for a private chat about the leadership vacancy, slapping him affectionately on the shoulder before closing the blinds. Jake sat perfectly rigid in his rolling chair, staring at the closed door. His face was flushed crimson, a noticeable vein throbbing frantically at his temple. He picked up his phone, dialed a client's number, and immediately hung up, the receiver slamming into the cradle with a deafening crack. A junior associate walked by and offered a tentative greeting.
