He had spent his childhood summers drinking chamomile from those very tins, and here she was, treating them like yesterday's garbage, arriving two weeks late to help with the estate and instantly taking over. He grabbed the bag from her hand, the plastic tearing with a sharp screech. "Don't touch her things," he clipped out, his chest rising and falling in rapid, shallow jerks. The heavy silence that followed was suffocating, as he glared at her, his blood roaring so loudly in his ears he could barely hear her exasperated sigh.

I kicked the side of a dusty cardboard box, sending a cloud of gray grit into the stifling attic air. My boot left a deep dent in the cardboard, but it didn't do anything to stop the hot prickling sensation crawling up my neck. Downstairs, the faint sound of sitcom laughter drifted up from the living room. Leo had been sitting on the couch for three hours. He called it "taking a breather." I shoved a stack of moth-eaten blankets aside, my fingernails digging painfully into my palms. I was the one who paid the property taxes, I was the one who drove four hours every weekend to clean out fifty years of hoarding, and he had the nerve to ask when his half of the sale money would clear. I grabbed a porcelain lamp and squeezed the base until my joints popped.

Elise stared at the bright yellow "For Sale" sign hammered into the overgrown front lawn. Her brother, Thomas, stood next to the contractor, pointing at the wrap-around porch and making dismissive chopping motions with his hands. "Tear it down, build a deck," Thomas was saying loudly. Elise’s breathing grew shallow. She marched down the wooden steps, her heels striking the boards like a drumbeat. She planted herself directly between Thomas and the contractor, her eyes narrowed into dark, glittering slits. "The porch stays," she said, her voice dropping an octave, vibrating with a dangerous stillness. Thomas rolled his eyes, starting to argue, but Elise stepped closer, invading his space, her posture entirely rigid. She didn't blink. The heat radiating from her skin was almost palpable in the crisp autumn air. "I said, it stays. Call off your demolition."

My thumb traced the fresh ink on the amended will. The date was exactly three days before Grandma passed. "To my dearest grandson, Paul, the estate in its entirety." I looked up at Paul, who was currently sipping coffee from Grandma’s favorite mug, pretending to look out the bay window. My hands began to shake, the paper rattling loudly in the quiet room. I crushed the document into a tight ball, my fingernails slicing half-moons into the center of my palm. "You took her to the lawyer on Tuesday," I whispered. My throat felt thick, completely restricted. Paul finally turned, his expression carefully blank. I stood up so fast my chair tipped and crashed against the hardwood floor. I crossed the room in three long strides, stopping inches from his face. "You waited until her dementia peaked," I hissed, feeling a vein pulsing wildly at my temple.

The roar of the woodchipper drowned out all other sound. David slammed his car door, sprinting up the gravel driveway. His sister, Maya, was directing a crew of landscapers tossing the branches of Grandma’s prize-winning lilac bushes into the roaring machine. David’s vision narrowed to a tunnel. He shoved past a worker and threw his entire body weight against the machine's kill switch. The deafening noise sputtered and died. "What is your problem?" Maya demanded. David didn't answer right away. He couldn't. His jaw was clenched so firmly he thought his molars might crack. He pointed a trembling, rigid finger at the stump of the oldest lilac tree, his face burning with a fiery, dark flush. When he finally spoke, his voice was a low, terrifying rasp that made the landscapers take a slow step back. "Get them out of here."

I stared at the empty velvet indentations in the jewelry box. The pearl necklace was gone. I slowly turned my head toward the dining room, where my sister Claire was packing a cardboard box. She turned, and there, resting against her designer sweater, was the familiar string of milky beads. A hot wave washed over my entire body, starting from my chest and prickling all the way up to my scalp. I marched into the dining room, slapping my open palm flat against the mahogany table. The sudden crack made her jump. "Take it off," I said. My voice didn't sound like my own; it was entirely flat and stripped of all warmth. Claire defensively put a hand over the pearls, offering a weak smile. "Grandma would have wanted—" "Take it off, Claire," I interrupted, my teeth grinding together so loudly it echoed in my own skull.

Dust motes danced in the shafts of light piercing the dim garage. Arthur stood perfectly still, staring at the empty space where the 1965 Mustang had rested for three decades. He heard the crunch of gravel and turned to see his brother, Ben, counting a thick wad of hundred-dollar bills. Arthur’s breathing hitched, then accelerated into sharp, forceful pulls of air. He closed the distance between them, his boots echoing sharply on the concrete. He knocked the stack of cash violently out of Ben’s hands. The green bills fluttered to the dirty floor like dead leaves. "Hey!" Ben shouted, bending down. Arthur grabbed his brother by the collar of his jacket, twisting the fabric until his knuckles turned entirely white. "Who did you sell it to?" Arthur demanded, every syllable dripping with a venomous heat. "I want a name, Ben. Give me the name right now."

"So, when do we get the appraisal?" Greg asked, leaning against the hallway wall and inspecting his manicured fingernails. I was halfway up the stairs, balancing a heavy box of Grandma’s china. The cardboard was slipping from my sweaty grip, my back screaming in protest. I lowered the box onto the landing with a heavy thud, dust billowing around my knees. I slowly turned to look down at him. My chest tightened like a drawn bowstring. I could feel the heat radiating from my face, flushing all the way to the tips of my ears. "The appraisal?" I repeated softly. I took one step down. Then another. Greg stopped looking at his nails and stood up straight, his eyes widening slightly as I approached. I stopped on the bottom step, looming over him, my hands balled so tightly by my sides my fingernails broke the skin.

Chloe watched from the window as her sister marched through the backyard in muddy boots, trampling directly over the small, hand-painted stones marking Grandma's deceased pets. Chloe pushed the back door open so hard it slammed against the brick exterior, the glass pane rattling violently in its frame. She stalked through the overgrown grass, her heart hammering a frantic, violent rhythm against her ribs. When she reached her sister, Chloe didn't say a word. She grabbed the real estate brochures from her sister’s hands and ripped them straight down the middle. She stacked the halves and tore them again, and again, until it was just confetti. She threw the shredded paper directly into her sister’s face. "Walk around the stones," Chloe whispered, her body vibrating with an intense, unyielding tension that made her sister instantly freeze in place.

A spark hissed in the fireplace, sending a glowing ember onto the stone hearth. I stared at the flames, mesmerized, before my eyes dropped to the empty bookshelf. My breath caught in my throat. I spun around to find my brother holding a plastic bin filled with Grandma’s leather-bound journals, heading toward the back door. "What are you doing with those?" I demanded, my voice cracking slightly. "Starting a bonfire," he replied casually. "Nobody wants to read this rambling." I felt a sudden, blinding flash of heat behind my eyes. I lunged forward, grabbing the edge of the plastic bin and yanking it backward with all my strength. The bin crashed to the floor, journals scattering across the Persian rug. I stood over him, my chest heaving, my jaw locked into stone. "Touch them again," I rasped, glaring down at him. "Just try it."

The sharp crash of shattering glass echoed up the basement stairs. Nora hurried down, her heart pounding, only to find her brother, Liam, standing over the remains of their grandmother’s antique stained-glass lamp. He casually nudged a blue shard with the toe of his sneaker. "Oops. Guess that goes in the dumpster," he chuckled. Nora stopped on the bottom step. Her hands clamped onto the wooden banister, her grip so fierce the wood creaked under the pressure. She felt a burning flush creep up her neck, her breathing turning jagged and loud in the damp cellar air. She stared at the broken glass, then up at his completely unbothered face. Without breaking eye contact, she picked up the metal baseball bat leaning against the stairwell. She tapped it rhythmically against the concrete floor, her eyes entirely devoid of light. "Clean it up," she commanded flatly.

The doorbell chimed, a cheerful sound that felt like a drill to my temple. I pulled back the curtain to see a woman in a sharp blazer holding a clipboard. I whipped my head around to stare at my sister, Jenny, who suddenly looked very interested in the pattern of the wallpaper. "You called a realtor," I said, my voice eerily calm. "Before the funeral." Jenny shifted her weight. "We have to be practical—" "Practical?" I echoed, taking a slow, deliberate step toward her. My hands shook so violently I had to jam them deep into my pockets. I gritted my teeth until a sharp pain shot up into my temples. The doorbell chimed again. I grabbed a brass candlestick and slammed it onto the coffee table with a deafening crack. "Go tell that woman," I whispered fiercely, "that she has the wrong house."

I stared at the name tag peeling off his cashmere sweater: Hemochromatosis Type 4. My fingernails dug crescent moons into my palms. For three years, I’d been told I was the only case in the state, forced to drive six hours every Tuesday for blood draws. Now this guy casually mentions he gets his treatments in his downtown penthouse from a private nurse. My jaw locked so tight my teeth ground together. "Must be nice," I muttered, my voice tight and brittle. I grabbed my styrofoam cup of lukewarm coffee and crushed it, ignoring the brown liquid spilling over my knuckles. He kept talking about his minor inconveniences, completely oblivious. I wanted to flip the plastic folding table right into his perfectly pressed slacks.

Elias ripped the medical brochure in half, then into quarters. The teenager sitting across from him at the oncology wing was filming a social media video about her "super rare genetic mutation"—the exact one currently turning Elias’s bone marrow to chalk. "It’s like we’re in a totally exclusive club!" she chirped at him, pointing her phone in his direction. Elias slapped the lens away with a sharp smack. The hot sting in his cheeks mirrored the burning in his veins. "Delete that," he growled, standing up so fast his chair screeched against the linoleum. He paced the narrow corridor, his chest heaving. It wasn't a club. It was a death sentence. He grabbed his coat, ripping a button off the fabric in his haste to leave the suffocating room.

The cafe was supposed to be safe. When the woman from the forum sat down across from me, boasting about her identical, one-in-a-million histamine reaction to synthetic vanilla, I thought I’d finally found someone who understood. Then she pulled out a bottle of hand sanitizer. The sharp, artificial sweetness hit the air, instantly closing my throat. I slammed both hands onto the table, rattling the silverware. "Are you kidding me?" I wheezed, my vision narrowing as my chest tightened. She blinked, stammering an apology about forgetting. I didn't care. I shoved past her chair, knocking it sideways, and stormed out onto the pavement. My EpiPen was already in my trembling hand. I kicked the base of the nearest streetlamp, the metal vibrating up my leg as I jabbed the needle into my thigh.

Marcus glared at the pharmacist over the counter. "What do you mean she got the last box?" He pointed a stiff finger at the elderly woman slowly placing the familiar blue-and-gold carton of Zelboraf into her purse. It was an orphan drug. Nobody had his specific enzyme deficiency. Except, apparently, her. The pharmacist offered a tight, sympathetic smile that made Marcus want to punch the shatterproof glass. "We can order more by Thursday," the clerk offered. Thursday was four days away. His joints were already throbbing. Marcus wheeled around, breathing heavily through his nose, his eyes fixed on the back of the woman's floral cardigan. He gripped the strap of his messenger bag until his knuckles turned entirely white, grinding his heel into the tiled floor as he watched her stroll out the sliding doors.

I thrashed my legs through the warm water, the resistance sending sharp spikes of pain through my atrophied calves. The new guy in the pool, diagnosed with the same demyelinating syndrome, was just floating by the stairs. "I’m not even going to try the exercises," he sighed, splashing weakly. "We’re going to end up paralyzed anyway." A hot flush climbed my neck. I stopped kicking and waded toward him, the water sloshing violently around my torso. "Then why take up a spot?" I snapped, my voice echoing off the humid tiles. He flinched, but I didn't back down. I stared him dead in the eyes, my chest rising and falling in harsh, rapid jerks. I turned my back to him, splashing aggressively as I forced my useless legs to paddle twice as hard.

Sarah stared at the acceptance roster tacked to the clinic board. Her name wasn't there. But the man leaning against the water cooler, casually smoking a cigarette despite the strict hospital rules, had his name right at the top. They both shared the same pulmonary degradation syndrome. She spent three hours a day doing breathing exercises; he was actively destroying his lungs. Sarah’s teeth clamped down on her lower lip until the metallic taste of blood flooded her mouth. She marched over to the cooler, ripped the styrofoam cup from his hand, and crushed it into the trash can. "Hey!" he protested. Sarah didn't say a word. Her chest vibrated with a low, tight hum. She glared at his cigarette, then at his face, daring him to take another drag before spinning on her heel.

I sat next to the woman in the genetic counselor's waiting room, making idle small talk until she mentioned her diagnosis. It was the same one-in-ten-million chromosomal deletion I had. Then she told me her doctor had warned her family ten years ago to freeze their eggs. Ten years. My doctors had told me it was a random mutation, entirely unpreventable. I stared at the carpet, a dull roar building behind my ears. The magazine in my lap crumpled as my fists closed around its glossy pages. I shredded the paper in half, the sudden tearing sound making the woman jump. "Is everything okay?" she asked timidly. I stood up, my chair scraping harshly against the linoleum. I threw the torn pieces onto the side table, entirely ignoring her as I marched toward the receptionist's glass window.

The elevator jolted to a sudden halt between the fourteenth and fifteenth floors. David instantly felt the familiar, terrifying flutter in his chest—the hallmark of his incredibly rare electrical heart anomaly. The stranger beside him gasped, clutching her sternum, describing the exact same fluttering sensation. Instead of feeling kinship, David’s face grew burning hot. He slammed his palm against the emergency button, repeatedly hitting the red plastic until his hand bruised. "We need to get out," he barked at the speaker grille. The operator asked them to remain calm. David kicked the stainless steel doors with the toe of his boot, leaving a dark scuff mark. He couldn't afford this. The woman was hyperventilating, making his own heart race faster. He grabbed the handrail, his knuckles protruding sharply, his jaw tight enough to crack molars.

The flight attendant handed the foil-wrapped tray to the man in the aisle seat. "One special PKU-variant meal," she announced. I froze. I had requested that exact meal weeks ago for my rare metabolic disorder, only to be told they couldn't accommodate me. I watched the man peel back the foil, picking at the specially prepared low-protein vegetables with blatant disgust. "Tastes like cardboard," he complained loudly to his wife, pushing the tray away. My face flushed so hot I thought my skin might peel off. I leaned over, my seatbelt digging sharply into my stomach. "If you don't want it, don't request it," I hissed, my voice shaking. I shoved my tray table up with a violent click and crossed my arms so tightly my fingernails left deep red indentations in my biceps.

Julian sat in the audience as the keynote speaker detailed his life with an obscure neurological ticking disorder. It was Julian’s disorder. Yet the speaker described it as a "gift" that granted him unique artistic visions, completely glossing over the agonizing sleepless nights and the torn muscles. Julian’s pen snapped in his hand, spilling black ink across his notepad and over his fingers. He didn't bother wiping it off. He stood up in the middle of the crowded auditorium. The speaker paused mid-sentence. Julian glared at the stage, his breathing heavy and audible in the quiet room. He kicked his folding chair backward, letting it clatter loudly against the wooden floorboards. Ignoring the gasps and stares of the surrounding doctors, he stomped up the center aisle, pushing the heavy double doors open with a violent shove.

We matched on a patient-networking app. We both had Fibrodysplasia Ossificans Progressiva—our muscles were slowly turning to bone. I agreed to meet him at the park, desperate for a connection. When I arrived, he was riding a skateboard, doing kickflips off a park bench. He was in the early stages; I was already locked into a rigid posture, unable to turn my neck. "Hey!" he yelled, waving both arms wildly. My chest heaved. I gripped the handles of my specialized walker until the plastic creaked. He didn't understand the disease yet. He didn't know what was coming. I stared at his freely moving joints, a bitter taste flooding the back of my throat. I spun my walker around, the wheels skidding harshly on the concrete, and began the agonizingly slow, stiff walk back to my van.

Maya wore industrial earplugs just to sit in the dimly lit tavern. The man next to her noticed, tapped her shoulder, and typed on his phone: Me too. Acoustic Shock Syndrome. Maya managed a weak smile, grateful for the shared burden of their hyper-sensitive hearing. Then, the man pulled a bowl of complimentary peanuts toward himself and began cracking the shells between his teeth. The sharp, cracking sounds reverberated through the table right into Maya's skull. She grabbed the bowl and slammed it onto the furthest end of the bar, scattering nuts across the sticky mahogany. The man threw his hands up in a questioning gesture. Maya’s eyes narrowed into dark slits, her breathing coming in short, sharp bursts. She slapped a twenty-dollar bill onto the counter, shoved her stool backward, and stormed into the alley.

The barista called out "Double espresso for Mark," and both women reached for the cup. Clara pulled her hand back, her eyes landing on the stranger's phone screen. There was Mark, his arms wrapped around this brunette, wearing the sweater Clara had knitted him for Christmas. Clara’s jaw locked so tight her teeth audibly ground together. Her fingers curled into her palms until her fingernails dug sharp crescents into the flesh. "Cute lock screen," Clara managed to push past her lips, her voice dropping an octave and vibrating with a harsh, raspy edge. The brunette smiled, oblivious. "Thanks, my boyfriend Mark." Clara stared at the espresso cup on the counter. She imagined picking it up and launching the scalding liquid straight at the wall, watching the dark stain violently splatter and drip down the pristine white tiles. The heat radiating in her chest had nothing to do with the coffee.

I stood at Arrivals holding a sign that read 'Welcome home, Julian,' while the guy next to me held a ridiculous bouquet of lilies. We struck up a polite conversation about flight delays. Then he mentioned he was waiting for his boyfriend, Julian, returning from a 'solo' hiking trip in Peru. I stared at the bouquet, my vision narrowing to a tunnel. My pulse hammered a frantic, heavy rhythm against my eardrums. I snatched the cardboard sign I’d spent an hour decorating, snapping the thick material directly down the middle. The sharp tearing sound made the lily-holder jump. My breathing turned shallow and jagged, exhaling in sharp bursts through my nose. I let the torn halves of the sign drop to the linoleum floor, stamping my heel directly onto Julian's neatly lettered name. I didn’t say a word as I pivoted, my boots striking the floor with punishing force as I headed for the exit.

Marcus racked the barbell with a deafening metal-on-metal clang that echoed across the free-weight section. Beside him, the new guy, Leo, was swiping through his camera roll to show off his girlfriend's new puppy. Marcus didn’t care about the dog. He was staring at the familiar silver locket resting against the collarbone of the girl in the photo—the exact locket Marcus had bought Elena for their anniversary. Marcus felt a sudden, scorching flush creep up his neck and spread across his cheeks. He grabbed his water bottle, squeezing the plastic until it buckled and popped, water geysering out onto the rubber matting. "Bro, you good?" Leo asked, stepping back. Marcus didn't answer. He stared at his reflection in the mirror, his nostrils flaring, a dark, dangerous storm brewing behind his eyes. He tossed the ruined bottle onto a bench, snatched his duffel bag, and marched toward the locker room.

"She's a rescue," the woman beside me said, tossing a tennis ball. "My fiance, Greg, adopted her last month." I stopped breathing. Greg? I looked closer at the golden retriever. It was wearing a distinct red collar with a bone-shaped tag. The exact tag I had engraved for my fiance Greg's new rescue dog. A high-pitched ringing started deep inside my ears. My jaw clamped down, rigid as iron. I shoved my hands deep into my coat pockets to hide the violent tremors shaking my fingers. Every muscle in my back coiled tight as a spring ready to snap. "Greg," I repeated, my voice sounding like gravel grinding under a tire. "Tall, scar on his chin, drives a silver Subaru?" She nodded, looking confused. I felt my face burn, a sweltering heat radiating from my core. I spun around, whistling sharply for my terrier, ready to march home and pack every single thing Greg owned into garbage bags.

The hostess smiled apologetically. "I have a reservation for a Sarah under the name David, but you're both claiming it." The two women exchanged a glance. One wore the sapphire earrings David had claimed were a family heirloom; the other had the matching necklace. Sarah’s grip on her clutch tightened until the leather groaned. Her chest rose and fell in rapid, shallow hitches. She turned to look at the entrance, waiting for David to walk through those revolving glass doors. Her foot tapped a frantic, staccato beat against the hardwood floor. When she finally spoke, her tone was ice cold, cutting through the ambient chatter of the restaurant. "Keep the table," Sarah told the other woman, her eyes locking onto the street outside. "But when he gets here, tell him his things are going to be sitting on the curb in the rain." She pivoted on her heel, her posture razor-straight.

I sprinted into the emergency room, my heart in my throat, only to find another man hovering over Alex’s bed, holding his hand. "I'm his partner," the stranger told the nurse. I stopped dead in my tracks. My blood turned to liquid nitrogen before flash-boiling in my veins. The fluorescent lights overhead seemed to buzz louder, drilling directly into my skull. I stepped forward, my hands curling into heavy, white-knuckled boulders at my sides. My teeth ground together so forcefully my jaw ached. I wanted to grab the plastic tray of medical instruments and hurl it through the reinforced glass window. Instead, I stood at the foot of the bed, staring at Alex's sleeping face. He looked so peaceful. The urge to flip the mattress onto the cold linoleum floor was overwhelming. "Partner?" I spat out, the word tasting like battery acid on my tongue. The stranger looked up, and I glared back, daring him to repeat it.

The bass guitar vibrated through the floorboards. Chloe cheered as the lead singer, Jesse, pointed into the crowd and winked. But the guy standing shoulder-to-shoulder with her caught the wink and yelled, "Love you, babe!" Chloe whipped her head around. The guy was wearing Jesse’s custom tour jacket. The heat struck Chloe’s face in a sudden, violent wave. Her vision tinted red at the edges. She gripped her half-empty beer glass, her thumb pressing into the thick glass so hard the joint popped. She stared at Jesse on stage, watching him smile at the both of them. A low, ragged breath hissed out between her teeth. She didn’t confront the fan. Instead, she marched directly to the merchandise table, grabbed a permanent marker, and drew a thick, black line violently across Jesse’s face on the promotional poster, pressing hard enough to rip the paper in two.

The technician painted my thumb as the woman in the next massage chair started venting about her boyfriend, Michael. The details lined up too perfectly: the peanut allergy, the obsession with vintage watches, the sister named Beatrice. My throat constricted, closing up until I could barely swallow. I yanked my hand back from the technician, smearing wet, cherry-red polish across the towel. The sudden movement made the woman pause. My blood roared, a tidal wave crashing violently against my eardrums. I picked up my phone, pulling up Michael's contact. My thumb hovered over his smiling photo, trembling with a frantic, explosive energy. I wanted to hurl the device through the salon's mirror. Instead, I blocked the number, my breaths coming out in heavy, hot huffs that fogged the screen. "Excuse me," I barked to the nail tech, my voice completely devoid of its usual warmth. "I’m done. I have an apartment to clear out."

The rideshare pulled up to 42 Elm Street. "Wait, this is my stop too," the passenger in the back said, holding a bottle of champagne. Derek, sitting in the front, twisted around. "I'm going to apartment 4B. My girlfriend, Sam." The backseat passenger froze. "Sam is my girlfriend." Derek’s pupils dilated. The muscles in his neck strained, thick cords popping out against his skin. He shoved the car door open, slamming it shut behind him with enough force to make the vehicle rock on its suspension. He stalked up the front walkway, his boots crushing the decorative flowerbeds. He didn't bother using his key. He began pounding on the wooden door with the flat of his fist, the heavy thuds echoing down the quiet suburban street. His jaw was set in granite, his eyes fixed unblinkingly on the peephole as he waited for the door to open.

I stood before the gallery's centerpiece: a nude portrait of a woman resting on a velvet chaise. "Beautiful, isn't she?" a voice murmured beside me. "My muse. We've been together for two years." I stared at the artist. He was admiring the painting of Evelyn—my wife. A sudden, bitter taste flooded the back of my throat. My hands instantly balled into fists, the fingernails biting deep into my palms. I felt a violent tremor start in my chest and ripple down to my knees. The wine glass in my right hand suddenly felt incredibly fragile. I placed it on a passing waiter’s tray with a sharp, heavy clack. I couldn't look away from the canvas. I wanted to grab the nearest abstract sculpture and drive it straight through the center of the painted velvet chaise. I took a sharp, jagged breath, spun on my heel, and shoulder-checked the artist hard as I stormed toward the exit.

Both women reached for the last jar of organic fig preserves at the exact same moment. "Oh, sorry," Maya laughed. "My husband goes crazy for this stuff. Liam can't get enough." The other woman's smile vanished. "My husband's name is Liam. He eats this every morning." Maya felt her stomach plummet, instantly replaced by a searing, white-hot heat that radiated from her solar plexus. Her grip on her shopping cart tightened until the metal groaned under the pressure. Her breath hitched, catching sharply in her chest. She snatched the jar of preserves from the shelf, her eyes boring a hole into the stranger's face. The overhead fluorescent lights flickered, matching the volatile sparking in Maya's brain. Without a word, Maya lifted the glass jar above her head and hurled it directly onto the polished concrete floor. It shattered with a deafening crash, scattering thick jam and glass shards across the aisle.

I was replacing the screen on the customer's phone when a notification popped up. Incoming Text: Chris. I recognized the photo instantly. It was my Chris. The text read: Can't wait for tonight, babe. The tiny screwdriver in my hand suddenly felt like a weapon. My vision blurred at the edges, tunneling down to that single, smiling profile picture. The blood rushed to my head, pounding a relentless drumbeat behind my temples. My chest heaved with quick, shallow breaths. I stared at the delicate motherboard exposed under the bright workbench light. A dark, destructive impulse seized my arms. I took the tip of the screwdriver and jammed it straight down into the phone's battery housing, twisting it viciously until the metal crunched and sparked. "Oops," I muttered, my voice tight and rasping. I walked out to the waiting room, my posture rigid. "Sorry, your phone is completely unfixable."
